50 in s: false
Time O(1) membership, O(n) aggregatesSpace O(1)
Do

Replace x in some_list (O(n) scan) by x in some_set (O(1)) whenever the same collection is tested many times — the single most common hashing speed-up in interview solutions.

Set algebra: union, intersection, difference
The four set operations on two sets that share one element
s1 = {10, 20, 30}      s2 = {30, 40, 50}

union          s1 | s2   = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}   everything in either
intersection   s1 & s2   = {30}                   only what is in both
difference     s1 - s2   = {10, 20}               in s1 but not in s2
symmetric diff s1 ^ s2   = {10, 20, 40, 50}       in exactly one of them

Each operation iterates one set and tests membership in the other, so it costs O(|s1| + |s2|). Python has operators and named methods (s1.union(s2)); C++ needs a loop (or std::set_union on sorted containers); Java uses the mutating addAll / retainAll / removeAll on a copy; JavaScript gained union, intersection, difference and symmetricDifference methods on Set in ES2025 (Node 22+).

Python
def show(label, s):
    print(label + ":", *sorted(s))

s1 = {10, 20, 30}
s2 = {30, 40, 50}
show("union", s1 | s2)                      # also s1.union(s2)
show("intersection", s1 & s2)               # s1.intersection(s2)
show("difference", s1 - s2)                 # s1.difference(s2)
show("symmetric difference", s1 ^ s2)       # s1.symmetric_difference(s2)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <string>
using namespace std;
using Set = unordered_set<int>;

void show(const string& label, const Set& s) {
    vector<int> v(s.begin(), s.end());
    sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    cout << label << ":";
    for (int x : v) cout << " " << x;
    cout << "\n";
}

Set unionOf(const Set& a, const Set& b) { Set r = a; r.insert(b.begin(), b.end()); return r; }
Set intersection(const Set& a, const Set& b) {
    Set r;
    for (int x : a) if (b.count(x)) r.insert(x);     // in both
    return r;
}
Set difference(const Set& a, const Set& b) {
    Set r;
    for (int x : a) if (!b.count(x)) r.insert(x);    // in a, not in b
    return r;
}
Set symmetricDifference(const Set& a, const Set& b) {
    return unionOf(difference(a, b), difference(b, a));
}

int main() {
    Set s1 = {10, 20, 30}, s2 = {30, 40, 50};
    show("union", unionOf(s1, s2));
    show("intersection", intersection(s1, s2));
    show("difference", difference(s1, s2));
    show("symmetric difference", symmetricDifference(s1, s2));
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static void show(String label, Set<Integer> s) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(label + ":");
        for (int x : new TreeSet<>(s)) sb.append(" ").append(x);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<Integer> s1 = Set.of(10, 20, 30), s2 = Set.of(30, 40, 50);

        Set<Integer> union = new HashSet<>(s1); union.addAll(s2);
        Set<Integer> inter = new HashSet<>(s1); inter.retainAll(s2);      // keep only what is in s2
        Set<Integer> diff = new HashSet<>(s1); diff.removeAll(s2);        // drop what is in s2
        Set<Integer> sym = new HashSet<>(union); sym.removeAll(inter);    // union minus intersection

        show("union", union);
        show("intersection", inter);
        show("difference", diff);
        show("symmetric difference", sym);
    }
}
JavaScript
const show = (label, s) => console.log(label + ":", [...s].sort((a, b) => a - b).join(" "));

const s1 = new Set([10, 20, 30]);
const s2 = new Set([30, 40, 50]);
show("union", s1.union(s2));                            // ES2025 Set methods
show("intersection", s1.intersection(s2));
show("difference", s1.difference(s2));
show("symmetric difference", s1.symmetricDifference(s2));
Output
union: 10 20 30 40 50
intersection: 30
difference: 10 20
symmetric difference: 10 20 40 50
Time O(|s1| + |s2|)Space O(|s1| + |s2|)
Key point

The mutating forms update a set in place: Python s1 |= s2, s1 &= s2, s1 -= s2 (or update, intersection_update, difference_update); Java's addAll / retainAll / removeAll are only mutating, which is why the sample copies first.

Subset, superset and disjoint tests
TestMeaningPythonCost
a.isdisjoint(b)No common elementa.isdisjoint(b)O(min(|a|, |b|))
a <= bEvery element of a is in b (subset, possibly equal)a.issubset(b)O(|a|)
a < bSubset and a != b (proper subset)a < bO(|a|)
a >= ba contains every element of b (superset)a.issuperset(b)O(|b|)
a > bProper superseta > bO(|b|)
Python
def b(x): return "true" if x else "false"

s1 = {10, 20}
s2 = {40, 30, 50}
print("s1 disjoint s2:", b(s1.isdisjoint(s2)))   # no common element
print("s2 disjoint s1:", b(s2.isdisjoint(s1)))
print("s1 disjoint s1:", b(s1.isdisjoint(s1)))   # a non-empty set shares everything with itself
print("s1 <= s2:", b(s1 <= s2))                   # subset
print("s1 < s2:", b(s1 < s2))                     # proper subset
print("s1 >= s2:", b(s1 >= s2))                   # superset
print("s1 > s2:", b(s1 > s2))                     # proper superset
print("{10} <= s1:", b({10} <= s1))
print("{10} < s1:", b({10} < s1))
print("s1 <= s1:", b(s1 <= s1))                   # a set is a subset of itself …
print("s1 < s1:", b(s1 < s1))                     # … but not a proper one
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <unordered_set>
using namespace std;
using Set = unordered_set<int>;

bool isDisjoint(const Set& a, const Set& b) {
    const Set& small = a.size() < b.size() ? a : b;
    const Set& big = a.size() < b.size() ? b : a;
    for (int x : small) if (big.count(x)) return false;
    return true;
}
bool isSubset(const Set& a, const Set& b) {          // a ⊆ b
    if (a.size() > b.size()) return false;
    for (int x : a) if (!b.count(x)) return false;
    return true;
}
bool isProperSubset(const Set& a, const Set& b) { return a.size() < b.size() && isSubset(a, b); }
const char* B(bool x) { return x ? "true" : "false"; }

int main() {
    Set s1 = {10, 20}, s2 = {40, 30, 50}, one = {10};
    cout << "s1 disjoint s2: " << B(isDisjoint(s1, s2)) << "\n";
    cout << "s2 disjoint s1: " << B(isDisjoint(s2, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 disjoint s1: " << B(isDisjoint(s1, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 <= s2: " << B(isSubset(s1, s2)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 < s2: " << B(isProperSubset(s1, s2)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 >= s2: " << B(isSubset(s2, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 > s2: " << B(isProperSubset(s2, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "{10} <= s1: " << B(isSubset(one, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "{10} < s1: " << B(isProperSubset(one, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 <= s1: " << B(isSubset(s1, s1)) << "\n";
    cout << "s1 < s1: " << B(isProperSubset(s1, s1)) << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static boolean isDisjoint(Set<Integer> a, Set<Integer> b) { return Collections.disjoint(a, b); }
    static boolean isSubset(Set<Integer> a, Set<Integer> b) { return b.containsAll(a); }     // a ⊆ b
    static boolean isProperSubset(Set<Integer> a, Set<Integer> b) { return a.size() < b.size() && b.containsAll(a); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<Integer> s1 = Set.of(10, 20), s2 = Set.of(40, 30, 50), one = Set.of(10);
        System.out.println("s1 disjoint s2: " + isDisjoint(s1, s2));
        System.out.println("s2 disjoint s1: " + isDisjoint(s2, s1));
        System.out.println("s1 disjoint s1: " + isDisjoint(s1, s1));
        System.out.println("s1 <= s2: " + isSubset(s1, s2));
        System.out.println("s1 < s2: " + isProperSubset(s1, s2));
        System.out.println("s1 >= s2: " + isSubset(s2, s1));
        System.out.println("s1 > s2: " + isProperSubset(s2, s1));
        System.out.println("{10} <= s1: " + isSubset(one, s1));
        System.out.println("{10} < s1: " + isProperSubset(one, s1));
        System.out.println("s1 <= s1: " + isSubset(s1, s1));
        System.out.println("s1 < s1: " + isProperSubset(s1, s1));
    }
}

Pitfall

< and > on sets are not a total order: for s1 = {10, 20} and s2 = {30, 40, 50} every one of s1 < s2, s1 > s2 and s1 == s2 is false. Never sort a list of sets with these operators.

Iteration order
Watch out

A hash set iterates in slot order, which depends on the hash values and the table size — it is not insertion order, not sorted order, and it can change after a rehash. Any program whose output depends on it is a bug waiting to happen.

ContainerIteration order
Python setArbitrary (small ints often look sorted because hash(i) == i — do not rely on it); string hashes are randomised per process
C++ unordered_setArbitrary, implementation defined
Java HashSetArbitrary; LinkedHashSet = insertion order; TreeSet = sorted
JavaScript SetInsertion order, guaranteed by the language specification
Do

When the output must be reproducible, sort first (sorted(s)), or use an insertion-ordered container (LinkedHashSet, JS Set, Python dict.fromkeys(items)) when the original order is what you want.

Typical uses

De-duplication

len(set(arr)) counts distinct values; set(arr) drops repeats in O(n) instead of O(n²).

Fast lookups

Turn a list of allowed values / visited states / seen ids into a set and test membership in O(1).

Visited markers

BFS/DFS on graphs store visited nodes in a set — see the Graph topics.

Pair problems

Two-sum, pair with a given difference: scan once, test whether target - x has been seen.

Set algebra

Common friends = intersection; who left = difference; symmetric difference = what changed.

Frequency counting

Needs counts, not just presence — that is a dictionary (next topic).

Problem: count distinct elements in an array
Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 20, 10, 30]
Output: 3
Input: arr = [5, 5, 5]
Output: 1

Idea

Insert every element into a set; duplicates vanish automatically, so the set's size is the number of distinct values. One pass, O(1) average per insert.

Python
def count_distinct(arr):
    return len(set(arr))                  # duplicates collapse on insert

for arr in ([10, 20, 20, 10, 30], [5, 5, 5], [1, 2, 3, 4]):
    print(*arr, "→", count_distinct(arr), "distinct")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_set>
using namespace std;

int countDistinct(const vector<int>& arr) {
    unordered_set<int> seen(arr.begin(), arr.end());   // duplicates collapse on insert
    return (int)seen.size();
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> tests = {{10, 20, 20, 10, 30}, {5, 5, 5}, {1, 2, 3, 4}};
    for (const auto& arr : tests) {
        for (int x : arr) cout << x << " ";
        cout << "→ " << countDistinct(arr) << " distinct\n";
    }
}

Problem: do two arrays have a common element?
Example

Input: a = [3, 8, 12, 5], b = [7, 1, 12]
Output: Yes (12)
Input: a = [1, 2], b = [3, 4]
Output: No

Idea

Put the smaller array in a set, then scan the other array testing membership — O(n + m) instead of the O(n · m) nested loop. This is the intersection operation stopped at the first hit.

Python
def common_element(a, b):
    seen = set(a)                          # O(len(a))
    for x in b:                            # O(len(b)) membership tests
        if x in seen:
            return x
    return None

for a, b in (([3, 8, 12, 5], [7, 1, 12]), ([1, 2], [3, 4])):
    found = common_element(a, b)
    result = f"Yes ({found})" if found is not None else "No"
    print(f"[{' '.join(map(str, a))}] and [{' '.join(map(str, b))}] →", result)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

bool commonElement(const vector<int>& a, const vector<int>& b, int& found) {
    unordered_set<int> seen(a.begin(), a.end());   // O(len(a))
    for (int x : b)                                // O(len(b)) membership tests
        if (seen.count(x)) { found = x; return true; }
    return false;
}

string join(const vector<int>& v) {
    string s = "[";
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); i++) s += (i ? " " : "") + to_string(v[i]);
    return s + "]";
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<vector<int>, vector<int>>> tests = {{{3, 8, 12, 5}, {7, 1, 12}}, {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}};
    for (auto& [a, b] : tests) {
        int found;
        bool ok = commonElement(a, b, found);
        cout << join(a) << " and " << join(b) << " → " << (ok ? "Yes (" + to_string(found) + ")" : "No") << "\n";
    }
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static Integer commonElement(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) seen.add(x);                   // O(len(a))
        for (int x : b) if (seen.contains(x)) return x; // O(len(b)) membership tests
        return null;
    }

    static String join(int[] v) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
        for (int i = 0; i < v.length; i++) sb.append(i > 0 ? " " : "").append(v[i]);
        return sb + "]";
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][][] tests = {{{3, 8, 12, 5}, {7, 1, 12}}, {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}};
        for (int[][] t : tests) {
            Integer found = commonElement(t[0], t[1]);
            System.out.println(join(t[0]) + " and " + join(t[1]) + " → " + (found != null ? "Yes (" + found + ")" : "No"));
        }
    }
}
JavaScript
function commonElement(a, b) {
    const seen = new Set(a);                 // O(len(a))
    for (const x of b)                       // O(len(b)) membership tests
        if (seen.has(x)) return x;
    return null;
}

const join = (v) => "[" + v.join(" ") + "]";
for (const [a, b] of [[[3, 8, 12, 5], [7, 1, 12]], [[1, 2], [3, 4]]]) {
    const found = commonElement(a, b);
    console.log(join(a), "and", join(b), "→", found !== null ? `Yes (${found})` : "No");
}

[1 2] and [3 4] → No
Time O(n + m) averageSpace O(min(n, m))
Interview Q&A
How is a set different from a list / array?

A set holds each value at most once, has no positions (no s[i], no order), and tests membership in O(1) average via hashing. A list keeps duplicates and order, supports O(1) indexing, but membership is an O(n) scan. Use a list when order or duplicates matter, a set when you ask is it there? repeatedly.

Why must set elements be hashable / immutable?

The element's hash decides which slot it lives in. If the element could change after insertion, its hash would change and it would be in the wrong slot — lookups would miss it. Python therefore refuses list and dict elements (TypeError: unhashable type) and offers tuple and frozenset; Java and C++ let you insert mutable objects but break if you mutate them inside the set.

What are the complexities of union, intersection and difference?

All three iterate one set and test membership in the other: O(|a| + |b|) for union and symmetric difference, O(min(|a|, |b|)) for intersection if you iterate the smaller one, O(|a|) for a - b. With sorted (tree) sets the same operations are O(|a| + |b|) by merging.

When would you pick a TreeSet / std::set over a hash set?

When you need the elements sorted, the smallest/largest element, the nearest value above or below a given one (ceiling/floor, lower_bound), or a range of elements. A hash set cannot answer any of those without a full scan; a tree set does each in O(log n).

How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping the original order?

A set alone loses order. Keep a seen set and append to a result only when the element was not yet seen — O(n). In Python list(dict.fromkeys(items)) does the same in one line because dicts preserve insertion order; in Java use LinkedHashSet; JavaScript's [...new Set(items)] works because Set keeps insertion order.

Hashing

Dictionary

A dictionary (hash map) stores key → value pairs and finds the value for any key in O(1) on average. It is the most used data structure in practice: counting, grouping, caching and indexing are all one hash lookup away.

Dictionary / hash map — a collection of key–value pairs with distinct keys, backed by a hash table: the key is hashed to a slot and the value is stored alongside it. Python dict, C++ unordered_map, Java HashMap, JavaScript Map.

A hash map is a hash table whose slots hold key–value pairs
d = {110: 'xyz', 101: 'abc', 105: 'pqr'}     with  h(key) = key % 4

slot 0 │            │
slot 1 │ 101 → abc  │──▶│ 105 → pqr │     101 % 4 = 1 and 105 % 4 = 1 collide → chained
slot 2 │ 110 → xyz  │
slot 3 │            │

lookup d[105]: h(105) = 1 → walk slot 1: 101? no, 105? yes → 'pqr'
Properties of a dictionary

Key–value pairs

Each entry maps a key to exactly one value: d[110] = 'xyz'.

Distinct keys

Assigning to an existing key replaces its value; there are never two entries with the same key.

Values may repeat

Many keys can map to the same value — only keys are unique.

Unordered (conceptually)

Entries live in hash slots. Python 3.7+ and JavaScript additionally remember insertion order; C++ and Java do not.

Hashing internally

Every lookup hashes the key — O(1) average, O(n) worst case.

Hashable keys

Keys must be immutable with a stable hash (numbers, strings, tuples). Values can be anything.

OperationPythonAverageWhy
insert / updated[k] = vO(1)Hash k; store or overwrite in its slot
lookupd[k] (KeyError if missing) / d.get(k, default)O(1)Hash k; compare keys in that one slot
membershipk in dO(1)Same lookup, returns a boolean
deletedel d[k] / d.pop(k)O(1)Hash k; unlink the entry
sizelen(d)O(1)A stored counter
iteratefor k, v in d.items()O(n)Walk every slot
Map containers in the four languages
LanguageHash map (unordered, O(1) avg)Ordered map (sorted keys, O(log n))
Pythondict (insertion-ordered since 3.7); collections.Counter, defaultdict— (use sorted(d); sortedcontainers third-party)
C++std::unordered_mapstd::map (red-black tree)
JavaHashMap; LinkedHashMap keeps insertion orderTreeMap (red-black tree)
JavaScriptMap (insertion-ordered); plain objects {} for string keys only— (sort the keys)
Key point

JavaScript objects {} convert every key to a string (obj[1] and obj["1"] are the same key). Use Map when keys are numbers, objects or mixed types, and whenever you need size without Object.keys(...).length.

Creating a dictionary, adding and reading entries

A dictionary is created from a literal or built up one assignment at a time. Reading d[key] returns the value; keys(), values() and items() give the three views. Below, the keys are sorted before printing because iteration order differs between languages.

Python
d = {}                       # same as {110: 'xyz', 101: 'abc', 105: 'pqr'}
d[110] = 'xyz'
d[101] = 'abc'
d[105] = 'pqr'
print("size:", len(d))
print("d[101] =", d[101])                        # O(1) lookup
print("keys:", *sorted(d.keys()))
print("values:", *[d[k] for k in sorted(d)])
print("items:", *[f"{k}={d[k]}" for k in sorted(d)])
d[101] = 'ABC'                                   # existing key → value replaced
print("after d[101] = 'ABC':", *[f"{k}={d[k]}" for k in sorted(d)])
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

vector<int> sortedKeys(const unordered_map<int, string>& d) {
    vector<int> keys;
    for (auto& kv : d) keys.push_back(kv.first);
    sort(keys.begin(), keys.end());
    return keys;
}

int main() {
    unordered_map<int, string> d;    // same as {{110, "xyz"}, {101, "abc"}, {105, "pqr"}}
    d[110] = "xyz";
    d[101] = "abc";
    d[105] = "pqr";
    cout << "size: " << d.size() << "\n";
    cout << "d[101] = " << d[101] << "\n";                 // O(1) lookup
    cout << "keys:"; for (int k : sortedKeys(d)) cout << " " << k; cout << "\n";
    cout << "values:"; for (int k : sortedKeys(d)) cout << " " << d[k]; cout << "\n";
    cout << "items:"; for (int k : sortedKeys(d)) cout << " " << k << "=" << d[k]; cout << "\n";
    d[101] = "ABC";                                          // existing key → value replaced
    cout << "after d[101] = 'ABC':"; for (int k : sortedKeys(d)) cout << " " << k << "=" << d[k]; cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static String items(Map<Integer, String> d) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int k : new TreeSet<>(d.keySet())) sb.append(" ").append(k).append("=").append(d.get(k));
        return sb.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Integer, String> d = new HashMap<>();   // same as Map.of(110, "xyz", 101, "abc", 105, "pqr")
        d.put(110, "xyz");
        d.put(101, "abc");
        d.put(105, "pqr");
        System.out.println("size: " + d.size());
        System.out.println("d[101] = " + d.get(101));          // O(1) lookup
        TreeSet<Integer> keys = new TreeSet<>(d.keySet());
        StringBuilder ks = new StringBuilder("keys:"), vs = new StringBuilder("values:");
        for (int k : keys) { ks.append(" ").append(k); vs.append(" ").append(d.get(k)); }
        System.out.println(ks);
        System.out.println(vs);
        System.out.println("items:" + items(d));
        d.put(101, "ABC");                                      // existing key → value replaced
        System.out.println("after d[101] = 'ABC':" + items(d));
    }
}

Pitfall

In C++ d[key] on a missing key silently inserts a default value (empty string, 0) and returns it. Use d.find(key), d.count(key), d.contains(key) (C++20) or d.at(key) (throws) when you only want to read.

Missing keys and default values

What happens when the key is absent is where the languages differ most, and the source of most dictionary bugs:

LanguageRead of a missing keySafe read with defaultMembership
Pythond[k] raises KeyErrord.get(k, default); d.setdefault(k, default) also insertsk in d
C++d[k] inserts a default and returns it; d.at(k) throwsauto it = d.find(k); it != d.end() ? it->second : defaultd.count(k) / d.contains(k)
Javad.get(k) returns nulld.getOrDefault(k, default)d.containsKey(k)
JavaScriptd.get(k) returns undefinedd.get(k) ?? defaultd.has(k)
Python
d = {110: 'xyz', 101: 'abc', 105: 'pqr'}
print("get 101:", d.get(101))
print("get 999:", d.get(999, "none"))           # no KeyError
print("999 in d:", "true" if 999 in d else "false")

counts = {}
counts['abc'] = counts.get('abc', 0) + 1       # the counting idiom
print("count of 'abc' with default 0 →", counts['abc'])
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

string getOr(const unordered_map<int, string>& d, int k, const string& def) {
    auto it = d.find(k);                          // find does not insert
    return it != d.end() ? it->second : def;
}

int main() {
    unordered_map<int, string> d = {{110, "xyz"}, {101, "abc"}, {105, "pqr"}};
    cout << "get 101: " << getOr(d, 101, "none") << "\n";
    cout << "get 999: " << getOr(d, 999, "none") << "\n";
    cout << "999 in d: " << (d.contains(999) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";

    unordered_map<string, int> counts;
    counts["abc"]++;                              // operator[] inserts 0 then increments — the counting idiom
    cout << "count of 'abc' with default 0 → " << counts["abc"] << "\n";
}

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Integer, String> d = new HashMap<>(Map.of(110, "xyz", 101, "abc", 105, "pqr"));
        System.out.println("get 101: " + d.get(101));
        System.out.println("get 999: " + d.getOrDefault(999, "none"));   // get(999) alone would be null
        System.out.println("999 in d: " + d.containsKey(999));

        Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        counts.merge("abc", 1, Integer::sum);           // the counting idiom
        System.out.println("count of 'abc' with default 0 → " + counts.get("abc"));

Key point

Python's collections.defaultdict(int) and Counter build the default-value idiom into the container: counts[x] += 1 just works. Counter(arr).most_common(k) is the one-liner for top-k frequency questions.

Removing entries

pop(key) removes an entry and returns its value (Python, and the same shape in Java's remove); del d[key] just removes it. Python's popitem() removes and returns the last inserted pair — handy as a stack of pairs — and has no equivalent in the other languages.

Python

def show(): print("remaining:", *[f"{k}={d[k]}" for k in sorted(d)])

show()
print("delete 105:", "true" if d.pop(105, None) is not None else "false")
print("delete 999:", "true" if d.pop(999, None) is not None else "false")   # default avoids KeyError
show()

Iteration order
Watch out

Conceptually a hash map has no order. Two of the four languages guarantee insertion order anyway, two do not — code that works in Python and breaks in Java or C++ is a classic porting bug.

ContainerIteration order
Python dictInsertion order (guaranteed since 3.7)
C++ unordered_mapArbitrary; std::map = sorted by key
Java HashMapArbitrary; LinkedHashMap = insertion order; TreeMap = sorted by key
JavaScript MapInsertion order; plain objects list integer-like keys first in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order
Do

Need sorted output? Sort the keys explicitly (for k in sorted(d)) or use a tree map. Need first-seen order in C++/Java? Keep a separate vector/list of keys in insertion order or use LinkedHashMap.

Typical uses

Frequency counting

count[x] += 1 over an array or text — then answer most frequent, appears exactly once, anagram check.

Lookup tables

id → record, name → phone number, word → definition. A database index in miniature.

Memoisation / caching

key = function arguments, value = result; dynamic programming top-down uses exactly this.

Grouping

key = group label (first letter, sorted letters, remainder), value = list of members.

Pair problems

Two-sum: for each x, has target - x been seen? Store value → index.

Graphs

Adjacency lists for sparse graphs with arbitrary vertex labels: adj[u] = [v, …].

Problem: word frequencies
Example

Input: text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"
Output: and 2 / bat 1 / cat 1 / hat 1 / the 3

Idea

Split into words and do freq[word] += 1 for each — a hash map update is O(1) on average, so the whole text costs O(n). Print the keys in sorted order so the result does not depend on the language's iteration order.

Python
def word_freq(text):
    freq = {}
    for w in text.split():
        freq[w] = freq.get(w, 0) + 1      # O(1) average
    for w in sorted(freq):
        print(w, freq[w])

word_freq("the cat and the hat and the bat")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

void wordFreq(const string& text) {
    unordered_map<string, int> freq;
    istringstream in(text);
    string w;
    while (in >> w) freq[w]++;            // O(1) average
    vector<string> words;
    for (auto& kv : freq) words.push_back(kv.first);
    sort(words.begin(), words.end());
    for (const string& x : words) cout << x << " " << freq[x] << "\n";
}

int main() {
    wordFreq("the cat and the hat and the bat");
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static void wordFreq(String text) {
        Map<String, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (String w : text.split(" ")) freq.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);   // O(1) average
        for (String w : new TreeSet<>(freq.keySet()))
            System.out.println(w + " " + freq.get(w));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        wordFreq("the cat and the hat and the bat");
    }
}

function wordFreq(text) {
    const freq = new Map();
    for (const w of text.split(" ")) freq.set(w, (freq.get(w) ?? 0) + 1);   // O(1) average
    for (const w of [...freq.keys()].sort()) console.log(w, freq.get(w));

Problem: two sum with a hash map
Example

Input: arr = [8, 3, 5, 11, 2], target = 13
Output: 8 + 5 = 13
Input: arr = [1, 2, 3], target = 10
Output: no pair

Idea

Scan once. For each x, the partner we need is target - x; if it has already been seen, we are done, otherwise record x. One hash lookup per element replaces the inner loop of the O(n²) brute force.

1
Create an empty map
seen maps a value to its index (a set suffices if indices are not needed).
2
For each element x
Compute need = target - x.
3
Check the map
If need is in seen, report the pair (need, x).
4
Record
Otherwise store seen[x] = index and continue.
Python
def two_sum(arr, target):
    seen = {}                               # value → index
    for i, x in enumerate(arr):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:                    # O(1) instead of an inner loop
            return seen[need], i
        seen[x] = i
    return None

for arr, target in (([8, 3, 5, 11, 2], 13), ([1, 2, 3], 10)):
    res = two_sum(arr, target)
    label = f"[{' '.join(map(str, arr))}] target {target} →"
    if res is None:
        print(label, "no pair")
    else:
        i, j = res
        print(label, f"{arr[i]} + {arr[j]} = {target} (indices {i}, {j})")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

bool twoSum(const vector<int>& arr, int target, int& i, int& j) {
    unordered_map<int, int> seen;           // value → index
    int n = arr.size();
    for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
        int need = target - arr[k];
        auto it = seen.find(need);          // O(1) instead of an inner loop
        if (it != seen.end()) { i = it->second; j = k; return true; }
        seen[arr[k]] = k;
    }
    return false;
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<vector<int>, int>> tests = {{{8, 3, 5, 11, 2}, 13}, {{1, 2, 3}, 10}};
    for (auto& [arr, target] : tests) {
        cout << "[";
        for (int k = 0; k < (int)arr.size(); k++) cout << (k ? " " : "") << arr[k];
        cout << "] target " << target << " → ";
        int i, j;
        if (twoSum(arr, target, i, j))
            cout << arr[i] << " + " << arr[j] << " = " << target << " (indices " << i << ", " << j << ")\n";
        else
            cout << "no pair\n";
    }
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static int[] twoSum(int[] arr, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();   // value → index
        for (int k = 0; k < arr.length; k++) {
            int need = target - arr[k];
            if (seen.containsKey(need))                 // O(1) instead of an inner loop
                return new int[]{seen.get(need), k};
            seen.put(arr[k], k);
        }
        return null;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] arrays = {{8, 3, 5, 11, 2}, {1, 2, 3}};
        int[] targets = {13, 10};
        for (int t = 0; t < arrays.length; t++) {
            int[] arr = arrays[t];
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
            for (int k = 0; k < arr.length; k++) sb.append(k > 0 ? " " : "").append(arr[k]);
            sb.append("] target ").append(targets[t]).append(" → ");
            int[] res = twoSum(arr, targets[t]);
            if (res == null) sb.append("no pair");
            else sb.append(arr[res[0]]).append(" + ").append(arr[res[1]]).append(" = ").append(targets[t])
                   .append(" (indices ").append(res[0]).append(", ").append(res[1]).append(")");
            System.out.println(sb);
        }
    }
}
JavaScript
function twoSum(arr, target) {
    const seen = new Map();                   // value → index
    for (let k = 0; k < arr.length; k++) {
        const need = target - arr[k];
        if (seen.has(need)) return [seen.get(need), k];   // O(1) instead of an inner loop
        seen.set(arr[k], k);
    }
    return null;
}

for (const [arr, target] of [[[8, 3, 5, 11, 2], 13], [[1, 2, 3], 10]]) {
    const label = `[${arr.join(" ")}] target ${target} →`;
    const res = twoSum(arr, target);
    if (res === null) console.log(label, "no pair");
    else console.log(label, `${arr[res[0]]} + ${arr[res[1]]} = ${target} (indices ${res[0]}, ${res[1]})`);
}

[1 2 3] target 10 → no pair
Time O(n) averageSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Insert x into the map after checking for its partner, not before — otherwise target = 2x would match an element with itself ([5], target 10 → "5 + 5").

Interview Q&A
How does a dictionary achieve O(1) lookup?

The key is hashed to an array index; the value sits in that slot (or in a short chain / probe sequence starting there). No scanning, no comparisons with unrelated keys. The cost is O(1) average: a bad hash function or an overfull table lengthens chains, and rehashing keeps the load factor bounded.

Dictionary vs set — when do you need which?

Both are hash tables with distinct keys. A set answers is x present?; a dictionary additionally attaches a value to each key — a count, an index, a list of members. If you catch yourself using a dictionary with all values True, you want a set.

What can be a dictionary key?

Anything hashable and immutable in Python: numbers, strings, tuples of hashables, frozenset — not lists, dicts or sets. Java and C++ require a consistent hashCode/equals pair (or std::hash plus ==) and the object must not change while it is a key. JavaScript Map accepts any value including objects (compared by identity), whereas plain objects stringify every key.

What is the difference between HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap (or dict vs std::map)?

HashMap/unordered_map/dict: hash table, O(1) average, no ordering guarantee (Python dict and JS Map keep insertion order). LinkedHashMap: hash table plus a linked list through the entries — insertion order at the same O(1). TreeMap/std::map: red-black tree, keys sorted, O(log n) per operation, supports floor/ceiling/range queries. Pick by whether you need order.

How would you find the first non-repeating character in a string?

Two passes with a dictionary: count every character (O(n)), then scan the string again and return the first character whose count is 1. The second pass uses the string's order, so the hash map's iteration order never matters.

Linked Lists

Linked List

A linked list is a linear collection whose elements are not stored next to each other in memory: every node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Insertion and deletion at a known position are O(1), at the price of O(n) access by index.

Singly linked list — a sequence of nodes, each containing a data field and a next reference to the following node. The first node is the head; the list ends at the node whose next is None/null. Only the head is stored — everything else is reached by following next pointers.

A singly linked list with three nodes — only the head reference is stored by the program
head
 ↓
┌──────┬──────┐    ┌──────┬──────┐    ┌──────┬──────┐
│  10  │  ●───┼───▶│  20  │  ●───┼───▶│  30  │  ∅   │
└──────┴──────┘    └──────┴──────┘    └──────┴──────┘
  data   next        data   next        data   next = None (end of list)
Structure of a node

A node is a tiny object (or struct) with two fields. Nodes are allocated one at a time, so the list grows and shrinks without ever copying or resizing an array. Traversal starts at the head and follows next until it becomes None.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None             # no next node yet

def show(head):
    parts = []
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:          # traversal: follow next until the end
        parts.append(str(curr.data))
        curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts))

def length(head):
    n, curr = 0, head
    while curr:
        n += 1
        curr = curr.next
    return n

head = Node(10)                      # build by hand: 10 -> 20 -> 30
head.next = Node(20)
head.next.next = Node(30)
show(head)
print("length:", length(head))
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data;
    Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}   // no next node yet
};

void show(Node* head) {
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next) {   // traversal: follow next until null
        cout << curr->data;
        if (curr->next) cout << " -> ";
    }
    cout << "\n";
}

int length(Node* head) {
    int n = 0;
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next) n++;
    return n;
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10);           // build by hand: 10 -> 20 -> 30
    head->next = new Node(20);
    head->next->next = new Node(30);
    show(head);
    cout << "length: " << length(head) << "\n";
}

Key point

The list has no size unless you maintain a counter: length walks all nodes in O(n). Real implementations wrap the head in a LinkedList class that also stores size (and often a tail).

Why — and why not — a linked list

Dynamic size

Grows one node at a time; no capacity to guess, no O(n) resize copy.

O(1) insert / delete at a known node

Re-link two pointers. An array must shift every later element.

No contiguous block needed

Nodes can live anywhere in memory — useful when large arrays cannot be allocated.

No random access

list[i] means walking i nodes: O(n). Binary search is impossible.

Extra memory

One pointer per element (8 bytes on 64-bit) — a list of small ints doubles its footprint.

Cache unfriendly

Nodes are scattered; each next is a potential cache miss, so traversals are slower than over an array of the same size.

Linked lists are the building block of other structures: stacks and queues (O(1) at the ends), hash-table chains, adjacency lists in graphs, and the LRU cache (a doubly linked list plus a hash map).

Operations and their cost
OperationTimeWhy
Insert at beginningO(1)New node points at the old head; the head reference moves. No traversal.
Insert at endO(n) — O(1) with a tail pointerWithout a tail you must walk to the last node first.
Delete headO(1)Head moves to head.next.
Delete lastO(n)Need the second-to-last node to clear its next; a singly linked list cannot go backwards.
Insert / delete after a given nodeO(1)Only pointers of the given node and its neighbour change.
SearchO(n)Sequential scan; nothing better is possible without random access.
Access by indexO(n)Walk i links.
Insert at the beginning
Example

Input: list = 20 -> 30, insert 10 at the beginning
Output: 10 -> 20 -> 30

Idea

Create the node, make it point at the current head, and return it as the new head. No node is visited, so it is O(1) regardless of the list length — the one place where a linked list beats an array outright.

Insert at the beginning: two pointer assignments
before:   head ──▶ [20] ──▶ [30] ──▶ ∅

step 1:   new = [10]           new.next = head        [10] ──▶ [20] ──▶ [30] ──▶ ∅
step 2:   head = new                                   head ──▶ [10] ──▶ [20] ──▶ [30] ──▶ ∅
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def insert_at_beginning(head, data):
    new_node = Node(data)
    new_node.next = head         # new node points at the old head
    return new_node              # it is the new head — caller must store it

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts))

head = None
for x in (30, 20, 10):           # insert in reverse to get 10 -> 20 -> 30
    head = insert_at_beginning(head, x)
    show(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* insertAtBeginning(Node* head, int data) {
    Node* newNode = new Node(data);
    newNode->next = head;        // new node points at the old head
    return newNode;              // it is the new head — caller must store it
}

void show(Node* head) {
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << head->data << (head->next ? " -> " : "\n");
}

int main() {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int x : {30, 20, 10}) {     // insert in reverse to get 10 -> 20 -> 30
        head = insertAtBeginning(head, x);
        show(head);
    }
}
Java

    static class Node {
        int data; Node next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node insertAtBeginning(Node head, int data) {
        Node newNode = new Node(data);
        newNode.next = head;         // new node points at the old head
        return newNode;              // it is the new head — caller must store it
    }

    static void show(Node head) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (; head != null; head = head.next) sb.append(head.data).append(head.next != null ? " -> " : "");
        System.out.println(sb);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node head = null;
        for (int x : new int[]{30, 20, 10}) {   // insert in reverse to get 10 -> 20 -> 30
            head = insertAtBeginning(head, x);

        }
    }
}

    const newNode = new Node(data);
    newNode.next = head;             // new node points at the old head
    return newNode;                  // it is the new head — caller must store it
}

function show(head) {
    const parts = [];
    for (; head !== null; head = head.next) parts.push(head.data);

Time O(1)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Functions that change the head must return the new head (or work on a wrapper object). Writing insert_at_beginning(head, 10) without head = … leaves the caller pointing at the old second node — the new node is lost.

Insert at the end
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 20, insert 30 at the end
Output: 10 -> 20 -> 30
Input: list = empty, insert 10
Output: 10

Idea

Walk to the last node (the one whose next is None) and hang the new node there. The walk makes it O(n); keeping a tail pointer in a wrapper class makes it O(1). The empty list is a special case: the new node simply becomes the head.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def insert_at_end(head, data):
    new_node = Node(data)
    if head is None:                 # empty list: the new node is the head
        return new_node
    current = head
    while current.next is not None:  # O(n) walk to the last node
        current = current.next
    current.next = new_node
    return head                      # head is unchanged

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts))

head = None
for x in (10, 20, 30):
    head = insert_at_end(head, x)
    show(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* insertAtEnd(Node* head, int data) {
    Node* newNode = new Node(data);
    if (!head) return newNode;           // empty list: the new node is the head
    Node* current = head;
    while (current->next) current = current->next;   // O(n) walk to the last node
    current->next = newNode;
    return head;                         // head is unchanged
}

void show(Node* head) {
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << head->data << (head->next ? " -> " : "\n");
}

int main() {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30}) {
        head = insertAtEnd(head, x);
        show(head);
    }
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node insertAtEnd(Node head, int data) {
        Node newNode = new Node(data);
        if (head == null) return newNode;    // empty list: the new node is the head
        Node current = head;
        while (current.next != null) current = current.next;   // O(n) walk to the last node
        current.next = newNode;
        return head;                         // head is unchanged
    }

    static void show(Node head) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (; head != null; head = head.next) sb.append(head.data).append(head.next != null ? " -> " : "");
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node head = null;
        for (int x : new int[]{10, 20, 30}) {
            head = insertAtEnd(head, x);
            show(head);
        }
    }
}

    constructor(data) { this.data = data; this.next = null; }

    const newNode = new Node(data);

    let current = head;

Key point

Building a list of n elements by repeated insert_at_end costs O(n²) without a tail pointer. Either keep a tail, or insert at the beginning and reverse once at the end.

Delete the head
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 20 -> 30
Output: 20 -> 30
Input: list = 10
Output: empty

Idea

The second node becomes the head: return head.next. In C++ free the old node; in Python, Java and JavaScript the garbage collector reclaims it once nothing refers to it. An empty list stays empty.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def delete_head(head):
    if head is None:
        return None                  # nothing to delete
    return head.next                 # the old head is garbage-collected

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts) if parts else "empty")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(20); head.next.next = Node(30)
show(head)
for _ in range(4):
    head = delete_head(head)
    print("after delete head: ", end="")
    show(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* deleteHead(Node* head) {
    if (!head) return nullptr;           // nothing to delete
    Node* next = head->next;
    delete head;                         // free the old head
    return next;
}

void show(Node* head) {
    if (!head) { cout << "empty\n"; return; }
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << head->data << (head->next ? " -> " : "\n");
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); head->next = new Node(20); head->next->next = new Node(30);
    show(head);
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
        head = deleteHead(head);
        cout << "after delete head: ";
        show(head);
    }
}

Delete the last node
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 20 -> 30
Output: 10 -> 20
Input: list = 10
Output: empty

Idea

A singly linked list cannot step backwards, so to drop the last node we must stop at the second-to-last one (current.next.next is None) and clear its next. That walk is what makes the operation O(n), while deleting the head is O(1).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def delete_last(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return None                          # 0 or 1 node → empty list
    current = head
    while current.next.next is not None:     # stop at the second-to-last node
        current = current.next
    current.next = None
    return head

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts) if parts else "empty")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(20); head.next.next = Node(30)
show(head)
for _ in range(3):
    head = delete_last(head)
    print("after delete last: ", end="")
    show(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* deleteLast(Node* head) {
    if (!head || !head->next) { delete head; return nullptr; }   // 0 or 1 node → empty list
    Node* current = head;
    while (current->next->next) current = current->next;        // stop at the second-to-last node
    delete current->next;
    current->next = nullptr;
    return head;
}

void show(Node* head) {
    if (!head) { cout << "empty\n"; return; }
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << head->data << (head->next ? " -> " : "\n");
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); head->next = new Node(20); head->next->next = new Node(30);
    show(head);
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        head = deleteLast(head);
        cout << "after delete last: ";
        show(head);
    }
}

        Node current = head;

        current.next = null;

    static void show(Node head) {
        if (head == null) { System.out.println("empty"); return; }
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

    head = deleteLast(head);
    process.stdout.write("after delete last: ");
    show(head);
}

Search in a linked list
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 20 -> 30, target = 20
Output: position 2
Input: target = 40
Output: -1

Idea

Walk from the head comparing each node's data with the target and counting positions (1-indexed). Return the position on a match, -1 after falling off the end. Without random access, a linear scan is the only option — even on a sorted list.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def search_list(head, target):
    current, position = head, 1
    while current is not None:
        if current.data == target:
            return position
        current = current.next
        position += 1
    return -1                            # fell off the end

def report(head, x):
    pos = search_list(head, x)
    print(f"search {x}:", f"position {pos}" if pos != -1 else -1)

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(20); head.next.next = Node(30)
for x in (20, 10, 40):
    report(head, x)
C++
#include <iostream>

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;

int searchList(Node* head, int target) {
    int position = 1;
    for (Node* current = head; current; current = current->next, position++)
        if (current->data == target) return position;
    return -1;                           // fell off the end
}

void report(Node* head, int x) {
    int pos = searchList(head, x);
    cout << "search " << x << ": ";
    if (pos != -1) cout << "position " << pos << "\n"; else cout << "-1\n";
}

}

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Array vs linked list
OperationArray / dynamic array (contiguous)Linked list (pointers)
Access by indexO(1) — address = base + i · sizeO(n) — walk i links
Search (unsorted)O(n)O(n)
Search (sorted)O(log n) binary searchO(n) — no random access, binary search impossible
Insert / delete at startO(n) — shift every elementO(1) — re-link the head
Insert / delete at endO(1) amortised (occasional resize copy)O(n), or O(1) with a tail pointer (delete last stays O(n) for singly linked)
Insert / delete in the middle (position known)O(n) — shift the tailO(1) — once you hold the previous node
Extra memoryNone per element; unused capacity in dynamic arraysOne next pointer per node
Memory layoutContiguous — cache friendly, prefetchableScattered — pointer chasing, cache misses
SizeFixed, or resized by copyingGrows node by node
Do

Default to an array / dynamic array: random access and cache locality win most of the time. Reach for a linked list when you need many O(1) insertions or deletions at known nodes (queues, LRU caches, adjacency lists, splicing lists together) or cannot afford resize copies.

Interview Q&A
Why is inserting at the front O(1) in a linked list but O(n) in an array?

An array keeps elements contiguous, so making room at index 0 means moving every existing element one slot right. A linked list has no positions — a new node just points at the old head and becomes the new head; nothing else moves.

Why is binary search not possible on a linked list?

Binary search needs the middle element in O(1). In a linked list reaching the middle costs O(n/2) pointer hops, so every probe is O(n) and the search becomes O(n) overall — no better than a linear scan.

How do you find the middle of a linked list in one pass?

Two pointers: slow moves one node per step, fast two. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. The same trick (Floyd's algorithm) detects a cycle: if fast ever meets slow, the list loops.

How would you reverse a singly linked list?

Iterate with three pointers prev, curr, next: save next = curr.next, redirect curr.next = prev, then advance prev = curr, curr = next. When curr is None, prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.

When is a linked list a better choice than a dynamic array?

When the workload is dominated by inserts/deletes at the ends or at nodes you already hold (a queue, an LRU cache, merging sorted lists), when element moves are expensive, or when a guaranteed O(1) without occasional resize pauses matters. For index-heavy or cache-sensitive code, arrays win.

Linked Lists

Circular Linked List

A circular linked list is a singly linked list whose last node points back to the head instead of to None. There is no end, so the list can be traversed from any node, and keeping a single pointer gives O(1) access to both the first and the last element.

Circular linked list — a linked list in which the next of the last node refers to the first node. A one-node list points to itself. Traversal stops when we return to the node where we started, not when next is None — because it never is.

10 → 5 → 20 → 15 → back to 10
head
 ↓
┌──────┬────┐    ┌──────┬────┐    ┌──────┬────┐    ┌──────┬────┐
│  10  │ ●──┼───▶│   5  │ ●──┼───▶│  20  │ ●──┼───▶│  15  │ ●──┼──┐
└──────┴────┘    └──────┴────┘    └──────┴────┘    └──────┴────┘  │
  ▲                                                               │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                the last node links back to the head
Building and traversing

The nodes are the same as in a singly linked list; only the last link differs. Traversal must stop when it comes back to the head, so the loop prints the head first and then walks until curr == head again. A while curr.next != head loop (as in the original notes) also works but needs the last node printed separately.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def print_circular(head):
    if head is None:
        print("empty")
        return
    parts = [str(head.data)]
    curr = head.next
    while curr != head:              # stop when we are back at the start
        parts.append(str(curr.data))
        curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head = Node(10)
head.next = Node(5)
head.next.next = Node(20)
head.next.next.next = Node(15)
head.next.next.next.next = head      # close the circle
print_circular(head)

#include <iostream>

struct Node {

void printCircular(Node* head) {
    if (!head) { cout << "empty\n"; return; }
    cout << head->data;
    for (Node* curr = head->next; curr != head; curr = curr->next)   // stop when back at the start
        cout << " -> " << curr->data;

    Node* head = new Node(10);

    head->next->next->next = new Node(15);
    head->next->next->next->next = head;    // close the circle

}

Time O(n) traversalSpace O(1)
Pitfall

A while curr is not None loop never terminates on a circular list. Every traversal must remember where it started and stop there.

Advantages and disadvantages

Traverse from any node

Starting anywhere, following next visits every node — no need to find the head first.

Round-robin scheduling

The OS gives each process a time slice and moves to next; after the last process comes the first again. Also: multiplayer turns, circular buffers, music playlists on repeat.

O(1) at both ends with one pointer

Keep a reference to the tail: the head is tail.next, so insert at the beginning, insert at the end and delete the head are all O(1).

More complex code

Every operation must handle the empty list, the one-node list (which points at itself) and the wrap-around; an off-by-one gives an infinite loop instead of a crash.

Operation (holding head only)NaiveEfficient trickHolding tail instead
Insert at beginningO(n): walk to the last node to fix its nextO(1): insert after head and swap dataO(1)
Insert at endO(n): walk to the last nodeO(1): same trick, return the new node as headO(1)
Delete headO(n): walk to the last node to re-point itO(1): copy head.next into head and unlink head.nextO(1)
Delete k-th nodeO(k)—O(k)
SearchO(n)—O(n)
Insert at the beginning
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 (circular), insert 25 at the beginning
Output: 25 -> 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 -> (back to 25)

Naive, O(n). The last node must point at the new head, and the only way to reach the last node is to walk the whole circle.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def insert_beginning_naive(head, x):
    temp = Node(x)
    if head is None:
        temp.next = temp               # one node points at itself
        return temp
    curr = head
    while curr.next != head:           # O(n) walk to the last node
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = temp                   # last node → new node
    temp.next = head                   # new node → old head
    return temp

def print_circular(head):
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(5); head.next.next = Node(20); head.next.next.next = Node(15)
head.next.next.next.next = head
head = insert_beginning_naive(head, 25)
print_circular(head)
Output
25 -> 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 -> (back to 25)
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Idea

Efficient, O(1). Insert the new node right after the head (two pointer changes — no walk) and then swap the data of the head and the new node. The head node now carries the new value and the old head value sits in second position: exactly the result of inserting at the front. The head reference does not even change.

Insert at the beginning in O(1): insert after the head, then swap the two values
before:          head ──▶ [10] ──▶ [5] ──▶ [20] ──▶ [15] ──▶ back to 10
insert after head:   head ──▶ [10] ──▶ [25] ──▶ [5] ──▶ [20] ──▶ [15] ──▶ back to 10
swap data:           head ──▶ [25] ──▶ [10] ──▶ [5] ──▶ [20] ──▶ [15] ──▶ back to 25
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def insert_beginning(head, x):
    temp = Node(x)
    if head is None:
        temp.next = temp                             # one node points at itself
        return temp
    temp.next = head.next                            # insert temp right after head
    head.next = temp
    head.data, temp.data = temp.data, head.data      # swap values: head now holds x
    return head

def print_circular(head):
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head.next.next.next.next = head

head = insert_beginning(head, 30); print_circular(head)

Node* insertBeginning(Node* head, int x) {

    temp->next = head->next;                         // insert temp right after head
    head->next = temp;

}

void printCircular(Node* head) {
    cout << head->data;

    cout << " -> (back to " << head->data << ")\n";

Pitfall

The swap trick moves a value into a different node. If other code holds references to specific nodes (or the data is large/expensive to copy), use the tail-pointer design instead: with tail known, head = tail.next and both ends are O(1) without any swapping.

Insert at the end
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 (circular), insert 35 at the end
Output: 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 -> 35 -> (back to 10)

Naive, O(n). Walk to the last node, link it to the new node and link the new node back to the head.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def insert_end_naive(head, x):
    temp = Node(x)
    if head is None:
        temp.next = temp
        return temp
    curr = head
    while curr.next != head:           # O(n) walk to the last node
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = temp                   # last → new
    temp.next = head                   # new → head
    return head

def print_circular(head):
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(5); head.next.next = Node(20); head.next.next.next = Node(15)
head.next.next.next.next = head
head = insert_end_naive(head, 35)
print_circular(head)
Output
10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 -> 35 -> (back to 10)
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Idea

Efficient, O(1). Same trick as before — insert the new node after the head and swap the values — but now return the new node as the head. Reading the circle from that node gives the old sequence first and the new value last: the head node (which now holds x) comes just before it.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def insert_end(head, x):
    temp = Node(x)
    if head is None:
        temp.next = temp
        return temp
    temp.next = head.next                            # insert temp right after head
    head.next = temp
    head.data, temp.data = temp.data, head.data      # old head value moves to temp
    return temp                                      # temp is the new head; x sits just before it

def print_circular(head):
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

Delete the head
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 (circular)
Output: 5 -> 20 -> 15 -> (back to 5)
Input: list = 10 (one node)
Output: empty

Naive, O(n). The last node points at the head, so after removing the head the last node must be found and re-pointed at the second node — a full walk.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def delete_head_naive(head):
    if head is None or head.next == head:   # empty or single node → empty
        return None
    curr = head
    while curr.next != head:                # O(n) walk to the last node
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = head.next                   # last → second node
    return curr.next                        # second node is the new head

def print_circular(head):
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(5); head.next.next = Node(20); head.next.next.next = Node(15)
head.next.next.next.next = head
head = delete_head_naive(head)
print_circular(head)
Output
5 -> 20 -> 15 -> (back to 5)
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Idea

Efficient, O(1). Instead of removing the head node, copy the second node's value into it and unlink the second node. The head node object survives, so the last node's back-pointer stays valid without any walk.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def delete_head(head):
    if head is None or head.next == head:   # empty or single node → empty
        return None
    head.data = head.next.data               # pull the second value into the head node
    head.next = head.next.next               # unlink the second node
    return head

def print_circular(head):
    if head is None:
        print("empty"); return
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(5); head.next.next = Node(20); head.next.next.next = Node(15)
head.next.next.next.next = head
for _ in range(4):
    head = delete_head(head)
    print_circular(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* deleteHead(Node* head) {
    if (!head) return nullptr;
    if (head->next == head) { delete head; return nullptr; }   // single node → empty
    Node* second = head->next;
    head->data = second->data;               // pull the second value into the head node
    head->next = second->next;               // unlink the second node
    delete second;
    return head;
}

void printCircular(Node* head) {
    if (!head) { cout << "empty\n"; return; }
    cout << head->data;
    for (Node* curr = head->next; curr != head; curr = curr->next) cout << " -> " << curr->data;
    cout << " -> (back to " << head->data << ")\n";
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); head->next = new Node(5); head->next->next = new Node(20);
    head->next->next->next = new Node(15); head->next->next->next->next = head;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
        head = deleteHead(head);
        printCircular(head);
    }
}

Delete the k-th node
Example

Input: list = 10 -> 5 -> 20 -> 15 (circular), k = 2
Output: 10 -> 20 -> 15 -> (back to 10)
Input: k = 1
Output: 5 -> 20 -> 15 -> (back to 5)

Idea

k = 1 is the head — reuse delete_head. Otherwise walk to the (k-1)-th node, which takes k - 2 steps from the head, and bypass its successor: curr.next = curr.next.next. The circle stays closed because the bypassed node's next is reused.

1
Empty list
Return None.
2
k == 1
Return delete_head(head) — the O(1) version above.
3
Walk
curr = head; move k - 2 times → curr is the (k-1)-th node.
4
Bypass
curr.next = curr.next.next removes the k-th node.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def delete_head(head):
    if head is None or head.next == head:
        return None
    head.data = head.next.data
    head.next = head.next.next
    return head

def delete_kth(head, k):
    if head is None:
        return None
    if k == 1:
        return delete_head(head)
    curr = head
    for _ in range(k - 2):                   # k-2 steps reach the (k-1)-th node
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = curr.next.next               # bypass the k-th node
    return head

def print_circular(head):
    parts, curr = [str(head.data)], head.next
    while curr != head:
        parts.append(str(curr.data)); curr = curr.next
    print(" -> ".join(parts), f"-> (back to {head.data})")

head = Node(10); head.next = Node(5); head.next.next = Node(20); head.next.next.next = Node(15)
head.next.next.next.next = head
print_circular(head)
for k, label in ((2, "2nd"), (3, "3rd"), (1, "1st")):
    head = delete_kth(head, k)
    print(f"delete {label}: ", end=""); print_circular(head)

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* deleteHead(Node* head) {
    if (!head) return nullptr;
    if (head->next == head) { delete head; return nullptr; }
    Node* second = head->next;
    head->data = second->data; head->next = second->next;
    delete second;

Node* deleteKth(Node* head, int k) {
    if (!head) return nullptr;
    if (k == 1) return deleteHead(head);
    Node* curr = head;
    for (int i = 0; i < k - 2; i++) curr = curr->next;   // k-2 steps reach the (k-1)-th node
    Node* victim = curr->next;
    curr->next = victim->next;                           // bypass the k-th node
    delete victim;
    return head;
}

    cout << head->data;
    for (Node* curr = head->next; curr != head; curr = curr->next) cout << " -> " << curr->data;

}

}

Pitfall

The original notes looped for i in range(1, k-2), which takes k - 3 steps and deletes the wrong node for every k > 2. Count the steps on paper: from node 1, reaching node k-1 is exactly k - 2 hops. The code also assumes k ≤ length; add a length check (or stop when curr.next == head) for untrusted input.

Interview Q&A
How do you detect that a linked list is circular?

Traverse with a fast pointer moving two steps and a slow pointer moving one (Floyd's cycle detection). In a circular list they eventually meet; in a normal list fast reaches None. O(n) time, O(1) space — a visited-set would also work but costs O(n) memory.

Why keep a tail pointer rather than a head pointer in a circular list?

Because tail.next is the head. With the tail you can insert at the front (new.next = tail.next; tail.next = new), insert at the back (same, then tail = new) and delete the front, all in O(1), without the value-swapping trick. Queues built on circular lists do exactly this.

Where are circular linked lists used in practice?

Round-robin CPU scheduling, turn order in games, circular buffers for streaming data, Fibonacci heaps (the root list is circular doubly linked), and the Josephus problem — every k-th person around a circle is eliminated until one remains.

What goes wrong if you forget the single-node case?

A one-node circular list has head.next == head. A delete_head that does head.next = head.next.next would leave the node pointing at itself and return it — the list never becomes empty. Always test the empty, one-node and two-node lists.

Linked Lists

Doubly Linked List

A doubly linked list gives every node a prev pointer in addition to next, so the list can be walked in both directions and any node can be removed in O(1) given only a reference to it. It costs one extra pointer per node and a little more bookkeeping.

Doubly linked list — a linked list whose nodes hold data, next (the following node) and prev (the preceding node). The head's prev and the tail's next are None. Every link is mirrored: a.next == b always implies b.prev == a.

A doubly linked list: every node knows both its neighbours
         head                                                   tail
          ↓                                                       ↓
     ┌────┬──────┬────┐     ┌────┬──────┬────┐     ┌────┬──────┬────┐
∅ ◀──┼ ●  │  10  │ ●──┼────▶│ ●  │  20  │ ●──┼────▶│ ●  │  30  │ ●──┼──▶ ∅
     └────┴──────┴────┘◀────┼─●  │      │    │◀────┼─●  │      │    │
      prev  data  next      └────┴──────┴────┘     └────┴──────┴────┘

None <-> 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 <-> None
Structure of a node and traversal in both directions

Linking two nodes now means setting two pointers: a.next = b and b.prev = a. Forgetting one of them is the classic doubly-linked bug — the list looks fine going forward and breaks going backward. Traversal backwards starts from the last node and follows prev.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def show(head):
    parts, curr, last = [], head, None
    while curr is not None:
        parts.append(str(curr.data))
        last = curr                          # remember the tail for the way back
        curr = curr.next
    print("forward:", " <-> ".join(parts))
    parts, curr = [], last
    while curr is not None:                  # walk back along prev
        parts.append(str(curr.data))
        curr = curr.prev
    print("backward:", " <-> ".join(parts))

head = Node(10); temp1 = Node(20); temp2 = Node(30)
head.next = temp1;  temp1.prev = head        # every link is set in both directions
temp1.next = temp2; temp2.prev = temp1
show(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* prev; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {}
};

void show(Node* head) {
    Node* last = nullptr;
    cout << "forward:";
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next) {
        cout << (curr == head ? " " : " <-> ") << curr->data;
        last = curr;                             // remember the tail for the way back
    }
    cout << "\nbackward:";
    for (Node* curr = last; curr; curr = curr->prev)   // walk back along prev
        cout << (curr == last ? " " : " <-> ") << curr->data;
    cout << "\n";
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); Node* temp1 = new Node(20); Node* temp2 = new Node(30);
    head->next = temp1;  temp1->prev = head;     // every link is set in both directions
    temp1->next = temp2; temp2->prev = temp1;
    show(head);
}

Advantages and disadvantages

Traversal in both directions

Walk forward with next, backward with prev — browsers' back/forward history, text editor cursors, undo/redo.

Delete a node in O(1) given its reference

node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev. A singly linked list would first need an O(n) walk to find the predecessor.

Insert / delete before a given node

The predecessor is one pointer away, so inserting before is as cheap as inserting after.

O(1) at both ends with a tail

Keeping tail makes insert and delete at both ends O(1) — the basis of deque and the LRU cache.

Extra space

A second pointer per node: 16 bytes of links per element on a 64-bit machine.

More complex code

Every operation updates up to four pointers and must keep prev/next consistent; more special cases for the head and tail.

OperationSingly linkedDoubly linkedWhy the difference
Insert at beginningO(1)O(1)Both just re-point the head; doubly also sets the old head's prev.
Insert at endO(n) / O(1) with tailO(n) / O(1) with tailSame walk unless a tail is kept.
Delete headO(1)O(1)Doubly also clears the new head's prev.
Delete lastO(n) even with tailO(1) with tailThe tail's prev gives the new last node for free.
Delete a given nodeO(n)O(1)The predecessor is node.prev; singly must search for it.
Insert before a given nodeO(n)O(1)Same reason.
ReverseO(n)O(n)Doubly: swap prev and next in every node.
Insert at the beginning
Example

Input: list = 10 <-> 20 <-> 30, insert 5 at the beginning
Output: 5 <-> 10 <-> 20 <-> 30

Idea

Point the new node's next at the old head, point the old head's prev back at the new node, and return the new node as head. Two pointer writes — O(1). The empty list needs a guard: there is no old head whose prev could be set (the original notes crashed on this case).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def insert_at_beginning(head, data):
    temp = Node(data)
    temp.next = head                 # new → old head
    if head is not None:
        head.prev = temp             # old head → new (guard the empty list)
    return temp

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data)); head = head.next
    print(" <-> ".join(parts))

head = Node(10); t1 = Node(20); t2 = Node(30)
head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1
show(head)
head = insert_at_beginning(head, 5); show(head)
head = insert_at_beginning(head, 1); show(head)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* prev; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* insertAtBeginning(Node* head, int data) {
    Node* temp = new Node(data);
    temp->next = head;               // new → old head
    if (head) head->prev = temp;     // old head → new (guard the empty list)
    return temp;
}

void show(Node* head) {
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << head->data << (head->next ? " <-> " : "\n");
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); Node* t1 = new Node(20); Node* t2 = new Node(30);
    head->next = t1; t1->prev = head; t1->next = t2; t2->prev = t1;
    show(head);
    head = insertAtBeginning(head, 5); show(head);
    head = insertAtBeginning(head, 1); show(head);
}

Insert at the end
Example

Input: list = 10 <-> 20 <-> 30, insert 40 at the end
Output: 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 <-> 40
Input: list = empty, insert 40
Output: 40

Idea

Walk to the last node, link it forward to the new node and link the new node back with prev. O(n) because of the walk; a class that stores tail does the same two writes in O(1).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def insert_end(head, x):
    temp = Node(x)
    if head is None:
        return temp                      # empty list: new node is the head
    curr = head
    while curr.next is not None:         # O(n) walk to the last node
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = temp                     # last → new
    temp.prev = curr                     # new → last
    return head

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data)); head = head.next
    print(" <-> ".join(parts))

head = Node(10); t1 = Node(20); t2 = Node(30)
head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1
head = insert_end(head, 40); show(head)
empty = insert_end(None, 40); show(empty)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* prev; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* insertEnd(Node* head, int x) {
    Node* temp = new Node(x);
    if (!head) return temp;                  // empty list: new node is the head
    Node* curr = head;
    while (curr->next) curr = curr->next;    // O(n) walk to the last node
    curr->next = temp;                       // last → new
    temp->prev = curr;                       // new → last
    return head;
}

void show(Node* head) {
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << head->data << (head->next ? " <-> " : "\n");
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); Node* t1 = new Node(20); Node* t2 = new Node(30);

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node prev, next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node insertEnd(Node head, int x) {
        Node temp = new Node(x);
        if (head == null) return temp;               // empty list: new node is the head
        Node curr = head;
        while (curr.next != null) curr = curr.next;  // O(n) walk to the last node
        curr.next = temp;                            // last → new
        temp.prev = curr;                            // new → last
        return head;
    }

    static void show(Node head) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (; head != null; head = head.next) sb.append(head.data).append(head.next != null ? " <-> " : "");
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node head = new Node(10), t1 = new Node(20), t2 = new Node(30);
        head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1;
        head = insertEnd(head, 40); show(head);
        Node empty = insertEnd(null, 40); show(empty);
    }
}

Delete the head
Example

Input: list = 10 <-> 20 <-> 30
Output: 20 <-> 30
Input: list = 10
Output: empty

Idea

Move the head to the second node and clear its prev — without that step the new head would still point back at a node that is no longer in the list. A one-node list becomes empty.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def delete_head(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return None                      # 0 or 1 node → empty
    head = head.next
    head.prev = None                     # the new head has no predecessor
    return head

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data)); head = head.next
    print(" <-> ".join(parts) if parts else "empty")

head = Node(10); t1 = Node(20); t2 = Node(30)
head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1
for _ in range(3):

    print("after delete head: ", end=""); show(head)
