Delete the last node
Example

Input: list = 10 <-> 20 <-> 30
Output: 10 <-> 20
Input: list = 10
Output: empty

Idea

Walk to the last node and cut it off via last.prev.next = None. Thanks to prev the predecessor is one hop away; the only O(n) part is reaching the last node, which disappears when a tail pointer is kept — the operation a singly linked list cannot do in O(1) even with a tail.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def delete_last(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return None                      # 0 or 1 node → empty
    curr = head
    while curr.next is not None:         # walk to the last node (O(1) with a tail pointer)
        curr = curr.next
    curr.prev.next = None                # predecessor is one hop away via prev
    return head

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data)); head = head.next
    print(" <-> ".join(parts) if parts else "empty")

head = Node(10); t1 = Node(20); t2 = Node(30)
head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1

    print("after delete last: ", end=""); show(head)

Delete a node given its reference
Example

Input: list = 10 <-> 20 <-> 30, node = the node holding 20
Output: 10 <-> 30

Idea

This is the operation that justifies the extra pointer. With node.prev and node.next both known, unlink in O(1): the predecessor's next skips to the successor and the successor's prev skips back to the predecessor. Guard the ends: if node is the head there is no predecessor (the head moves), if it is the tail there is no successor.

Deleting a node in O(1): two pointer writes on its neighbours
before:   [10] ◀──▶ [20] ◀──▶ [30]
                    node

node.prev.next = node.next     [10] ───────▶ [30]       (10's next skips 20)
node.next.prev = node.prev     [10] ◀─────── [30]       (30's prev skips 20)

after:    [10] ◀──▶ [30]
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def delete_node(head, node):
    if node.prev is not None:
        node.prev.next = node.next       # predecessor skips over node
    else:
        head = node.next                 # node was the head
    if node.next is not None:
        node.next.prev = node.prev       # successor skips back over node
    return head

def show(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data)); head = head.next
    print(" <-> ".join(parts) if parts else "empty")

head = Node(10); t1 = Node(20); t2 = Node(30)
head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1
show(head)
head = delete_node(head, t1); print("delete node 20: ", end=""); show(head)
head = delete_node(head, head); print("delete node 10 (head): ", end=""); show(head)

    else head = node->next;                          // node was the head

Key point

This is exactly how an LRU cache evicts and promotes entries: a hash map gives the node for a key in O(1), and the doubly linked list moves that node to the front in O(1). Neither structure alone can do both.

Reverse a doubly linked list
Example

Input: list = 10 <-> 20 <-> 30
Output: 30 <-> 20 <-> 10

Idea

Reversing means every node's next becomes its prev and vice versa — so swap the two pointers in each node. After the swap, the old next is reachable as curr.prev, which is how the loop advances. The last node visited is the new head.

1
Walk the list
curr = head, remembering the node just processed in prev.
2
Swap in place
curr.next, curr.prev = curr.prev, curr.next.
3
Advance
curr = curr.prev — that field now holds the old next.
4
Finish
When curr is None, prev is the last node processed: the new head.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def reverse_dll(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr is not None:
        prev = curr
        curr.next, curr.prev = curr.prev, curr.next   # swap the two links
        curr = curr.prev                              # old next now lives in prev
    return prev                                       # last node processed = new head

def show(label, head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data)); head = head.next
    print(label + ":", " <-> ".join(parts))

head = Node(10); t1 = Node(20); t2 = Node(30)
head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1
show("forward", head)
head = reverse_dll(head); show("reversed", head)
head = reverse_dll(head); show("back again", head)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* prev; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* reverseDLL(Node* head) {
    Node* prev = nullptr;
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->prev) {   // after the swap, prev holds the old next
        prev = curr;
        swap(curr->next, curr->prev);                      // swap the two links
    }
    return prev;                                           // last node processed = new head
}

void show(const char* label, Node* head) {
    cout << label << ":";
    for (; head; head = head->next) cout << " " << head->data << (head->next ? " <->" : "");
    cout << "\n";
}

int main() {
    Node* head = new Node(10); Node* t1 = new Node(20); Node* t2 = new Node(30);
    head->next = t1; t1->prev = head; t1->next = t2; t2->prev = t1;
    show("forward", head);
    head = reverseDLL(head); show("reversed", head);
    head = reverseDLL(head); show("back again", head);
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node prev, next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node reverseDLL(Node head) {
        Node prev = null;
        for (Node curr = head; curr != null; curr = curr.prev) {   // after the swap, prev holds the old next
            prev = curr;
            Node t = curr.next; curr.next = curr.prev; curr.prev = t;   // swap the two links
        }
        return prev;                                               // last node processed = new head
    }

    static void show(String label, Node head) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(label + ":");
        for (; head != null; head = head.next) sb.append(" ").append(head.data).append(head.next != null ? " <->" : "");
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node head = new Node(10), t1 = new Node(20), t2 = new Node(30);
        head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1;
        show("forward", head);
        head = reverseDLL(head); show("reversed", head);
        head = reverseDLL(head); show("back again", head);
    }
}

class Node {
    constructor(data) { this.data = data; this.prev = null; this.next = null; }
}

function reverseDLL(head) {
    let prev = null;
    for (let curr = head; curr !== null; curr = curr.prev) {   // after the swap, prev holds the old next
        prev = curr;
        [curr.next, curr.prev] = [curr.prev, curr.next];        // swap the two links
    }
    return prev;                                                // last node processed = new head
}

function show(label, head) {
    const parts = [];
    for (; head !== null; head = head.next) parts.push(head.data);
    console.log(label + ":", parts.join(" <-> "));
}

head.next = t1; t1.prev = head; t1.next = t2; t2.prev = t1;

head = reverseDLL(head); show("reversed", head);

reversed: 30 <-> 20 <-> 10

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Advancing with curr = curr.next after the swap walks backwards into the part already reversed and loops forever (or stops after one node). The old next is in curr.prev once the swap has happened.

Interview Q&A
What does the extra prev pointer buy you?

O(1) deletion of a node you hold a reference to, O(1) insertion before a node, O(1) removal from the tail (with a tail pointer) and backward traversal. The price is one more pointer per node and twice as many links to keep consistent.

How does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list?

Entries are nodes ordered from most to least recently used; a hash map points from each key to its node. On access, the node is unlinked in O(1) (possible only because of prev) and re-inserted at the front. On eviction the tail node is removed in O(1). All operations are O(1).

Singly vs doubly linked list — how do you choose?

Singly when you only move forward and operate at the head (stacks, hash chains, adjacency lists) — it is smaller and simpler. Doubly when you need deletions in the middle by reference, both-end operations (deques) or backward iteration. Java's LinkedList and C++ std::list are doubly linked; std::forward_list is singly linked.

How would you reverse a doubly linked list?

Swap next and prev in every node and return the last node visited. One pass, no extra memory. Because the old next ends up in prev, the loop advances with curr = curr.prev.

What is an XOR linked list?

A memory-saving trick: each node stores prev XOR next in a single field. Walking forward from a known predecessor, next = stored XOR prev. It halves the pointer overhead but defeats garbage collectors and makes the code fragile — an interview curiosity rather than a production structure.

Stacks & Queues

Stack

A stack is a Last In, First Out (LIFO) collection: you can only add to or remove from one end, the top. It is the data structure behind function calls, undo, bracket matching and expression evaluation.

Stack — a linear data structure where insertion (push) and deletion (pop) happen at the same end, called the top. The element pushed last is popped first.

A stack after push(10), push(20), push(30), push(40)
push(40)  →   ┌────┐  ← top        pop()  →  returns 40
              │ 40 │
              ├────┤
              │ 30 │
              ├────┤
              │ 20 │
              ├────┤
              │ 10 │  ← bottom
              └────┘
Operations
OperationWhat it doesTime
push(x)Insert x at the topO(1)
pop()Remove and return the top elementO(1)
peek() / top()Return the top element without removing itO(1)
isEmpty()true when the stack has no elementsO(1)
size()Number of elementsO(1)
Watch out

Underflow — calling pop() or peek() on an empty stack. Overflow — calling push() on a fixed-capacity stack that is full. Always check isEmpty() before popping; the built-in containers below raise an error (Python/Java) or return undefined (JavaScript) instead.

Using the built-in containers

Every language already has a container that works as a stack. Use the end of a dynamic array (append / pop at the back are amortised O(1)) — never the front, where every operation shifts all elements.

Python
stack = []                 # a list used as a stack
stack.append('a')          # push
stack.append('b')
stack.append('c')
print("top:", stack[-1])   # peek
print("popped:", stack.pop())
print("popped:", stack.pop())
print("size:", len(stack))
print("empty:", len(stack) == 0)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    stack<char> st;            // std::stack adapts a deque
    st.push('a');
    st.push('b');
    st.push('c');
    cout << "top: " << st.top() << "\n";
    cout << "popped: " << st.top() << "\n"; st.pop();   // pop() returns nothing in C++
    cout << "popped: " << st.top() << "\n"; st.pop();
    cout << "size: " << st.size() << "\n";
    cout << "empty: " << (st.empty() ? "True" : "False") << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();   // preferred over the legacy java.util.Stack
        stack.push('a');
        stack.push('b');
        stack.push('c');
        System.out.println("top: " + stack.peek());
        System.out.println("popped: " + stack.pop());
        System.out.println("popped: " + stack.pop());
        System.out.println("size: " + stack.size());
        System.out.println("empty: " + (stack.isEmpty() ? "True" : "False"));
    }
}

Key point

Python's collections.deque and queue.LifoQueue also work as stacks. deque is the right choice when the same container must also behave as a queue; LifoQueue is thread-safe and meant for producer/consumer code, not for algorithms.

Implementing a stack with a linked list

Pushing and popping at the head of a singly linked list are both O(1), so a linked list gives a stack that never needs resizing. The head node is the top.

push(10), push(20), push(30) — the newest node becomes the head
top
 ↓
┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐
│ 30 │ ●─┼──▶│ 20 │ ●─┼──▶│ 10 │ ∅ │
└────┴───┘   └────┴───┘   └────┴───┘
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

class Stack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None
        self.size = 0

    def push(self, value):
        node = Node(value)
        node.next = self.head      # new node points at the old top
        self.head = node
        self.size += 1

    def pop(self):
        if self.head is None:
            raise IndexError("pop from empty stack")
        node = self.head
        self.head = node.next
        self.size -= 1
        return node.value

    def peek(self):
        return None if self.head is None else self.head.value

    def is_empty(self):
        return self.head is None

s = Stack()
for x in (10, 20, 30):
    s.push(x)
node = s.head
while node:                      # print top → bottom
    print(node.value, end=" ")
    node = node.next
print()
print("size:", s.size)
print("popped:", s.pop())
print("peek:", s.peek())
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int value;
    Node* next;
    Node(int v) : value(v), next(nullptr) {}
};

class Stack {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    int count = 0;
public:
    ~Stack() { while (head) pop(); }
    void push(int v) {
        Node* node = new Node(v);
        node->next = head;           // new node points at the old top
        head = node;
        count++;
    }
    int pop() {
        if (!head) throw runtime_error("pop from empty stack");
        Node* node = head;
        int v = node->value;
        head = node->next;
        delete node;
        count--;
        return v;
    }
    int peek() const { return head->value; }
    bool isEmpty() const { return head == nullptr; }
    int size() const { return count; }
    Node* top() const { return head; }
};

int main() {
    Stack s;
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30}) s.push(x);
    for (Node* n = s.top(); n; n = n->next) cout << n->value << " ";
    cout << "\n";
    cout << "size: " << s.size() << "\n";
    cout << "popped: " << s.pop() << "\n";
    cout << "peek: " << s.peek() << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int value; Node next;
        Node(int v) { value = v; }
    }

    static class Stack {
        Node head; int size;
        void push(int v) {
            Node node = new Node(v);
            node.next = head;            // new node points at the old top
            head = node;
            size++;
        }
        int pop() {
            if (head == null) throw new RuntimeException("pop from empty stack");
            int v = head.value;
            head = head.next;
            size--;
            return v;
        }
        Integer peek() { return head == null ? null : head.value; }
        boolean isEmpty() { return head == null; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Stack s = new Stack();
        for (int x : new int[]{10, 20, 30}) s.push(x);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Node n = s.head; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.value).append(' ');
        System.out.println(sb.toString().trim());
        System.out.println("size: " + s.size);
        System.out.println("popped: " + s.pop());
        System.out.println("peek: " + s.peek());
    }
}

class Stack {

        node.next = this.head;           // new node points at the old top
        this.head = node;
        this.size++;
    }
    pop() {
        if (!this.head) throw new Error("pop from empty stack");
        const node = this.head;
        this.head = node.next;
        this.size--;
        return node.value;
    }
    peek() { return this.head ? this.head.value : null; }
    isEmpty() { return this.head === null; }
}

Where stacks are used

Function calls

The call stack stores one frame per active call; returning pops it. Deep recursion overflows it.

Balanced brackets

Push every opener, pop on every closer and check that it matches — see below.

Undo / redo, back / forward

Each action is pushed; undo pops it onto a second stack for redo.

Expression evaluation

Infix → postfix conversion and postfix evaluation both run on a stack.

Reversing

Push everything, then pop everything — the order reverses.

Monotonic stack problems

Next greater element, stock span, histogram area (DSA Advanced → Stack).

Problem: check for balanced parentheses
Example

Input: s = "([])"
Output: Yes
Input: s = "([)]"
Output: No
Input: s = "(("
Output: No

Idea

Scan left to right. Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener — pop it. At the end the stack must be empty. Any violation means the string is unbalanced.

1
Opening bracket
Push it onto the stack.
2
Closing bracket
If the stack is empty → unbalanced. Pop the top; if it is not the matching opener → unbalanced.
3
End of string
Balanced only if the stack is empty (every opener was closed).
Python
def is_balanced(s):
    match = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in '([{':
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in match:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != match[ch]:
                return False
    return not stack

for s in ["([])", "([)]", "((", "{[()]}"]:
    print(s, "→", "Yes" if is_balanced(s) else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

bool isBalanced(const string& s) {
    stack<char> st;
    for (char ch : s) {
        if (ch == '(' || ch == '[' || ch == '{') {
            st.push(ch);
        } else {
            if (st.empty()) return false;
            char open = st.top(); st.pop();
            if ((ch == ')' && open != '(') || (ch == ']' && open != '[') || (ch == '}' && open != '{'))
                return false;
        }
    }
    return st.empty();
}

int main() {
    for (string s : {"([])", "([)]", "((", "{[()]}"})
        cout << s << " → " << (isBalanced(s) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static boolean isBalanced(String s) {
        Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (ch == '(' || ch == '[' || ch == '{') {
                stack.push(ch);
            } else {
                if (stack.isEmpty()) return false;
                char open = stack.pop();
                if ((ch == ')' && open != '(') || (ch == ']' && open != '[') || (ch == '}' && open != '{'))
                    return false;
            }
        }
        return stack.isEmpty();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[]{"([])", "([)]", "((", "{[()]}"})
            System.out.println(s + " → " + (isBalanced(s) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}
JavaScript
function isBalanced(s) {
    const match = { ')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{' };
    const stack = [];
    for (const ch of s) {
        if ('([{'.includes(ch)) {
            stack.push(ch);
        } else if (ch in match) {
            if (!stack.length || stack.pop() !== match[ch]) return false;
        }
    }
    return stack.length === 0;
}

for (const s of ["([])", "([)]", "((", "{[()]}"])
    console.log(s, "→", isBalanced(s) ? "Yes" : "No");
Output

([)] → No
(( → No
{[()]} → Yes
Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

Forgetting the final stack is empty check accepts "(("; forgetting the empty before pop check crashes on ")". Both are classic interview slips.

Interview Q&A
Array or linked list for a stack — which is better?

Both give O(1) push/pop. An array (dynamic) is cache-friendly and usually faster; occasionally a push triggers an O(n) resize, but the amortised cost stays O(1). A linked list never resizes and has no capacity limit, at the price of one pointer per element and scattered memory.

What is stack overflow in the context of recursion?

Every call pushes a frame on the call stack. Recursion that goes too deep (no base case, or a very large input) exhausts the stack's fixed size — Python raises RecursionError at about 1000 frames; C++ and Java crash with a stack overflow. Convert to iteration or use an explicit stack when depth can be large.

How would you implement a queue using two stacks?

Push into stack in. To dequeue, if out is empty, pop everything from in and push onto out (this reverses the order), then pop from out. Each element moves at most twice, so operations are amortised O(1). See the Queue topic.

Stacks & Queues

Queue

A queue is a First In, First Out (FIFO) collection: elements enter at the rear and leave from the front, exactly like a line at a ticket counter. It is the data structure behind scheduling, buffering and breadth-first search.

Queue — a linear data structure where insertion (enqueue) happens at one end, the rear, and deletion (dequeue) happens at the other end, the front. The element that has waited longest is served first.

A queue after enqueue(10), enqueue(15), enqueue(20), enqueue(30), enqueue(40) — 10 leaves first
dequeue()  ◀──  ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐  ◀──  enqueue(x)
                │ 10 │ 15 │ 20 │ 30 │ 40 │
                └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
                  ↑                   ↑
                front               rear
Operations
OperationWhat it doesTime
enqueue(x)Insert x at the rearO(1)
dequeue()Remove and return the front elementO(1)
front() / getFront()Return the front element without removing itO(1)
rear() / getRear()Return the rear element without removing itO(1)
isEmpty()true when the queue has no elementsO(1)
size()Number of elementsO(1)

Every operation is O(1) — provided the implementation is right. A plain array where dequeue removes index 0 is the classic way to get this wrong: every remaining element shifts one slot left, so dequeue becomes O(n). The circular-array section below fixes that.

Watch out

Underflow — dequeue() or front() on an empty queue. Overflow — enqueue() on a fixed-capacity queue that is full. Check isEmpty() / isFull() first; the built-in containers raise (Python/C++ UB/Java remove) or return null/undefined (Java poll, JavaScript shift).

Where queues are used

One resource, many consumers

Ticket counters, printer spooling, a single CPU shared by many processes — whoever asked first is served first.

Buffers between fast and slow devices

The keyboard buffer, network sockets and audio/video pipelines queue data produced faster than it is consumed.

Operating systems

FCFS (first-come, first-served) scheduling, semaphore wait lists, I/O request queues, spooling.

Networks and messaging

Routers and switches queue packets; mail servers and message brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka) queue jobs.

Breadth-first search

BFS on graphs and level-order traversal of trees visit nodes in the order they were discovered — a queue (see Trees and Graphs).

Variations

Deque (both ends), priority queue (served by priority, not arrival), double-ended priority queue (min and max).

Using the built-in containers

Every language ships a ready-made queue. The rule is the same everywhere: add at the back, remove at the front, and make sure removing at the front is O(1).

Python
from collections import deque

q = deque()                       # O(1) at both ends
q.append(10)                      # enqueue at the rear
q.append(20)
q.append(30)
print("front:", q[0])
print("rear:", q[-1])
print("dequeued:", q.popleft())   # dequeue from the front
print("dequeued:", q.popleft())
print("size:", len(q))
print("empty:", len(q) == 0)

#include <queue>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    queue<int> q;                 // std::queue adapts a std::deque
    q.push(10);                   // enqueue at the back
    q.push(20);
    q.push(30);
    cout << "front: " << q.front() << "\n";
    cout << "rear: " << q.back() << "\n";
    cout << "dequeued: " << q.front() << "\n"; q.pop();   // pop() returns nothing in C++

}

Pitfall

Using a Python list as a queue. q.pop(0) shifts every remaining element, so a loop that dequeues n items costs O(n²). The notes' original list version is shown below only to make the point — reach for collections.deque.

Python
q = []
q.append(10)
q.append(20)
q.append(30)
print(q)          # [10, 20, 30]
print(q.pop(0))   # 10   ← removes the front, but shifts 20 and 30 left: O(n)
print(q)          # [20, 30]
q.pop(0)
print(q)          # [30]
Key point

queue.Queue is for threads: get() blocks until an item arrives, so calling it on an empty queue in single-threaded code hangs the program. Use get_nowait() / put_nowait() if you must use it outside a producer/consumer setting.

Python
from queue import Queue

q = Queue()
q.put(10)
q.put(20)
print(q.get())            # 10
print(q.qsize())          # 1
print(q.empty())          # False
print(q.get_nowait())     # 20
Implementing a queue with a linked list

Keep two pointers: front (the head, where we dequeue) and rear (the tail, where we enqueue). Appending at the tail and removing at the head of a singly linked list are both O(1), and the queue never needs resizing.

enqueue(10), enqueue(20), enqueue(30) — the oldest node is the head
front                                   rear
 ↓                                       ↓
┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐
│ 10 │ ●─┼──▶│ 20 │ ●─┼──▶│ 30 │ ∅ │   enqueue(40): rear.next = node, rear = node
└────┴───┘   └────┴───┘   └────┴───┘   dequeue():   front = front.next
1
enqueue(x)
Create a node. If the queue is empty, front = rear = node; otherwise rear.next = node and rear = node.
2
dequeue()
Save front.value, move front = front.next. If front became null, also set rear = null — the classic bug is leaving rear pointing at the freed node.
3
getFront / getRear
Read front.value / rear.value — O(1) because we keep both pointers.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

class Queue:
    def __init__(self):
        self.front = None        # dequeue here (head)
        self.rear = None         # enqueue here (tail)
        self.size = 0

    def enqueue(self, value):
        node = Node(value)
        if self.rear is None:            # empty: the node is both front and rear
            self.front = self.rear = node
        else:
            self.rear.next = node        # link after the old tail
            self.rear = node
        self.size += 1

    def dequeue(self):
        if self.front is None:
            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")
        node = self.front
        self.front = node.next
        if self.front is None:           # became empty: rear must not dangle
            self.rear = None
        self.size -= 1
        return node.value

    def get_front(self):
        return None if self.front is None else self.front.value

    def get_rear(self):
        return None if self.rear is None else self.rear.value

    def is_empty(self):
        return self.size == 0

q = Queue()
for x in (10, 20, 30):
    q.enqueue(x)
print("front:", q.get_front())
print("rear:", q.get_rear())
print("dequeued:", q.dequeue())
print("front:", q.get_front())
print("rear:", q.get_rear())
print("size:", q.size)
print("empty:", q.is_empty())
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int value;
    Node* next;
    Node(int v) : value(v), next(nullptr) {}
};

class Queue {
    Node* front = nullptr;     // dequeue here (head)
    Node* rear = nullptr;      // enqueue here (tail)
    int count = 0;
public:
    ~Queue() { while (front) dequeue(); }
    void enqueue(int v) {
        Node* node = new Node(v);
        if (!rear) front = rear = node;          // empty: the node is both front and rear
        else { rear->next = node; rear = node; } // link after the old tail
        count++;
    }
    int dequeue() {
        if (!front) throw runtime_error("dequeue from empty queue");
        Node* node = front;
        int v = node->value;
        front = node->next;
        if (!front) rear = nullptr;              // became empty: rear must not dangle
        delete node;
        count--;
        return v;
    }
    int getFront() const { return front->value; }
    int getRear() const { return rear->value; }
    bool isEmpty() const { return count == 0; }
    int size() const { return count; }
};

int main() {
    Queue q;
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30}) q.enqueue(x);
    cout << "front: " << q.getFront() << "\n";
    cout << "rear: " << q.getRear() << "\n";
    cout << "dequeued: " << q.dequeue() << "\n";
    cout << "front: " << q.getFront() << "\n";
    cout << "rear: " << q.getRear() << "\n";
    cout << "size: " << q.size() << "\n";
    cout << "empty: " << (q.isEmpty() ? "True" : "False") << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int value; Node next;
        Node(int v) { value = v; }
    }

    static class Queue {
        Node front, rear;          // dequeue at front (head), enqueue at rear (tail)
        int size;
        void enqueue(int v) {
            Node node = new Node(v);
            if (rear == null) front = rear = node;      // empty: the node is both front and rear
            else { rear.next = node; rear = node; }     // link after the old tail
            size++;
        }
        int dequeue() {
            if (front == null) throw new RuntimeException("dequeue from empty queue");
            int v = front.value;
            front = front.next;
            if (front == null) rear = null;             // became empty: rear must not dangle
            size--;
            return v;
        }
        Integer getFront() { return front == null ? null : front.value; }
        Integer getRear() { return rear == null ? null : rear.value; }
        boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Queue q = new Queue();
        for (int x : new int[]{10, 20, 30}) q.enqueue(x);
        System.out.println("front: " + q.getFront());
        System.out.println("rear: " + q.getRear());
        System.out.println("dequeued: " + q.dequeue());
        System.out.println("front: " + q.getFront());
        System.out.println("rear: " + q.getRear());
        System.out.println("size: " + q.size);
        System.out.println("empty: " + (q.isEmpty() ? "True" : "False"));

JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(value) { this.value = value; this.next = null; }
}

class Queue {
    constructor() { this.front = null; this.rear = null; this.size = 0; }
    enqueue(value) {
        const node = new Node(value);
        if (this.rear === null) this.front = this.rear = node;   // empty: both ends
        else { this.rear.next = node; this.rear = node; }        // link after the old tail
        this.size++;
    }
    dequeue() {
        if (this.front === null) throw new Error("dequeue from empty queue");
        const node = this.front;
        this.front = node.next;
        if (this.front === null) this.rear = null;               // became empty: rear must not dangle
        this.size--;
        return node.value;
    }
    getFront() { return this.front ? this.front.value : null; }
    getRear() { return this.rear ? this.rear.value : null; }
    isEmpty() { return this.size === 0; }
}

Pitfall

Enqueueing at the head and dequeueing at the tail would need the node before the tail, which a singly linked list cannot reach in O(1). Always enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head.

Implementing a queue with a circular array

A fixed array of capacity cap has two naive designs, and both are bad. If dequeue removes slots[0] and shifts everything, it is O(n). If instead it just advances a front index, each dequeue leaves a dead slot behind: after a few dequeues rear reaches the end and enqueue fails even though the array is half empty.

Advancing front without wrapping wastes every slot that has been dequeued
Plain array, dequeue by advancing front (capacity 5):

  index:   0     1     2     3     4
        ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
        │  ×  │  ×  │ 30  │ 40  │ 50  │   front = 2, rear = 5
        └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
           ↑ dead slots              ↑ rear is past the end:
                                       enqueue(60) fails although two slots are free

The fix is to let both indices wrap around with the modulo operator: rear = (rear + 1) % cap and front = (front + 1) % cap. The array is treated as a ring, so a dequeued slot is reused by the next enqueue.

The ring reuses the slots freed by dequeue; the logical order is read from front, wrapping with % cap
Circular array — same state, then enqueue(60), enqueue(70):

  index:   0     1     2     3     4
        ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
        │ 60  │ 70  │ 30  │ 40  │ 50  │   rear wrapped: 5 % 5 = 0, then 1
        └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
                       ↑ front = 2
           ↑ rear = 2 (next free slot) — equal to front, so size tells us: full

  logical order (front → rear):  30  40  50  60  70
Key point

When front == rear the ring is either empty or full — the indices alone cannot tell. Either keep a size counter (done below) or deliberately leave one slot unused and treat (rear + 1) % cap == front as full.

Example

Input: capacity = 5; enqueue 10 20 30 40 50; dequeue ×2; enqueue 60 70
Output: slots: 60 70 30 40 50 — logical order 30 40 50 60 70

Python
class CircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.slots = [None] * capacity
        self.cap = capacity
        self.front = 0          # index of the first element
        self.rear = 0           # index where the next element goes
        self.size = 0           # needed: front == rear for both empty and full

    def is_empty(self):
        return self.size == 0

    def is_full(self):
        return self.size == self.cap

    def enqueue(self, value):
        if self.is_full():
            raise OverflowError("queue is full")
        slot = self.rear
        self.slots[slot] = value
        self.rear = (self.rear + 1) % self.cap     # wrap around
        self.size += 1
        return slot

    def dequeue(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("queue is empty")
        value = self.slots[self.front]
        self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.cap   # wrap around
        self.size -= 1
        return value

    def get_front(self):
        return self.slots[self.front]

    def get_rear(self):
        return self.slots[(self.rear - 1 + self.cap) % self.cap]

q = CircularQueue(5)
for x in (10, 20, 30, 40, 50):
    q.enqueue(x)
print("front:", q.get_front())
print("rear:", q.get_rear())
print("full:", q.is_full())
print("dequeued:", q.dequeue())
print("dequeued:", q.dequeue())
print("enqueue 60 → slot", q.enqueue(60))
print("enqueue 70 → slot", q.enqueue(70))
print("slots:", *q.slots)
print("front =", q.front, "rear =", q.rear, "size =", q.size)
print("in order:", *(q.slots[(q.front + i) % q.cap] for i in range(q.size)))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class CircularQueue {
public:
    vector<int> slots;
    int cap, front = 0, rear = 0, size = 0;   // size: front == rear for both empty and full
    CircularQueue(int capacity) : slots(capacity, 0), cap(capacity) {}
    bool isEmpty() const { return size == 0; }
    bool isFull() const { return size == cap; }
    int enqueue(int value) {
        if (isFull()) throw runtime_error("queue is full");
        int slot = rear;
        slots[slot] = value;
        rear = (rear + 1) % cap;              // wrap around
        size++;
        return slot;
    }
    int dequeue() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw runtime_error("queue is empty");
        int value = slots[front];
        front = (front + 1) % cap;            // wrap around
        size--;
        return value;
    }
    int getFront() const { return slots[front]; }
    int getRear() const { return slots[(rear - 1 + cap) % cap]; }
};

int main() {
    CircularQueue q(5);
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}) q.enqueue(x);
    cout << "front: " << q.getFront() << "\n";
    cout << "rear: " << q.getRear() << "\n";
    cout << "full: " << (q.isFull() ? "True" : "False") << "\n";
    cout << "dequeued: " << q.dequeue() << "\n";
    cout << "dequeued: " << q.dequeue() << "\n";
    cout << "enqueue 60 → slot " << q.enqueue(60) << "\n";
    cout << "enqueue 70 → slot " << q.enqueue(70) << "\n";
    cout << "slots:";
    for (int v : q.slots) cout << " " << v;
    cout << "\n";
    cout << "front = " << q.front << " rear = " << q.rear << " size = " << q.size << "\n";
    cout << "in order:";
    for (int i = 0; i < q.size; i++) cout << " " << q.slots[(q.front + i) % q.cap];
    cout << "\n";
}

        return value;
    }

}

Pitfall

getRear() is not slots[rear - 1]: after a wrap rear can be 0, and index -1 is out of bounds in C++/Java (and silently the last element in Python). Use (rear - 1 + cap) % cap. Also note that a dequeued slot is not cleared — printing the raw array shows stale values until they are overwritten.

Key point

Dynamic-array queues (std::deque, Java ArrayDeque, Python deque) are circular buffers that double the capacity when full, so they never overflow: amortised O(1) enqueue.

Problem: implement a stack using queues
Example

Input: push(10), push(20), push(30), top(), pop(), top()
Output: 30, 30, 20

Idea

A queue gives you the oldest element; a stack needs the newest. Make push expensive: put the new element into an empty auxiliary queue, move everything else behind it, then swap the queues. The front of q1 is now always the most recently pushed element, so pop and top are plain O(1) queue operations.

1
push(x) — version 1
Move everything from q1 to q2, enqueue x into q1, move everything back from q2 to q1. Two full copies per push.
2
push(x) — optimised
Enqueue x into q2, move everything from q1 behind it, then swap q1 and q2. One copy per push, same effect.
3
pop() / top()
Dequeue / peek the front of q1 — O(1).
4
size() / isEmpty()
Delegate to q1; isFull() is always false for a dynamic queue.
The optimised push: the new element goes in first, older elements queue behind it
push(10):  q2 = [10]                 swap → q1 = [10]        q2 = []
push(20):  q2 = [20] ← move 10 →     q2 = [20 10]   swap → q1 = [20 10]
push(30):  q2 = [30] ← move 20 10 →  q2 = [30 20 10] swap → q1 = [30 20 10]
                                                              ↑ front = top of stack
Python
from collections import deque

class Stack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.q1 = deque()      # holds the items, newest at the front
        self.q2 = deque()      # auxiliary, empty between operations

    def push(self, x):
        self.q2.append(x)                      # a) x goes in first ...
        while self.q1:                         # b) ... then everything older behind it
            self.q2.append(self.q1.popleft())
        self.q1, self.q2 = self.q2, self.q1    # c) swap: q1 holds the items again

    def pop(self):
        return self.q1.popleft()               # front of q1 is the newest item

    def top(self):
        return self.q1[0]

    def size(self):
        return len(self.q1)

    def is_empty(self):
        return len(self.q1) == 0

s = Stack()
s.push(10)
s.push(20)
s.push(30)
print("top:", s.top())
print("popped:", s.pop())
print("top:", s.top())
print("size:", s.size())
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

class Stack {
    queue<int> q1, q2;         // q1 holds the items, newest at the front
public:
    void push(int x) {
        q2.push(x);                                            // a) x goes in first ...
        while (!q1.empty()) { q2.push(q1.front()); q1.pop(); } // b) ... older items behind it
        swap(q1, q2);                                          // c) q1 holds the items again
    }
    int pop() { int x = q1.front(); q1.pop(); return x; }     // front of q1 is the newest item
    int top() const { return q1.front(); }
    int size() const { return (int)q1.size(); }
    bool isEmpty() const { return q1.empty(); }
};

int main() {
    Stack s;
    s.push(10);
    s.push(20);
    s.push(30);
    cout << "top: " << s.top() << "\n";
    cout << "popped: " << s.pop() << "\n";
    cout << "top: " << s.top() << "\n";
    cout << "size: " << s.size() << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static class Stack {
        Queue<Integer> q1 = new ArrayDeque<>();   // holds the items, newest at the front
        Queue<Integer> q2 = new ArrayDeque<>();   // auxiliary
        void push(int x) {
            q2.offer(x);                                   // a) x goes in first ...
            while (!q1.isEmpty()) q2.offer(q1.poll());     // b) ... older items behind it
            Queue<Integer> tmp = q1; q1 = q2; q2 = tmp;    // c) swap
        }
        int pop() { return q1.poll(); }                    // front of q1 is the newest item
        int top() { return q1.peek(); }
        int size() { return q1.size(); }
        boolean isEmpty() { return q1.isEmpty(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Stack s = new Stack();
        s.push(10);
        s.push(20);
        s.push(30);
        System.out.println("top: " + s.top());
        System.out.println("popped: " + s.pop());
        System.out.println("top: " + s.top());
        System.out.println("size: " + s.size());
    }
}
JavaScript
class Stack {
    constructor() {
        this.q1 = [];          // holds the items, newest at the front
        this.q2 = [];          // auxiliary
    }
    push(x) {
        this.q2.push(x);                                   // a) x goes in first ...
        while (this.q1.length) this.q2.push(this.q1.shift()); // b) ... older items behind it
        [this.q1, this.q2] = [this.q2, this.q1];           // c) swap
    }
    pop() { return this.q1.shift(); }                      // front of q1 is the newest item
    top() { return this.q1[0]; }
    size() { return this.q1.length; }
    isEmpty() { return this.q1.length === 0; }
}

const s = new Stack();
s.push(10);
s.push(20);
s.push(30);

console.log("size:", s.size());

popped: 30
top: 20
size: 2
Time push O(n), pop/top O(1)Space O(n)
Key point

One queue is enough: enqueue x, then dequeue-and-re-enqueue the other size − 1 elements so x rotates to the front. Same O(n) push, no auxiliary queue. The mirror design — cheap push, O(n) pop that rotates all but the last element — is also valid; pick the one that matches which operation is more frequent.

Problem: implement a queue using two stacks
Example

Input: enqueue(10), enqueue(20), enqueue(30), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(40), front()
Output: 10, 20, 30

Idea

Two LIFO reversals make a FIFO. Push every new element onto inbox. To dequeue, pop from outbox; when outbox is empty, pour all of inbox into it first — popping and pushing reverses the order, so the oldest element ends up on top of outbox.

1
enqueue(x)
inbox.push(x) — O(1).
2
dequeue() / front()
If outbox is empty, move every element from inbox to outbox (pop one, push the other). Then pop / peek outbox.
3
Why not pour every time?
Only pour when outbox is empty. Elements already in outbox are older than anything in inbox, so the order stays correct, and each element is moved at most once.
Python
class Queue:
    def __init__(self):
        self.inbox = []        # enqueue pushes here
        self.outbox = []       # dequeue pops from here (reversed = FIFO order)

    def enqueue(self, x):
        self.inbox.append(x)

    def _pour(self):
        if not self.outbox:                    # only when outbox is empty
            while self.inbox:
                self.outbox.append(self.inbox.pop())

    def dequeue(self):
        self._pour()
        return self.outbox.pop()

    def front(self):
        self._pour()
        return self.outbox[-1]

    def size(self):
        return len(self.inbox) + len(self.outbox)

q = Queue()
for x in (10, 20, 30):
    q.enqueue(x)
print("front:", q.front())
print("dequeued:", q.dequeue())
print("dequeued:", q.dequeue())
q.enqueue(40)
print("front:", q.front())
print("size:", q.size())
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
using namespace std;

class Queue {
    stack<int> inbox, outbox;  // enqueue pushes to inbox; dequeue pops from outbox
    void pour() {
        if (outbox.empty())                              // only when outbox is empty
            while (!inbox.empty()) { outbox.push(inbox.top()); inbox.pop(); }
    }
public:
    void enqueue(int x) { inbox.push(x); }
    int dequeue() { pour(); int x = outbox.top(); outbox.pop(); return x; }
    int front() { pour(); return outbox.top(); }
    int size() const { return (int)(inbox.size() + outbox.size()); }
};

int main() {
    Queue q;
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30}) q.enqueue(x);
    cout << "front: " << q.front() << "\n";
    cout << "dequeued: " << q.dequeue() << "\n";
    cout << "dequeued: " << q.dequeue() << "\n";
    q.enqueue(40);
    cout << "front: " << q.front() << "\n";
    cout << "size: " << q.size() << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static class Queue {
        Deque<Integer> inbox = new ArrayDeque<>();    // enqueue pushes here
        Deque<Integer> outbox = new ArrayDeque<>();   // dequeue pops from here
        void enqueue(int x) { inbox.push(x); }
        void pour() {
            if (outbox.isEmpty())                     // only when outbox is empty
                while (!inbox.isEmpty()) outbox.push(inbox.pop());
        }
        int dequeue() { pour(); return outbox.pop(); }
        int front() { pour(); return outbox.peek(); }
        int size() { return inbox.size() + outbox.size(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Queue q = new Queue();
        for (int x : new int[]{10, 20, 30}) q.enqueue(x);
        System.out.println("front: " + q.front());
        System.out.println("dequeued: " + q.dequeue());
        System.out.println("dequeued: " + q.dequeue());
        q.enqueue(40);
        System.out.println("front: " + q.front());
        System.out.println("size: " + q.size());
    }
}

class Queue {
    constructor() {
        this.inbox = [];       // enqueue pushes here
        this.outbox = [];      // dequeue pops from here (reversed = FIFO order)
    }
    enqueue(x) { this.inbox.push(x); }
    pour() {
        if (this.outbox.length === 0)                  // only when outbox is empty
            while (this.inbox.length) this.outbox.push(this.inbox.pop());
    }
    dequeue() { this.pour(); return this.outbox.pop(); }
    front() { this.pour(); return this.outbox[this.outbox.length - 1]; }
    size() { return this.inbox.length + this.outbox.length; }
}

Time amortised O(1) per operationSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Pouring inbox into outbox while outbox still has elements breaks the order: the poured (newer) elements would land on top of older ones. Pour only when outbox is empty. Each element is pushed and popped at most twice, which is why the amortised cost is O(1) even though one dequeue can be O(n).

Interview Q&A
Stack vs queue — when do you use which?

A stack (LIFO) when the most recent thing matters: function calls, undo, bracket matching, DFS. A queue (FIFO) when arrival order matters: scheduling, buffering, BFS / level-order traversal. Both have O(1) insert and remove; the only difference is which end you remove from.

Why is a circular array better than a plain array for a queue?

A plain array either shifts all elements on every dequeue (O(n)) or wastes every slot it has dequeued, failing with a full error while most of the array is empty. Wrapping front and rear with % capacity lets freed slots be reused, so every operation is O(1) and all capacity slots are usable.

In a circular queue front == rear — is it empty or full?

Either, so the indices alone are ambiguous. Two standard fixes: keep a size counter (empty when size == 0, full when size == capacity), or sacrifice one slot and declare the queue full when (rear + 1) % capacity == front.

Why not use a Python list or a JavaScript array as a queue?

list.pop(0) and Array.shift() remove the first element by shifting every other element left — O(n) per dequeue, O(n²) for a loop that drains the queue. Use collections.deque (O(1) popleft) in Python; in JavaScript write a small linked-list or two-pointer queue (or keep a head index into the array) for anything large, e.g. BFS over a big graph.

How do you implement a queue with two stacks, and what is the complexity?

Push into inbox. To dequeue, if outbox is empty pour everything from inbox into outbox (which reverses it), then pop outbox. A single dequeue can cost O(n), but each element is moved at most once, so n operations cost O(n) in total — amortised O(1).

What is a priority queue, and how does it differ from a queue?

A queue serves elements in arrival order; a priority queue serves the element with the highest (or lowest) priority first, regardless of arrival. It is normally built on a binary heap: O(log n) insert and remove-top, O(1) peek. A deque is a different variation — a queue that allows insertion and removal at both ends.

Stacks & Queues

Deque

A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced “deck”) lets you insert and delete at both ends in O(1). It is a stack and a queue in one container, and the workhorse behind sliding-window problems, undo histories and work-stealing schedulers.

Deque — a linear data structure that generalises the stack and the queue: elements can be added or removed at the front and at the rear, all in O(1). Access to the middle may or may not be supported depending on the implementation.

A deque is a queue whose both ends are open — restrict yourself to one pattern and you get a stack or a queue
insertFront(x) ──▶  ┌────┬────┬────┬────┐  ◀── insertRear(x)
deleteFront()  ◀──  │ 10 │ 20 │ 30 │ 40 │  ──▶ deleteRear()
                    └────┴────┴────┴────┘
                      ↑              ↑
                    front           rear

use only the rear  →  a stack   (push = insertRear, pop = deleteRear)
rear in, front out →  a queue   (enqueue = insertRear, dequeue = deleteFront)
Operations
OperationWhat it doesTime
insertFront(x)Add x before the current frontO(1)
insertRear(x)Add x after the current rearO(1)
deleteFront()Remove and return the front elementO(1)
deleteRear()Remove and return the rear elementO(1)
getFront() / getRear()Peek at either endO(1)
isEmpty() / isFull()Empty check; isFull() only for fixed-capacity dequesO(1)
size()Number of elementsO(1)

The same operations have different names in every library — this table is worth memorising, because it is also the stack and queue API of each language:

Python collections.dequeC++ std::dequeJava ArrayDeque (Deque<T>)JavaScript Array
insertFrontappendleft(x)push_front(x)offerFirst(x) / addFirst(x) / push(x)unshift(x) — O(n)
insertRearappend(x)push_back(x)offerLast(x) / addLast(x) / offer(x)push(x)
deleteFrontpopleft()pop_front()pollFirst() / removeFirst() / pop() / poll()shift() — O(n)
deleteRearpop()pop_back()pollLast() / removeLast()pop()
getFront / getReard[0] / d[-1]front() / back()peekFirst() / peekLast()a[0] / a[a.length - 1]
Watch out

JavaScript has no built-in deque. unshift() and shift() re-index the whole array, so they are O(n). For small inputs that is fine; for sliding windows over large arrays, implement a deque yourself (circular array or doubly linked list — both below) or keep two indices into a plain array.

Where deques are used

Stack and queue in one

A deque does everything both do, so one implementation (Python's deque, Java's ArrayDeque) serves as the standard stack and the standard queue.

History of actions

Browser history, undo buffers, “recently used” lists: push new actions at one end, drop the oldest from the other when the history is full (deque(maxlen=n) does this automatically).

Work-stealing schedulers

Each worker thread keeps its tasks in a deque: it pushes and pops at the rear (LIFO, cache-warm); idle threads steal from the front (the oldest, largest tasks). Used by Java's ForkJoinPool and Go's runtime.

Two-level priority queue

Urgent items go to the front, normal items to the rear, always serve the front — a priority queue with exactly two priorities, as in 0-1 BFS on graphs with edge weights 0 and 1.

Sliding window maximum / minimum

Maximum of every subarray of size k in O(n): the deque keeps candidate indices in decreasing order of value — see DSA Advanced → Sliding Window.

Palindromes and symmetry checks

Compare the two ends and remove both until the middle is reached — solved below.

Using the built-in containers
Python
from collections import deque

def show(d):
    print(*d)

d = deque()
d.append(10)            # insert at the rear
d.append(20)
d.append(30)
show(d)
d.appendleft(100)       # insert at the front
show(d)
d.pop()                 # delete from the rear
show(d)
d.popleft()             # delete from the front
show(d)
print("front:", d[0], "rear:", d[-1])
C++
#include <deque>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void show(const deque<int>& d) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < d.size(); i++) cout << (i ? " " : "") << d[i];   // deque allows d[i]
    cout << "\n";
}

int main() {
    deque<int> d;
    d.push_back(10);        // insert at the rear
    d.push_back(20);
    d.push_back(30);
    show(d);
    d.push_front(100);      // insert at the front
    show(d);
    d.pop_back();           // delete from the rear
    show(d);
    d.pop_front();          // delete from the front
    show(d);
    cout << "front: " << d.front() << " rear: " << d.back() << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static void show(Deque<Integer> d) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int v : d) sb.append(sb.length() == 0 ? "" : " ").append(v);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Deque<Integer> d = new ArrayDeque<>();   // preferred over LinkedList
        d.addLast(10);          // insert at the rear
        d.addLast(20);
        d.addLast(30);
        show(d);
        d.addFirst(100);        // insert at the front
        show(d);
        d.removeLast();         // delete from the rear
        show(d);
        d.removeFirst();        // delete from the front
        show(d);
        System.out.println("front: " + d.peekFirst() + " rear: " + d.peekLast());
    }
}

Python's deque also has a handful of list-like extras. They are convenient, but note which of them walk the whole structure (next section).

Python
from collections import deque

d = deque([10, 20, 30, 40])
d.insert(2, 15)
print(list(d))          # [10, 20, 15, 30, 40]
print(d.count(10))      # 1
d.remove(10)            # removes the first occurrence
print(list(d))          # [20, 15, 30, 40]
d.extend([50, 60])
print(list(d))          # [20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 60]
d.extendleft([10, 20])
print(list(d))          # [20, 10, 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 60]   ← appendleft one by one, so the order flips
d.reverse()
print(list(d))          # [60, 50, 40, 30, 15, 20, 10, 20]
Python
from collections import deque

d = deque([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
d.rotate(2)             # positive: the last 2 elements move to the front
print(list(d))          # [40, 50, 10, 20, 30]
d.rotate(-2)            # negative: the first 2 elements move to the back
print(list(d))          # [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(d[2])             # 30   ← indexing works, but the middle is O(n)
d[2] = 100
print(list(d))          # [10, 20, 100, 40, 50]
print(d[0], d[-1])      # 10 50

history = deque(maxlen=3)        # bounded: a full deque drops the opposite end
for x in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    history.append(x)
print(list(history))    # [2, 3, 4]   ← 1 fell off the front
Pitfall

extendleft([10, 20]) produces 20, 10, … — it calls appendleft for each element in turn, so the sequence appears reversed. Pass reversed(items) if you want to keep their order.

Time complexities and internal working
ComplexityPython deque operationsWhy
O(1)append, appendleft, pop, popleft, len, d[0], d[-1]both ends are directly reachable
O(n)d[i] in the middle, count(x), insert(i, x), remove(x), x in d, reverse()must walk the blocks from one end
O(min(k, n − k))rotate(k)moves k elements one by one, going the shorter way round
O(len(l))extend(l), extendleft(l)one append / appendleft per element

CPython's deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 slots each). The ends live in the leftmost and rightmost blocks, so pushing or popping at either end touches one slot and occasionally allocates or frees one block; walking to d[i] means hopping i // 64 blocks, hence O(n) in the middle.

Why both ends are O(1) but the middle is not
collections.deque — a doubly linked list of 64-slot blocks

   leftblock               ...                 rightblock
  ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐
  │ · · · 10 20 30│◀──▶│ 40 50 … … 90  │◀──▶│ 100 110 · · · │
  └───────────────┘    └───────────────┘    └───────────────┘
         ↑ leftindex                             ↑ rightindex

  appendleft / popleft move leftindex   → O(1)
  append / pop move rightindex          → O(1)
  d[i] hops i // 64 blocks              → O(n) in the middle
LibraryInternal structureBoth endsRandom access d[i]
Python collections.dequedoubly linked list of 64-slot blocksO(1)O(n) in the middle, O(1) near the ends
C++ std::dequearray of pointers to fixed-size chunks (“map of blocks”)O(1)O(1) — two lookups
Java ArrayDequecircular, growable array (doubles when full)amortised O(1)not supported (no get(i))
Java LinkedListdoubly linked list of nodesO(1)O(n)
Key point

std::deque is the one standard deque with O(1) indexing, which is why std::stack and std::queue adapt it by default. Java's ArrayDeque is faster and leaner than LinkedList for stack/queue work (one array, no per-node objects) but refuses null elements.

Implementing a deque with a doubly linked list

A singly linked list gives O(1) at the head and, with a tail pointer, O(1) insertRear — but deleteRear needs the node before the tail, which only a walk from the head can find: O(n). A doubly linked list stores a prev pointer in every node, so tail = tail.prev is one step and every deque operation is O(1).

Each node knows both neighbours, so either end can be removed without a search
head (front)                                        tail (rear)
 ↓                                                   ↓
┌───┬────┬───┐     ┌───┬────┬───┐     ┌───┬────┬───┐
│ ∅ │ 10 │ ●─┼────▶│ ● │ 20 │ ●─┼────▶│ ● │ 30 │ ∅ │
│   │    │   │◀────┼─● │    │   │◀────┼─● │    │   │
└───┴────┴───┘     └───┴────┴───┘     └───┴────┴───┘
prev value next

deleteRear(): tail = tail.prev; tail.next = ∅         ← O(1) thanks to prev
insertFront(x): node.next = head; head.prev = node; head = node
1
insertFront(x) / insertRear(x)
Create a node. If empty, head = tail = node. Otherwise link it before head (set node.next, head.prev, head) or after tail (set node.prev, tail.next, tail).
2
deleteFront() / deleteRear()
Advance head = head.next (or tail = tail.prev). If the deque became empty set the other pointer to null too; otherwise clear the new end's dangling prev (or next).
3
Both empty cases matter
The original notes did head = head.next; head.prev = None without checking — deleting the last element then crashes on None.prev. Guard it.
Example

Input: insertRear 10 20 30; deleteFront; deleteRear; insertFront 100, 1000
Output: front/rear: 10/30 → 20/30 → 20/20; final order 1000 100 20

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

class Deque:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None       # front
        self.tail = None       # rear
        self.size = 0

    def is_empty(self):
        return self.size == 0

    def insert_front(self, value):
        node = Node(value)
        if self.is_empty():
            self.head = self.tail = node
        else:
            node.next = self.head
            self.head.prev = node
            self.head = node
        self.size += 1

    def insert_rear(self, value):
        node = Node(value)
        if self.is_empty():
            self.head = self.tail = node
        else:
            node.prev = self.tail
            self.tail.next = node
            self.tail = node
        self.size += 1

    def delete_front(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("deque is empty")
        value = self.head.value
        self.head = self.head.next
        if self.head is None:          # became empty
            self.tail = None
        else:
            self.head.prev = None
        self.size -= 1
        return value

    def delete_rear(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("deque is empty")
        value = self.tail.value
        self.tail = self.tail.prev     # O(1) thanks to prev
        if self.tail is None:          # became empty
            self.head = None
        else:
            self.tail.next = None
        self.size -= 1
        return value

    def get_front(self):
        return None if self.is_empty() else self.head.value

    def get_rear(self):
        return None if self.is_empty() else self.tail.value

    def display(self):
        node, parts = self.head, []
        while node:
            parts.append(str(node.value))
            node = node.next
        print(" ".join(parts))

d = Deque()
for x in (10, 20, 30):
    d.insert_rear(x)
print("front:", d.get_front(), "rear:", d.get_rear())
d.delete_front()
print("deleteFront → front:", d.get_front(), "rear:", d.get_rear())
d.delete_rear()
print("deleteRear → front:", d.get_front(), "rear:", d.get_rear())
print("size:", d.size, "empty:", d.is_empty())
d.insert_front(100)
d.insert_front(1000)
d.display()
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int value;
    Node* prev;
    Node* next;
    Node(int v) : value(v), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {}
};

class Deque {
    Node* head = nullptr;      // front
    Node* tail = nullptr;      // rear
    int count = 0;
public:
    ~Deque() { while (head) deleteFront(); }
    bool isEmpty() const { return count == 0; }
    int size() const { return count; }
    void insertFront(int v) {
        Node* node = new Node(v);
        if (isEmpty()) head = tail = node;
        else { node->next = head; head->prev = node; head = node; }
        count++;
    }
    void insertRear(int v) {
        Node* node = new Node(v);
        if (isEmpty()) head = tail = node;
        else { node->prev = tail; tail->next = node; tail = node; }
        count++;
    }
    int deleteFront() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw runtime_error("deque is empty");
        Node* node = head;
        int v = node->value;
        head = head->next;
        if (!head) tail = nullptr;             // became empty
        else head->prev = nullptr;
        delete node;
        count--;
        return v;
    }
    int deleteRear() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw runtime_error("deque is empty");
        Node* node = tail;
        int v = node->value;
        tail = tail->prev;                     // O(1) thanks to prev
        if (!tail) head = nullptr;             // became empty
        else tail->next = nullptr;
        delete node;
        count--;
        return v;
    }
    int getFront() const { return head->value; }
    int getRear() const { return tail->value; }
    void display() const {
        for (Node* n = head; n; n = n->next) cout << n->value << (n->next ? " " : "");
        cout << "\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    Deque d;
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30}) d.insertRear(x);
    cout << "front: " << d.getFront() << " rear: " << d.getRear() << "\n";
    d.deleteFront();
    cout << "deleteFront → front: " << d.getFront() << " rear: " << d.getRear() << "\n";
    d.deleteRear();
    cout << "deleteRear → front: " << d.getFront() << " rear: " << d.getRear() << "\n";
    cout << "size: " << d.size() << " empty: " << (d.isEmpty() ? "True" : "False") << "\n";
    d.insertFront(100);
    d.insertFront(1000);
    d.display();
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int value; Node prev, next;
        Node(int v) { value = v; }
    }

    static class Deque {
        Node head, tail;           // front, rear
        int size;
        boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
        void insertFront(int v) {
            Node node = new Node(v);
            if (isEmpty()) head = tail = node;
            else { node.next = head; head.prev = node; head = node; }
            size++;
        }
        void insertRear(int v) {
            Node node = new Node(v);
            if (isEmpty()) head = tail = node;
            else { node.prev = tail; tail.next = node; tail = node; }
            size++;
        }
        int deleteFront() {
            if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("deque is empty");
            int v = head.value;
            head = head.next;
            if (head == null) tail = null;         // became empty
            else head.prev = null;
            size--;
            return v;
        }
        int deleteRear() {
            if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("deque is empty");
            int v = tail.value;
            tail = tail.prev;                      // O(1) thanks to prev
            if (tail == null) head = null;         // became empty
            else tail.next = null;
            size--;
            return v;
        }
        Integer getFront() { return isEmpty() ? null : head.value; }
        Integer getRear() { return isEmpty() ? null : tail.value; }
        void display() {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.value).append(n.next != null ? " " : "");
            System.out.println(sb);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Deque d = new Deque();
        for (int x : new int[]{10, 20, 30}) d.insertRear(x);
        System.out.println("front: " + d.getFront() + " rear: " + d.getRear());
        d.deleteFront();
        System.out.println("deleteFront → front: " + d.getFront() + " rear: " + d.getRear());
        d.deleteRear();
        System.out.println("deleteRear → front: " + d.getFront() + " rear: " + d.getRear());
        System.out.println("size: " + d.size + " empty: " + (d.isEmpty() ? "True" : "False"));
        d.insertFront(100);
        d.insertFront(1000);
        d.display();
    }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(value) { this.value = value; this.prev = null; this.next = null; }
}

class Deque {
    constructor() { this.head = null; this.tail = null; this.size = 0; }   // front, rear
    isEmpty() { return this.size === 0; }
    insertFront(value) {
        const node = new Node(value);
        if (this.isEmpty()) this.head = this.tail = node;
        else { node.next = this.head; this.head.prev = node; this.head = node; }
        this.size++;
    }
    insertRear(value) {
        const node = new Node(value);
        if (this.isEmpty()) this.head = this.tail = node;
        else { node.prev = this.tail; this.tail.next = node; this.tail = node; }
        this.size++;
    }
    deleteFront() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("deque is empty");
        const value = this.head.value;
        this.head = this.head.next;
        if (this.head === null) this.tail = null;      // became empty
        else this.head.prev = null;
        this.size--;
        return value;
    }
    deleteRear() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("deque is empty");
        const value = this.tail.value;
        this.tail = this.tail.prev;                    // O(1) thanks to prev
        if (this.tail === null) this.head = null;      // became empty
        else this.tail.next = null;
        this.size--;
        return value;
    }
    getFront() { return this.isEmpty() ? null : this.head.value; }
    getRear() { return this.isEmpty() ? null : this.tail.value; }
    display() {
        const parts = [];
        for (let n = this.head; n; n = n.next) parts.push(n.value);
        console.log(parts.join(" "));
    }
}
