Implementing a deque with a circular array

The circular-array queue extends naturally: insertFront steps front backwards (wrapping from 0 to cap − 1), insertRear fills the slot after the rear (wrapping from cap − 1 to 0). Keeping front and size is enough — the rear index is always (front + size − 1) % cap, and size disambiguates empty from full.

Both ends wrap; the physical array order differs from the logical order
capacity 5: insertFront(10), insertFront(20), insertFront(30), insertRear(40), insertRear(50)

  index:   0     1     2     3     4
        ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
        │ 40  │ 50  │ 30  │ 20  │ 10  │
        └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
                       ↑ front = 2        rear = (front + size − 1) % 5 = 1

  insertFront moves front backwards:  0 → 4 (10) → 3 (20) → 2 (30)   wraps to the end
  insertRear fills the slot after rear: 4 → 0 (40) → 1 (50)          wraps to the start
  logical order (front → rear):  30  20  10  40  50
Example

Input: capacity = 5; insertFront 10 20 30; insertRear 40 50; deleteFront; deleteRear
Output: order 30 20 10 40 50 → after deletes 20 10 40

Python
class ArrayDeque:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.slots = [None] * capacity
        self.cap = capacity
        self.front = 0        # index of the first element
        self.size = 0         # rear index is derived: (front + size - 1) % cap

    def is_empty(self):
        return self.size == 0

    def is_full(self):
        return self.size == self.cap

    def insert_front(self, value):
        if self.is_full():
            raise OverflowError("deque is full")
        self.front = (self.front - 1 + self.cap) % self.cap   # step back, wrapping to the end
        self.slots[self.front] = value
        self.size += 1

    def insert_rear(self, value):
        if self.is_full():
            raise OverflowError("deque is full")
        self.slots[(self.front + self.size) % self.cap] = value   # next free slot after rear
        self.size += 1

    def delete_front(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("deque is empty")
        value = self.slots[self.front]
        self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.cap
        self.size -= 1
        return value

    def delete_rear(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("deque is empty")
        value = self.slots[(self.front + self.size - 1) % self.cap]
        self.size -= 1                                # rear simply moves back by one
        return value

    def get_front(self):
        return self.slots[self.front]

    def get_rear(self):
        return self.slots[(self.front + self.size - 1) % self.cap]

    def in_order(self):
        return [self.slots[(self.front + i) % self.cap] for i in range(self.size)]

d = ArrayDeque(5)
for x in (10, 20, 30):
    d.insert_front(x)
for x in (40, 50):
    d.insert_rear(x)
print("in order:", *d.in_order())
print("slots:", *d.slots)
print("front =", d.front, "size =", d.size)
print("full:", d.is_full())
print("deleteFront →", d.delete_front())
print("deleteRear →", d.delete_rear())
print("in order:", *d.in_order())
print("front:", d.get_front(), "rear:", d.get_rear())
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class ArrayDeque {
public:
    vector<int> slots;
    int cap, front = 0, size = 0;    // rear index is derived: (front + size - 1) % cap
    ArrayDeque(int capacity) : slots(capacity, 0), cap(capacity) {}
    bool isEmpty() const { return size == 0; }
    bool isFull() const { return size == cap; }
    void insertFront(int v) {
        if (isFull()) throw runtime_error("deque is full");
        front = (front - 1 + cap) % cap;              // step back, wrapping to the end
        slots[front] = v;
        size++;
    }
    void insertRear(int v) {
        if (isFull()) throw runtime_error("deque is full");
        slots[(front + size) % cap] = v;              // next free slot after rear
        size++;
    }
    int deleteFront() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw runtime_error("deque is empty");
        int v = slots[front];
        front = (front + 1) % cap;
        size--;
        return v;
    }
    int deleteRear() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw runtime_error("deque is empty");
        int v = slots[(front + size - 1) % cap];
        size--;                                       // rear simply moves back by one
        return v;
    }
    int getFront() const { return slots[front]; }
    int getRear() const { return slots[(front + size - 1) % cap]; }
    void printInOrder() const {
        cout << "in order:";
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) cout << " " << slots[(front + i) % cap];
        cout << "\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    ArrayDeque d(5);
    for (int x : {10, 20, 30}) d.insertFront(x);
    for (int x : {40, 50}) d.insertRear(x);
    d.printInOrder();
    cout << "slots:";
    for (int v : d.slots) cout << " " << v;
    cout << "\n";
    cout << "front = " << d.front << " size = " << d.size << "\n";
    cout << "full: " << (d.isFull() ? "True" : "False") << "\n";
    cout << "deleteFront → " << d.deleteFront() << "\n";
    cout << "deleteRear → " << d.deleteRear() << "\n";
    d.printInOrder();
    cout << "front: " << d.getFront() << " rear: " << d.getRear() << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class ArrayDeque {
        int[] slots;
        int cap, front = 0, size = 0;    // rear index is derived: (front + size - 1) % cap
        ArrayDeque(int capacity) { slots = new int[capacity]; cap = capacity; }
        boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
        boolean isFull() { return size == cap; }
        void insertFront(int v) {
            if (isFull()) throw new RuntimeException("deque is full");
            front = (front - 1 + cap) % cap;          // step back, wrapping to the end
            slots[front] = v;
            size++;
        }
        void insertRear(int v) {
            if (isFull()) throw new RuntimeException("deque is full");
            slots[(front + size) % cap] = v;          // next free slot after rear
            size++;
        }
        int deleteFront() {
            if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("deque is empty");
            int v = slots[front];
            front = (front + 1) % cap;
            size--;
            return v;
        }
        int deleteRear() {
            if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("deque is empty");
            int v = slots[(front + size - 1) % cap];
            size--;                                   // rear simply moves back by one
            return v;
        }
        int getFront() { return slots[front]; }
        int getRear() { return slots[(front + size - 1) % cap]; }
        void printInOrder() {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("in order:");
            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) sb.append(' ').append(slots[(front + i) % cap]);
            System.out.println(sb);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayDeque d = new ArrayDeque(5);
        for (int x : new int[]{10, 20, 30}) d.insertFront(x);
        for (int x : new int[]{40, 50}) d.insertRear(x);
        d.printInOrder();
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("slots:");
        for (int v : d.slots) sb.append(' ').append(v);
        System.out.println(sb);
        System.out.println("front = " + d.front + " size = " + d.size);
        System.out.println("full: " + (d.isFull() ? "True" : "False"));
        System.out.println("deleteFront → " + d.deleteFront());
        System.out.println("deleteRear → " + d.deleteRear());
        d.printInOrder();
        System.out.println("front: " + d.getFront() + " rear: " + d.getRear());
    }
}
JavaScript
class ArrayDeque {
    constructor(capacity) {
        this.slots = new Array(capacity).fill(null);
        this.cap = capacity;
        this.front = 0;       // index of the first element
        this.size = 0;        // rear index is derived: (front + size - 1) % cap
    }
    isEmpty() { return this.size === 0; }
    isFull() { return this.size === this.cap; }
    insertFront(value) {
        if (this.isFull()) throw new Error("deque is full");
        this.front = (this.front - 1 + this.cap) % this.cap;   // step back, wrapping to the end
        this.slots[this.front] = value;
        this.size++;
    }
    insertRear(value) {
        if (this.isFull()) throw new Error("deque is full");
        this.slots[(this.front + this.size) % this.cap] = value;   // next free slot after rear
        this.size++;
    }
    deleteFront() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("deque is empty");
        const value = this.slots[this.front];
        this.front = (this.front + 1) % this.cap;
        this.size--;
        return value;
    }
    deleteRear() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("deque is empty");
        const value = this.slots[(this.front + this.size - 1) % this.cap];
        this.size--;                                  // rear simply moves back by one
        return value;
    }
    getFront() { return this.slots[this.front]; }
    getRear() { return this.slots[(this.front + this.size - 1) % this.cap]; }
    inOrder() {
        const out = [];
        for (let i = 0; i < this.size; i++) out.push(this.slots[(this.front + i) % this.cap]);
        return out;
    }
}

const d = new ArrayDeque(5);
for (const x of [10, 20, 30]) d.insertFront(x);
for (const x of [40, 50]) d.insertRear(x);
console.log("in order:", d.inOrder().join(" "));
console.log("slots:", d.slots.join(" "));
console.log("front =", d.front, "size =", d.size);
console.log("full:", d.isFull() ? "True" : "False");
console.log("deleteFront →", d.deleteFront());
console.log("deleteRear →", d.deleteRear());
console.log("in order:", d.inOrder().join(" "));
console.log("front:", d.getFront(), "rear:", d.getRear());
Output
in order: 30 20 10 40 50
slots: 40 50 30 20 10
front = 2 size = 5
full: True
deleteFront → 30
deleteRear → 50
in order: 20 10 40
front: 20 rear: 40
Time O(1) per operationSpace O(cap)
Pitfall

Stepping the front backwards as front - 1 gives -1 when front == 0. In C++/Java that is an out-of-bounds read; in Python slots[-1] silently hits the last slot and leaves front negative. Always write (front - 1 + cap) % cap — and avoid the -1-means-empty sentinel of the original notes, which needs four special cases per operation; a size counter needs none.

Array or linked list?

The original notes list the array version's advantages as “random access, supports all operations, cache friendly, O(1) time”. Here is the full comparison:

Circular arrayDoubly linked list
Insert / delete at both endsO(1) (amortised O(1) if it grows by doubling)O(1)
Random access d[i]O(1) — slots[(front + i) % cap]O(n)
Memoryone contiguous block, no per-element overhead; some unused capacitytwo pointers per node, scattered allocations
Cache behaviourfriendly — neighbours are adjacent in memorypoor — every step is a pointer chase
Capacityfixed, or resize by doubling (copy O(n), rarely)unbounded, never copies
Used byJava ArrayDeque, C++ std::deque (chunked), Python deque (blocks)Java LinkedList
Do

Default to the array-based deque of your language: it is faster in practice and supports indexing. Reach for a linked list only when you need stable node references (an element must keep its identity while others are added) or truly unbounded growth without copying.

Problem: check whether a string is a palindrome
Example

Input: s = "Nurses run"
Output: Yes
Input: s = "hello"
Output: No

Idea

Load the cleaned characters into a deque, then repeatedly compare and remove the two ends. A palindrome reads the same from both directions, so every pair must match until at most one character is left.

Python
from collections import deque

def is_palindrome(s):
    d = deque(ch.lower() for ch in s if ch.isalnum())   # ignore spaces, case, punctuation
    while len(d) > 1:
        if d.popleft() != d.pop():                        # compare both ends, O(1) each
            return False
    return True

for s in ["racecar", "Nurses run", "hello", "No lemon, no melon"]:
    print(s, "→", "Yes" if is_palindrome(s) else "No")
C++
#include <cctype>
#include <deque>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

bool isPalindrome(const string& s) {
    deque<char> d;
    for (char ch : s)                                         // ignore spaces, case, punctuation
        if (isalnum((unsigned char)ch)) d.push_back((char)tolower((unsigned char)ch));
    while (d.size() > 1) {
        if (d.front() != d.back()) return false;              // compare both ends, O(1) each
        d.pop_front();
        d.pop_back();
    }
    return true;
}

int main() {
    for (string s : {"racecar", "Nurses run", "hello", "No lemon, no melon"})
        cout << s << " → " << (isPalindrome(s) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        Deque<Character> d = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray())                       // ignore spaces, case, punctuation
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(ch)) d.addLast(Character.toLowerCase(ch));
        while (d.size() > 1) {
            char a = d.pollFirst(), b = d.pollLast();         // unbox before comparing!
            if (a != b) return false;                         // compare both ends, O(1) each
        }
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[]{"racecar", "Nurses run", "hello", "No lemon, no melon"})
            System.out.println(s + " → " + (isPalindrome(s) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}
JavaScript
function isPalindrome(s) {
    const d = [];
    for (const ch of s.toLowerCase())                         // ignore spaces, case, punctuation
        if (/[a-z0-9]/.test(ch)) d.push(ch);
    while (d.length > 1) {
        if (d.shift() !== d.pop()) return false;              // compare both ends (shift is O(n) on arrays)
    }
    return true;
}

for (const s of ["racecar", "Nurses run", "hello", "No lemon, no melon"])
    console.log(s, "→", isPalindrome(s) ? "Yes" : "No");
Output
racecar → Yes
Nurses run → Yes
hello → No
No lemon, no melon → Yes
Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

In Java, d.pollFirst() != d.pollLast() compares two Character objects by reference. It happens to work for ASCII because of the small-value cache, and silently fails beyond it — unbox to char (or use .equals) first. In JavaScript the array shift() makes this O(n²); two indices i, j walking inwards give the same answer in O(n) with no deque at all.

Key point

The flagship deque problem — maximum of every window of size k in O(n) — keeps the deque sorted by value with indices, popping from the rear anything smaller than the new element and from the front anything that has left the window. It is worked through in DSA Advanced → Sliding Window.

Interview Q&A
What is a deque, and how does it relate to stacks and queues?

A double-ended queue: insert and delete in O(1) at both the front and the rear. Use only one end and it is a stack; insert at the rear and delete at the front and it is a queue. That is why collections.deque and ArrayDeque are the recommended stack and queue in Python and Java.

Why does a deque need a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?

deleteRear() must make the previous node the new tail. In a singly linked list that node is only reachable by walking from the head — O(n). A prev pointer makes it tail = tail.prev, O(1). Everything else (head operations, tail insert) a singly linked list with a tail pointer can already do in O(1).

How does Python's deque give O(1) at both ends, and why is d[i] O(n)?

It is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 slots). The two ends live in the leftmost and rightmost blocks, so pushing or popping there touches one slot. Indexing the middle has to hop block by block from the nearer end — O(n/64), i.e. O(n). Use a list when you need random access, a deque when you need both ends.

ArrayDeque or LinkedList in Java?

ArrayDeque for stacks and queues: a circular growable array, cache-friendly, no per-element node objects, faster in practice. LinkedList only when you also need List operations (index-based insert/remove via an iterator) or must store null, which ArrayDeque rejects.

How do you implement a deque with a fixed array, and how do you tell empty from full?

Treat the array as a ring. insertFront moves front to (front − 1 + cap) % cap; insertRear writes at (front + size) % cap. Keep a size counter: empty when size == 0, full when size == cap. Without the counter front and rear coincide in both states and you have to waste one slot to disambiguate.

Name a problem where a deque beats both a stack and a queue.

Sliding window maximum: for each window of size k, the deque holds indices of candidates in decreasing value order. New elements evict smaller ones from the rear (they can never be a maximum again), and indices that fall out of the window are dropped from the front. Each index enters and leaves once — O(n) overall, versus O(nk) naively.

Trees & Heaps

Tree Data Structures

A tree is a non-linear, hierarchical data structure: one root node with children, each of which is the root of a smaller tree. Folders, HTML documents, organisation charts, expression parsers, database indexes and every search tree and heap are trees — and most tree algorithms are five-line recursions once you see the structure.

Tree — a collection of nodes connected by edges such that there is exactly one root and every other node has exactly one parent — so there are no cycles and n nodes always have n − 1 edges. A binary tree is a tree in which every node has at most two children, called left and right.

The sample binary tree used in every example below
       10                  ← root (depth 0, level 0)
     /    \
   20      30              ← depth 1
  /  \       \
40    50      60           ← depth 2
     /  \
   70    80                ← depth 3 — 40, 70, 80, 60 are the leaves
Terminology
TermMeaningIn the sample tree
NodeOne element: a key plus links to its children10, 20, … (8 nodes)
EdgeThe link from a parent to a child; a tree of n nodes has n − 1 edges7 edges
RootThe topmost node — the only node without a parent10
Parent / childThe node directly above / directly below along an edge50 is the parent of 70 and 80
SiblingsChildren of the same parent70 and 80; 20 and 30
Leaf (external node)A node with no children40, 70, 80, 60
Internal nodeA node with at least one child10, 20, 30, 50
SubtreeA node together with all its descendants — itself a treethe subtree rooted at 20 is 20, 40, 50, 70, 80
AncestorsAll nodes on the path from a node up to the rootancestors of 70: 50, 20, 10
DescendantsAll nodes in a node's subtree except itselfdescendants of 20: 40, 50, 70, 80
Degree of a nodeNumber of children (at most 2 in a binary tree)degree of 20 is 2, of 30 is 1, of 40 is 0
Depth of a nodeNumber of edges from the root down to the nodedepth of 70 is 3, of the root is 0
LevelAll nodes at the same depth (level 0 = root)level 2 is 40 50 60
Height of a nodeNumber of edges on the longest downward path to a leaf (a leaf has height 0)height of 20 is 2
Height of the treeHeight of the root3 edges — or 4 if you count nodes on that path (the convention of these notes)
Key point

Two height conventions exist. Counting edges, the sample tree has height 3 and an empty tree has height −1. Counting nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path (what the notes and GeeksforGeeks do, and what the height() code below returns), it has height 4 and an empty tree has height 0. Interviewers accept either — just say which one you use.

Where trees are used

Trees are the natural representation of anything hierarchical, and the basis of most fast search structures.

Hierarchical data

Organisation structures, folder / file systems, XML and HTML documents (the DOM), nested JSON objects, class inheritance in OOP.

Binary search tree

Keys kept in sorted order with O(log n) search, insert and delete — std::map, TreeMap (next topic).

Binary heap

A complete binary tree in an array; the priority queue behind heap sort, Dijkstra and schedulers (topic after next).

B and B+ trees

Wide, shallow search trees that keep disk reads to a minimum — the indexes of every relational database.

Spanning and shortest-path trees

Prim's and Kruskal's minimum spanning trees, Dijkstra's shortest-path tree — the backbone of routing in computer networks.

Parse and expression trees

Compilers turn source code into a syntax tree; (a + b) * c is a tree with * at the root.

Special-purpose variations you will meet later in DSA Advanced:

VariationWhat it is for
Trie (prefix tree)Strings keyed character by character — autocomplete, spell check, IP routing tables
Suffix treeAll suffixes of a text — substring search in O(m)
Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick tree)Prefix sums with O(log n) point updates in a plain array
Segment treeRange queries (sum, min, max) with O(log n) updates
Kinds of binary tree

The same n keys can form very different binary trees. The shape decides the height, and the height decides how fast everything runs — so the special shapes have names.

The named shapes of a binary tree
FULL (0 or 2 children)      COMPLETE (left-filled)      PERFECT (all leaves same level)
         1                          1                            1
       /   \                      /   \                        /   \
      2     3                    2     3                      2     3
     / \                        / \   /                      / \   / \
    4   5                      4   5 6                      4   5 6   7

BALANCED (|hL − hR| ≤ 1 at every node)      DEGENERATE / SKEWED (a linked list)
         1                                      1
       /   \                                     \
      2     3                                      2
     /       \                                      \
    4         5                                       3
                                                       \
                                                        4
KindRuleWhy it matters
Full (strict / proper)Every node has either 0 or 2 childrenLeaves = internal nodes + 1; expression trees are full
CompleteEvery level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to rightCan be stored in an array with no gaps — this is what a binary heap is
PerfectAll internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are on the same levelExactly 2^h − 1 nodes for height h (in nodes); the densest possible tree
BalancedHeight is O(log n) — e.g. AVL: left and right heights differ by at most 1 at every nodeGuarantees O(log n) search, insert and delete in a BST
Degenerate (skewed)Every node has exactly one childHeight n − 1: it behaves like a linked list, every operation becomes O(n)

Useful facts (height counted in nodes): level l holds at most 2^l nodes; a tree of height h holds at most 2^h − 1 nodes; therefore n nodes need height at least ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉. A perfect tree is always complete and full; a complete tree need not be full (node 3 above has one child); a full tree need not be complete.

Binary tree node and building the sample tree

A binary tree is a linked data structure, like a linked list with two links. Each node stores a key and pointers to its left and right child; a missing child is None / nullptr / null. The tree is identified by its root pointer alone — there is no separate container object. Every program in this topic starts by building the sample tree with this node class.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

def is_leaf(node):
    return node.left is None and node.right is None

root = sample_tree()
print("root:", root.key)
print("children of root:", root.left.key, root.right.key)
print("left child of 20:", root.left.left.key)
print("right child of 30:", root.right.right.key)
print("30 has a left child:", "true" if root.right.left else "false")
print("70 is a leaf:", "true" if is_leaf(root.left.right.left) else "false")
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k) : key(k), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

Node* sampleTree() {                 // the tree from the notes
    Node* root = new Node(10);
    root->left = new Node(20);
    root->right = new Node(30);
    root->left->left = new Node(40);
    root->left->right = new Node(50);
    root->right->right = new Node(60);
    root->left->right->left = new Node(70);
    root->left->right->right = new Node(80);
    return root;
}

bool isLeaf(Node* node) { return !node->left && !node->right; }

int main() {
    Node* root = sampleTree();
    cout << "root: " << root->key << "\n";
    cout << "children of root: " << root->left->key << " " << root->right->key << "\n";
    cout << "left child of 20: " << root->left->left->key << "\n";
    cout << "right child of 30: " << root->right->right->key << "\n";
    cout << "30 has a left child: " << (root->right->left ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
    cout << "70 is a leaf: " << (isLeaf(root->left->right->left) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Node sampleTree() {           // the tree from the notes

        root.left.right.left = new Node(70);
        root.left.right.right = new Node(80);

}

}

left child of 20: 40
right child of 30: 60

70 is a leaf: true
Key point

Building a tree by hand like this is fine for examples. Real code builds trees by insertion (a BST), from an array (a heap, or a level-order array with -1 for missing nodes) or by parsing input.

Tree traversals

Traversing means visiting every node exactly once. A list has one natural order; a tree has several, and each one is useful for something.

TraversalOrderSample tree givesTypical use
Inorder (depth-first)Left subtree → Root → Right subtree40 20 70 50 80 10 30 60Sorted output of a binary search tree
Preorder (depth-first)Root → Left → Right10 20 40 50 70 80 30 60Copying / serialising a tree, prefix expressions
Postorder (depth-first)Left → Right → Root40 70 80 50 20 60 30 10Deleting a tree (children before parent), folder sizes, postfix expressions
Level order (breadth-first)Level 0, then level 1, … left to right10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80Shortest paths, printing by level, anything that needs closest first
The three depth-first orders differ only in when the root is visited relative to its subtrees
       10            Inorder   : (left of 10) 10 (right of 10)
     /    \                     = (40 20 70 50 80) 10 (30 60)
   20      30
  /  \       \      Preorder  : 10 (left of 10) (right of 10)
40    50      60                = 10 (20 40 50 70 80) (30 60)
     /  \
   70    80          Postorder : (left of 10) (right of 10) 10
                                = (40 70 80 50 20) (60 30) 10
Idea

All three depth-first traversals are the same recursion — visit(root.left), visit(root.right) and print the root — in a different order. The names say where the root goes: pre-order before the children, in-order in between, post-order after. Each recursive call handles one node and makes two calls, so the total work is O(n); the recursion stack is as deep as the tree, so auxiliary space is O(h).

Inorder traversal
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 20 70 50 80 10 30 60

Recurse into the left subtree, print the node, recurse into the right subtree. On a BST this prints the keys in sorted order, which is why inorder is the traversal you will use most.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

def inorder(root):
    if root is None:                 # base case: empty subtree
        return
    inorder(root.left)               # 1. left subtree
    print(root.key, end=" ")         # 2. root
    inorder(root.right)              # 3. right subtree

inorder(sample_tree())
print()

function inorder(root) {
    if (root === null) return;       // base case: empty subtree
    inorder(root.left);              // 1. left subtree
    process.stdout.write(root.key + " "); // 2. root
    inorder(root.right);             // 3. right subtree
}

inorder(sampleTree());
console.log();
Output
40 20 70 50 80 10 30 60
Time O(n)Space O(h) recursion stack — O(n) for a skewed tree, O(log n) when balanced
Pitfall

The notes' comment Auxiliary space Θ(n) is the worst case only. The stack holds one frame per ancestor of the current node, so its depth is the height h; it reaches n only for a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree.

Preorder traversal
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 40 50 70 80 30 60

Print the node first, then its subtrees. Preorder lists every node before its descendants, so writing a tree out in preorder (with markers for missing children) is enough to rebuild it — this is how trees are serialised and copied.

    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)

def preorder(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    print(root.key, end=" ")         # 1. root first
    preorder(root.left)              # 2. left subtree
    preorder(root.right)             # 3. right subtree

preorder(sample_tree())
print()

Example

Input: the sample tree

Key point

In C++ the destructor of a tree is a postorder traversal: delete the left subtree, delete the right subtree, then the node — deleting the node first would lose the pointers to its children.

Height of a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 4 (nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path 10 → 20 → 50 → 70)
Input: an empty tree
Output: 0

Idea

The height of a tree is one more than the taller of its two subtrees. That is the whole algorithm: recurse into both children, take the maximum, add 1. The base case — an empty subtree — has height 0 under the node-counting convention.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

def height(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0                             # empty tree (node convention)
    return max(height(root.left), height(root.right)) + 1   # +1 for the root

root = sample_tree()
print("height:", height(root))
print("height of left subtree:", height(root.left))
print("height of right subtree:", height(root.right))

Print nodes at distance K from the root
Example

Input: the sample tree, K = 2
Output: 40 50 60
Input: K = 1
Output: 20 30
Input: K = 3
Output: 70 80

Idea

A node is at distance K from the root exactly when it is at distance K − 1 from one of the root's children. So pass K down the recursion, decrementing at each level; when it reaches 0, the current node is one of the answers. Nothing needs to come back up — the recursion just needs to reach depth K.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

def print_k_distance(root, k):
    if root is None:
        return
    if k == 0:                           # reached distance K: this node is an answer
        print(root.key, end=" ")
    else:                                # both children are one step closer
        print_k_distance(root.left, k - 1)
        print_k_distance(root.right, k - 1)

root = sample_tree()
for k in range(4):
    print(f"k = {k}:", end=" ")
    print_k_distance(root, k)
    print()

Key point

The recursion visits at most all nodes down to depth K, so it is O(n) in the worst case but stops early for small K. Nodes at distance K from the root are exactly level K — the level-order traversal below produces the same groups without recursion.

Level order traversal (breadth-first)
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80
Input: the tree 3 → 4 → 5 (each the left child of the previous)
Output: 3 4 5

Idea

Recursion naturally goes deep. To go wide — whole level before the next — use a queue: start with the root, and every time you dequeue a node, enqueue its children. Because a queue is FIFO, all of level d is dequeued before anything from level d + 1, which was enqueued later.

1
Start
Push the root into an empty queue.
2
Loop while the queue is not empty
Pop the front node and print it.
3
Enqueue children
Push its left child, then its right child (if they exist) — they will be visited after everything already in the queue.
The queue holds at most one level (plus part of the next) at any time
queue →  [10]                 print 10, push 20 30
         [20 30]              print 20, push 40 50
         [30 40 50]           print 30, push 60
         [40 50 60]           print 40 (leaf)
         [50 60]              print 50, push 70 80
         [60 70 80]           print 60, 70, 80 (leaves)
         []                   done:  10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()               # oldest node first (FIFO)
        print(node.key, end=" ")
        if node.left:                    # its children join the back of the line
            q.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            q.append(node.right)

level_order(sample_tree())
print()
C++
#include <queue>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k) : key(k), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

Node* sampleTree() {                 // the tree from the notes
    Node* root = new Node(10);
    root->left = new Node(20);
    root->right = new Node(30);
    root->left->left = new Node(40);
    root->left->right = new Node(50);
    root->right->right = new Node(60);
    root->left->right->left = new Node(70);
    root->left->right->right = new Node(80);
    return root;
}

void levelOrder(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    queue<Node*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        Node* node = q.front(); q.pop();     // oldest node first (FIFO)
        cout << node->key << " ";
        if (node->left) q.push(node->left);  // its children join the back of the line
        if (node->right) q.push(node->right);
    }
}

int main() {
    levelOrder(sampleTree());
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Node sampleTree() {           // the tree from the notes
        Node root = new Node(10);
        root.left = new Node(20);
        root.right = new Node(30);
        root.left.left = new Node(40);
        root.left.right = new Node(50);
        root.right.right = new Node(60);
        root.left.right.left = new Node(70);
        root.left.right.right = new Node(80);
        return root;
    }

    static void levelOrder(Node root) {
        if (root == null) return;
        Queue<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            Node node = q.poll();                // oldest node first (FIFO)
            System.out.print(node.key + " ");
            if (node.left != null) q.offer(node.left);   // children join the back of the line
            if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        levelOrder(sampleTree());
        System.out.println();
    }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(key) { this.key = key; this.left = null; this.right = null; }
}

function sampleTree() {              // the tree from the notes
    const root = new Node(10);
    root.left = new Node(20);
    root.right = new Node(30);
    root.left.left = new Node(40);
    root.left.right = new Node(50);
    root.right.right = new Node(60);
    root.left.right.left = new Node(70);
    root.left.right.right = new Node(80);
    return root;
}

function levelOrder(root) {
    if (root === null) return;
    const q = [root];
    let head = 0;                        // index of the front: avoids O(n) shift()
    while (head < q.length) {
        const node = q[head++];          // oldest node first (FIFO)
        process.stdout.write(node.key + " ");
        if (node.left) q.push(node.left);    // its children join the back of the line
        if (node.right) q.push(node.right);
    }
}

levelOrder(sampleTree());
console.log();
Output
10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80
Time O(n)Space O(w) — the widest level, up to n/2 nodes for a perfect tree

Level by level. Interviewers usually want each level on its own line. Record the queue's size at the start of each round: exactly that many nodes belong to the current level, so pop just those, then start the next line.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

from collections import deque

def level_order_lines(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        count = len(q)                   # nodes of the current level
        for _ in range(count):
            node = q.popleft()
            print(node.key, end=" ")
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        print()                          # level finished

level_order_lines(sample_tree())
C++
#include <queue>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k) : key(k), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

Node* sampleTree() {                 // the tree from the notes
    Node* root = new Node(10);
    root->left = new Node(20);
    root->right = new Node(30);
    root->left->left = new Node(40);
    root->left->right = new Node(50);
    root->right->right = new Node(60);
    root->left->right->left = new Node(70);
    root->left->right->right = new Node(80);
    return root;
}

void levelOrderLines(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    queue<Node*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int count = (int)q.size();           // nodes of the current level
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
            Node* node = q.front(); q.pop();
            cout << node->key << " ";
            if (node->left) q.push(node->left);
            if (node->right) q.push(node->right);
        }
        cout << "\n";                        // level finished
    }
}

int main() { levelOrderLines(sampleTree()); }

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Node sampleTree() {           // the tree from the notes
        Node root = new Node(10);
        root.left = new Node(20);
        root.right = new Node(30);
        root.left.left = new Node(40);
        root.left.right = new Node(50);
        root.right.right = new Node(60);
        root.left.right.left = new Node(70);
        root.left.right.right = new Node(80);
        return root;
    }

    static void levelOrderLines(Node root) {
        if (root == null) return;
        Queue<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int count = q.size();                // nodes of the current level
            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
                Node node = q.poll();
                System.out.print(node.key + " ");
                if (node.left != null) q.offer(node.left);
                if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
            }
            System.out.println();                // level finished
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { levelOrderLines(sampleTree()); }
}

function levelOrderLines(root) {
    if (root === null) return;
    let level = [root];
    while (level.length) {               // the current level is a whole array
        const next = [];

Pitfall

Using a plain list / array as the queue and removing from the front (list.pop(0), Array.shift()) makes every dequeue O(n) and the traversal O(n²). Use collections.deque, std::queue, ArrayDeque, or an index into the array as above.

Size of a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 8
Input: an empty tree
Output: 0

Idea

The size of a tree is the size of the left subtree plus the size of the right subtree plus one for the root. Same shape as height(), with + instead of max.

Maximum value in a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 80
Input: an empty tree
Output: -inf (no maximum)

Idea

The maximum of a tree is the largest of three things: the root's key, the maximum of the left subtree and the maximum of the right subtree. The base case returns −∞ so that an empty subtree never wins. A plain binary tree has no ordering, so every node must be looked at — unlike a BST, where the maximum is simply the rightmost node.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def sample_tree():                   # the tree from the notes
    root = Node(10)
    root.left = Node(20)
    root.right = Node(30)
    root.left.left = Node(40)
    root.left.right = Node(50)
    root.right.right = Node(60)
    root.left.right.left = Node(70)
    root.left.right.right = Node(80)
    return root

import math

def get_max(root):
    if root is None:
        return -math.inf                     # identity for max: never wins
    return max(root.key, get_max(root.left), get_max(root.right))

root = sample_tree()
print("max:", get_max(root))
print("max of right subtree:", get_max(root.right))

Pitfall

Recursion on trees: the pattern

Height, size, maximum, and most other tree problems have the same three-line shape — remember it and you can derive the others in an interview.

1
Base case
if root is None: return <identity> — 0 for counting, 0/-1 for height, −∞ for max, +∞ for min, True for is valid.
2
Recurse
Solve the problem for root.left and root.right — trust the recursion to return the right answer for each subtree.
3
Combine
Mix the two answers with the root: max(l, r) + 1, l + r + 1, max(key, l, r), l and r and <condition on root>.
ProblemBase caseCombine
Height0max(l, r) + 1
Size0l + r + 1
Maximum−∞max(key, l, r)
Sum of keys0l + r + key
Count leaves0; a leaf returns 1l + r
Is balancedTruel and r and |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1
Interview Q&A
What is the difference between a binary tree and a binary search tree?

A binary tree only limits every node to at most two children — the keys can be anywhere. A binary search tree adds an ordering invariant: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. That invariant is what makes search O(h) instead of O(n).

Why is the height of a tree so important?

Almost every operation walks one root-to-leaf path, so it costs O(h). For a balanced tree h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = n − 1, and the tree degrades into a linked list. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist purely to keep h logarithmic.

Which traversal would you use to delete every node of a tree, and why?

Postorder: both children are freed before the parent, so no pointer to a child is ever lost. Preorder would free the parent — and the links to its children — first.

How do you get the inorder sequence without recursion?

Use an explicit stack: walk left pushing every node, pop one and print it, then move to its right child and repeat. It is the same O(n) time and O(h) space, but the stack is yours instead of the call stack — useful in languages with a small recursion limit (Python stops at about 1000 frames).

Is level order traversal depth-first or breadth-first, and what data structure does it need?

Breadth-first — it finishes a level before starting the next. It needs a queue; the three depth-first traversals need a stack (the call stack when written recursively). Space is O(w) for the widest level versus O(h) for depth-first; for a perfect tree the last level holds about n/2 nodes, so BFS can use far more memory.

Can you rebuild a binary tree from its traversals?

From inorder plus preorder (or inorder plus postorder), yes: the first preorder element is the root, its position in the inorder sequence splits the inorder into the left and right subtrees, and you recurse. Preorder plus postorder alone is not enough — a node with a single child is ambiguous. A single traversal with null markers is also enough, which is how serialisation works.

Trees & Heaps

Binary Search Tree

A binary search tree keeps keys in order: smaller keys to the left, larger to the right, at every node. That one rule turns search, insert, delete, floor and ceiling into a single walk down one path — O(log n) when the tree is balanced — and makes an inorder traversal print the keys sorted.

Binary search tree (BST) — a binary tree in which, for every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller than the node's key and all keys in its right subtree are greater. Keys are usually assumed distinct. Like a linked list it is a linked data structure: nodes connected by pointers, no fixed capacity.

The sample BST: an empty tree after inserting 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7 in that order
          20
       /      \
     15        30
    /  \         \
  12    18        40
 /               /  \
7              35    50
                       \
                        80

Check the invariant at any node: left of 20 are 15 12 18 7 (all smaller), right are 30 40 35 50 80 (all larger). Left of 40 is 35, right is 50 80. It holds for the whole subtree, not just the two children — a tree where 35 sat under 15 would have every child in order and still be wrong.

Watch out

The invariant is left subtree < node < right subtree, not left child < node < right child. A node's right child may have a left child, and that grandchild must still be greater than the node — e.g. 35 is a left child of 40 but greater than 30.

Why a BST: comparison with other structures

A BST is the structure for data that must stay sorted while it changes. Arrays are fast at one thing and slow at the other; a hash table is fastest for exact lookups but knows nothing about order.

OperationUnsorted arraySorted arrayLinked listBST (balanced)Hash table
SearchO(n)O(log n)O(n)O(log n)O(1) average
InsertO(1)O(n)O(1)O(log n)O(1) average
DeleteO(n)O(n)O(n)O(log n)O(1) average
Find closest (floor / ceiling)O(n)O(log n)O(n)O(log n)O(n)
Sorted traversalO(n log n)O(n)O(n log n)O(n)O(n log n)

Every BST operation walks one root-to-leaf path, so it costs O(h) where h is the height. The balanced column assumes h = O(log n); the self-balancing section shows how libraries guarantee it. Those libraries are the ready-made BSTs you should normally use:

LanguageOrdered setOrdered mapImplementation
C++std::set, std::multisetstd::map, std::multimapred-black tree
JavaTreeSetTreeMapred-black tree
Python— (use sortedcontainers.SortedList, or bisect on a list)—no BST in the standard library
JavaScript——none built in — implement one or use a library
Operations and their cost
OperationHowTime
search(k)Go left if k is smaller, right if larger, stop on match or nullO(h)
insert(k)Search for k; attach a new leaf where the search fell offO(h)
delete(k)Search, then one of three cases (leaf, one child, two children)O(h)
min() / max()Follow left / right pointers to the endO(h)
floor(k) / ceil(k)Search, remembering the last candidate on the way downO(h)
inorder()Left, node, right — visits keys in sorted orderO(n)

h is ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ for a perfectly balanced tree and n for a degenerate one, so the same code runs in O(log n) or O(n) depending only on the shape.

Insert
Example

Input: insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7 into an empty tree
Output: the sample BST; inorder 7 12 15 18 20 30 35 40 50 80
Input: then insert 60
Output: 60 becomes the left child of 80

Idea

Search for the key. If you find it, do nothing (no duplicates). If you fall off the tree at a null pointer, that is exactly where the key belongs: create a leaf there. The recursive version returns the (possibly new) root of each subtree so the parent can re-attach it — root.left = insert(root.left, key) — which handles the empty-tree case for free.

Every insert adds a new leaf at the point where the search ends
insert 7:   20 → smaller, go left            20
            15 → smaller, go left          /    \
            12 → smaller, go left        15      30
            null → create 7 here        /  \       \
                                      12    18      40
                                     /             /  \
                                   [7]           35    50
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):               # insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root                      # duplicates are ignored

def inorder(root):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left)
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        inorder(root.right)

def sample_bst():                    # insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    root = None
    for key in (20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7):
        root = insert(root, key)
    return root

root = sample_bst()
print("inorder:", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
print("root:", root.key)
root = insert(root, 40)              # already present: tree unchanged
print("after insert 40 (duplicate):", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
root = insert(root, 60)              # 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → 80 → left of 80
print("after insert 60:", end=" "); inorder(root); print()

Time O(h)Space O(h) recursion stack

Iterative insert avoids the recursion stack: walk down with a parent pointer until curr is null, then hang the new node on the correct side of parent. Same O(h) time, O(1) extra space.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert_iter(root, key):
    node = Node(key)
    if root is None:
        return node                      # empty tree: the new node is the root
    parent, curr = None, root
    while curr is not None:              # search, remembering the parent
        if key == curr.key:
            return root                  # duplicate: nothing to do
        parent = curr
        curr = curr.left if key < curr.key else curr.right
    if key < parent.key:                 # hang the leaf on the correct side
        parent.left = node
    else:
        parent.right = node
    return root

def inorder(root):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left)
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        inorder(root.right)

root = None
for key in (20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7):
    root = insert_iter(root, key)
print("inorder:", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
print("root:", root.key)
root = insert_iter(root, 40)
print("after insert 40 (duplicate):", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
root = insert_iter(root, 60)
print("after insert 60:", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k) : key(k), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

Node* insertIter(Node* root, int key) {
    Node* node = new Node(key);
    if (!root) return node;                   // empty tree: the new node is the root
    Node* parent = nullptr;
    Node* curr = root;
    while (curr) {                            // search, remembering the parent
        if (key == curr->key) { delete node; return root; }   // duplicate
        parent = curr;
        curr = key < curr->key ? curr->left : curr->right;
    }
    if (key < parent->key) parent->left = node;   // hang the leaf on the correct side
    else parent->right = node;
    return root;
}

void inorder(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    inorder(root->left);
    cout << root->key << " ";
    inorder(root->right);
}

int main() {
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int key : {20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7}) root = insertIter(root, key);
    cout << "inorder: "; inorder(root); cout << "\n";
    cout << "root: " << root->key << "\n";
    root = insertIter(root, 40);
    cout << "after insert 40 (duplicate): "; inorder(root); cout << "\n";
    root = insertIter(root, 60);
    cout << "after insert 60: "; inorder(root); cout << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Node insertIter(Node root, int key) {
        Node node = new Node(key);
        if (root == null) return node;             // empty tree: the new node is the root
        Node parent = null, curr = root;
        while (curr != null) {                     // search, remembering the parent
            if (key == curr.key) return root;      // duplicate: nothing to do
            parent = curr;
            curr = key < curr.key ? curr.left : curr.right;
        }
        if (key < parent.key) parent.left = node;  // hang the leaf on the correct side
        else parent.right = node;
        return root;
    }

    static void inorder(Node root) {
        if (root == null) return;
        inorder(root.left);
        System.out.print(root.key + " ");
        inorder(root.right);
    }

Time O(h)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Inserting keys that arrive already sorted (1, 2, 3, 4, …) builds a right-skewed chain of height n: every later operation is O(n). Shuffle the input, or use a self-balancing tree.

Key point

Inorder traversal of a BST always prints the keys in ascending order — so build a BST, traverse inorder is a sorting algorithm (tree sort), O(n log n) when the tree stays balanced.

Search
Example

Input: the sample BST, key = 7
Output: true
Input: key = 25
Output: false

Idea

Compare the key with the current node. Equal — found. Smaller — the key can only be in the left subtree, so go left. Larger — go right. Reaching null means the key is absent. Each step discards an entire subtree, which is why it is O(h) and not O(n): binary search on a tree.

A search follows one path from the root
search 7:  20 → 15 → 12 → 7  ✓ found (4 comparisons)
search 25: 20 → 30 → null    ✗ 25 > 20 go right, 25 < 30 go left, nothing there
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):               # insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root                      # duplicates are ignored

def inorder(root):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left)
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        inorder(root.right)

def sample_bst():                    # insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    root = None
    for key in (20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7):
        root = insert(root, key)
    return root

def search(root, key):                   # recursive
    if root is None:
        return False
    if key == root.key:
        return True
    if key < root.key:
        return search(root.left, key)    # only the left subtree can hold it
    return search(root.right, key)

def search_iter(root, key):              # iterative: O(1) space
    while root is not None:
        if key == root.key:
            return True
        root = root.left if key < root.key else root.right
    return False

root = sample_bst()
print("search 7:", "true" if search(root, 7) else "false")
print("search 25:", "true" if search(root, 25) else "false")
print("search 35 (iterative):", "true" if search_iter(root, 35) else "false")
print("search 100 (iterative):", "true" if search_iter(root, 100) else "false")

    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);

bool search(Node* root, int key) {            // recursive
    if (!root) return false;
    if (key == root->key) return true;

    return search(root->right, key);
}

bool searchIter(Node* root, int key) {        // iterative: O(1) space
    while (root) {

Key point

The recursion here is a tail call — nothing happens after it returns — which is why the iterative version is a trivial rewrite and the one to prefer in production code.

Delete
Example

Input: the sample BST, delete 7 (a leaf)
Output: inorder 12 15 18 20 30 35 40 50 80
Input: delete 30 (one child)
Output: 40 takes its place: 12 15 18 20 35 40 50 80
Input: delete 20 (two children)
Output: replaced by its inorder successor 35: 12 15 18 35 40 50 80

Idea

Search for the key, then fix the hole it leaves. A leaf can simply go. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children cannot be unlinked without breaking the shape — instead copy the inorder successor (the smallest key of the right subtree, found by walking left from right) into the node and delete the successor from the right subtree; the successor has no left child, so that second deletion is always case 1 or 2.

The three cases of BST deletion
Case 1 — leaf: unlink it            Case 2 — one child: parent adopts the child
        15                                   20                 20
       /  \        delete 7                   \     delete 30     \
     12    18     ────────▶    12             30   ──────────▶    40
    /                                            \               /  \
   7                                              40           35    50

Case 3 — two children: copy the inorder successor, then delete the successor
        20          successor of 20 = min of right subtree = 35
     /      \                                   35
   15        40        delete 20             /      \
  /  \      /  \      ────────▶            15        40
12    18  35    50                        /  \         \
 /               \                      12    18        50
7                 80                     /                \
                                        7                  80
1
Find the node
Recurse left or right as in search; root.left = delete(root.left, key) re-attaches whatever comes back.
2
Leaf, or one child
Return the child (or null) to the parent — the node is bypassed.
3
Two children
Find succ = min(root.right), copy succ.key into root, then root.right = delete(root.right, succ.key).
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):               # insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root                      # duplicates are ignored

def inorder(root):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left)
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        inorder(root.right)

def sample_bst():                    # insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    root = None
    for key in (20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7):
        root = insert(root, key)
    return root

def min_node(node):                      # leftmost node of a subtree
    while node.left is not None:
        node = node.left
    return node

def delete_key(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return None
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = delete_key(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = delete_key(root.right, key)
    else:                                # found it
        if root.left is None:            # case 1 & 2: zero or one child
            return root.right
        if root.right is None:
            return root.left
        succ = min_node(root.right)      # case 3: two children
        root.key = succ.key              # copy the inorder successor ...
        root.right = delete_key(root.right, succ.key)   # ... and remove it from the right
    return root

root = sample_bst()
root = delete_key(root, 7)
print("delete 7 (leaf):", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
root = delete_key(root, 30)
print("delete 30 (one child):", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
root = delete_key(root, 20)
print("delete 20 (two children):", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
print("new root:", root.key)

    Node(int k) : key(k), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {       // insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    return root;                          // duplicates are ignored
}

void inorder(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    inorder(root->left);
    cout << root->key << " ";
    inorder(root->right);
}

Node* sampleBST() {                       // insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int key : {20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7}) root = insert(root, key);
    return root;
}

Node* minNode(Node* node) {                   // leftmost node of a subtree
    while (node->left) node = node->left;
    return node;
}

Node* deleteKey(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return nullptr;
    if (key < root->key) root->left = deleteKey(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = deleteKey(root->right, key);
    else {                                    // found it
        if (!root->left || !root->right) {    // case 1 & 2: zero or one child
            Node* child = root->left ? root->left : root->right;
            delete root;
            return child;
        }
        Node* succ = minNode(root->right);    // case 3: two children
        root->key = succ->key;                // copy the inorder successor ...
        root->right = deleteKey(root->right, succ->key);   // ... and remove it from the right
    }
    return root;
}

    root = deleteKey(root, 20);
    cout << "delete 20 (two children): "; inorder(root); cout << "\n";
    cout << "new root: " << root->key << "\n";
}

Time O(h)Space O(h)
Pitfall

In case 3 you may equally use the inorder predecessor (max of the left subtree). What you must not do is move the successor node without removing it from where it was, or forget to re-attach the result of the recursive delete — the classic bug is delete_key(root.right, succ.key) without the root.right =.

Key point

Why O(h): the search is one path down, and the successor walk plus its deletion continue down the same path (successor is in the right subtree, and deleting it is another walk down). Total work is at most twice the height.

Floor in a BST
Example

Input: the sample BST, x = 14
Output: 12 (the largest key ≤ 14)
Input: x = 1
Output: none (every key is larger)
Input: x = 20
Output: 20
Input: x = 100
Output: 80

Floor of x — the largest key in the tree that is ≤ x. Ceiling is the smallest key ≥ x. Together they answer what is closest to x — something a hash table cannot do.

Idea

Walk down as in search, keeping the best candidate seen so far. At a node with key < x the node is a candidate — remember it, then go right to look for something closer to x. At a node with key > x it cannot be the floor, go left. On an exact match the answer is the node itself. When the walk hits null, the remembered candidate is the floor.

1
key == x
Return this node — nothing can be closer.
2
key > x
Too big; the floor must be in the left subtree: root = root.left.
3
key < x
A valid candidate; a larger one may exist to the right: res = root; root = root.right.
The candidate is updated only when we step right
floor(14):  20 > 14  → go left           candidate: —
            15 > 14  → go left           candidate: —
            12 < 14  → remember, go right  candidate: 12
            null     → answer 12
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):               # insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root                      # duplicates are ignored

def inorder(root):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left)
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        inorder(root.right)

def sample_bst():                    # insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    root = None
    for key in (20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7):
        root = insert(root, key)
    return root

def floor(root, x):
    res = None
    while root is not None:
        if root.key == x:
            return root                  # exact match
        if root.key > x:
            root = root.left             # too big: look left
        else:
            res = root                   # candidate; a larger one may be on the right
            root = root.right
    return res

root = sample_bst()
for x in (14, 1, 20, 100):
    node = floor(root, x)
    print(f"floor({x}) =", node.key if node else "none")

    Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k) : key(k), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {       // insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    return root;                          // duplicates are ignored
}

void inorder(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    inorder(root->left);
    cout << root->key << " ";
    inorder(root->right);
}

Node* sampleBST() {                       // insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int key : {20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7}) root = insert(root, key);
    return root;
}

Node* floorNode(Node* root, int x) {
    Node* res = nullptr;
    while (root) {
        if (root->key == x) return root;      // exact match
        if (root->key > x) root = root->left; // too big: look left
        else { res = root; root = root->right; }   // candidate; a larger one may be on the right
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    Node* root = sampleBST();
    for (int x : {14, 1, 20, 100}) {
        Node* node = floorNode(root, x);
        cout << "floor(" << x << ") = ";
        if (node) cout << node->key << "\n"; else cout << "none\n";
    }
}

Ceiling in a BST
Example

Input: the sample BST, x = 21
Output: 30 (the smallest key ≥ 21)
Input: x = 5
Output: 7
Input: x = 7
Output: 7
Input: x = 81
Output: none

Idea

The mirror image of floor. A key > x is a candidate — remember it and go left for something closer; a key < x is useless, go right; an exact match is the answer.

1
key == x
Return this node.
2
key < x
Too small; the ceiling must be on the right: root = root.right.
3
key > x
A valid candidate; a smaller one may exist to the left: res = root; root = root.left.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):               # insert key, keeping the BST invariant
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root                      # duplicates are ignored

def inorder(root):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left)
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        inorder(root.right)

def sample_bst():                    # insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
    root = None
    for key in (20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7):
        root = insert(root, key)
    return root

def ceil(root, x):
    res = None
    while root is not None:
        if root.key == x:
            return root                  # exact match
        if root.key < x:
            root = root.right            # too small: look right
        else:
            res = root                   # candidate; a smaller one may be on the left
            root = root.left
    return res

root = sample_bst()
for x in (21, 5, 7, 81):
    node = ceil(root, x)
    print(f"ceil({x}) =", node.key if node else "none")
