Key point

Floor and ceiling in a sorted array are binary search (bisect_right(a, x) - 1 and bisect_left(a, x) in Python). The BST versions are the same idea on a structure that also supports O(log n) insert and delete — which is exactly what floor / ceiling in a stream needs.

Self-balancing BSTs: why and how

The same set of keys can make BSTs of very different heights — it depends only on the insertion order. The operations above are O(h), so the whole point of balancing is to keep h = O(log n) no matter what order the keys arrive in.

Same keys, two heights: every operation is O(n) on the left and O(log n) on the right
insert 7, 10, 11, 15, 30, 35, 40          insert 15, 10, 35, 7, 11, 30, 40
(sorted order → height 7)                 (balanced → height 3)

  7                                                  15
   \                                               /    \
    10                                           10      35
      \                                         /  \    /  \
       11                                      7    11 30   40
         \
          15
            \
             30
               \
                35
                  \
                   40

If all keys were known in advance we could build the perfectly balanced tree directly (insert the middle of the sorted keys, then recurse on each half). With random insertions and deletions we cannot — so a self-balancing tree restructures itself after every insert or delete that makes it lopsided.

Inserting 100, 200, 300 produces a chain; one rotation turns it back into a balanced tree
insert 100          insert 200          insert 300           restructure
                                                             (rotate left at 100)
   100                 100                 100                     200
                          \                   \                   /   \
                           200                 200              100     300
                                                  \
                                                   300

The restructuring tool is the rotation: a local change of two or three pointers that moves a subtree one level up on one side and one level down on the other without breaking the BST order — the inorder sequence T1 y T2 x T3 is the same before and after.

A rotation re-hangs T2 on the other node and is O(1)
        P                                            P
        |                                            |
        x            Right rotation at x             y
      /   \         ─────────────────────▶         /   \
     y     T3                                     T1    x
    / \             ◀─────────────────────             / \
  T1   T2            Left rotation at y              T2   T3

inorder before:  T1  y  T2  x  T3          inorder after:  T1  y  T2  x  T3   (unchanged)
RotationPointer changesEffect
Right rotation at xy = x.left; x.left = y.right; y.right = x; P now points at yLeft subtree gets one level shorter, right subtree one level taller
Left rotation at yx = y.right; y.right = x.left; x.left = y; P now points at xThe mirror image

The two famous self-balancing BSTs differ only in what counts as balanced and therefore in when they rotate: the AVL tree (strict, by height) and the red-black tree (looser, by colouring).

AVL tree

AVL tree — a BST in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. The balance factor bf = height(left) − height(right) is therefore always −1, 0 or +1; a node with |bf| > 1 is unbalanced and must be rotated.

Named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962). The height condition guarantees h ≤ 1.44 log₂ n, so every operation is O(log n). Each node stores its height so the balance factor is O(1) to compute.

1
Normal BST insert
Walk down and attach the new leaf as usual.
2
Walk back up updating heights
The recursion returns through every ancestor of the new node; recompute height = 1 + max(hL, hR) at each.
3
Find the first unbalanced ancestor
The lowest node with |bf| > 1. Only ancestors can be unbalanced, and fixing the lowest one fixes everything above it for an insert.
4
Rotate according to one of four cases
Decided by which grandchild subtree the new key went into.
CaseWhere the key wentFixRotations
Left-Left (LL)Left child's left subtree (bf > 1 and key < left.key)Right rotation at the unbalanced node1 (single)
Right-Right (RR)Right child's right subtree (bf < −1 and key > right.key)Left rotation at the unbalanced node1 (single)
Left-Right (LR)Left child's right subtree (bf > 1 and key > left.key)Left rotation at the left child, then right rotation at the node2 (double)
Right-Left (RL)Right child's left subtree (bf < −1 and key < right.key)Right rotation at the right child, then left rotation at the node2 (double)
The LL case: the chain 20 → 15 → 5 becomes a balanced tree rooted at 15 (from the notes)
insert 20         insert 15         insert 5             Left-Left at 20:
                                                         right rotation
   20                20                20                      15
                    /                 /                      /    \
                  15                15                      5      20
                                   /
                                  5          bf(20) = 2 - 0 = +2 → unbalanced
The double-rotation cases: the first rotation turns them into LL / RR, the second fixes the balance
Left-Right at 30 (insert 30, 10, 20):      Right-Left at 10 (insert 10, 30, 20):

    30            30            20            10           10            20
   /    left     /    right    /  \            \   right    \   left    /  \
 10   rotate   20   rotate   10    30          30  rotate   20  rotate 10    30
   \  at 10    /     at 30                     /   at 30      \   at 10
    20       10                              20                30
Example

Input: insert 20, 15, 5
Output: root 15 — preorder 15 5 20
Input: insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
Output: preorder 20 15 12 7 18 40 30 35 50 80, height 4 (a plain BST has height 5)

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = self.right = None
        self.height = 1                  # a new node is a leaf (node-counting convention)

def height(node):
    return node.height if node else 0

def balance(node):
    return height(node.left) - height(node.right)

def update(node):
    node.height = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

def rotate_right(x):                     # x's left child y becomes the subtree root
    y = x.left
    x.left = y.right                     # T2 moves across
    y.right = x
    update(x); update(y)                 # x first: it is now below y
    return y

def rotate_left(x):                      # mirror image
    y = x.right
    x.right = y.left
    y.left = x
    update(x); update(y)
    return y

def insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    else:
        return root                      # duplicate
    update(root)                         # on the way back up
    bf = balance(root)
    if bf > 1 and key < root.left.key:   # Left-Left
        return rotate_right(root)
    if bf < -1 and key > root.right.key: # Right-Right
        return rotate_left(root)
    if bf > 1 and key > root.left.key:   # Left-Right
        root.left = rotate_left(root.left)
        return rotate_right(root)
    if bf < -1 and key < root.right.key: # Right-Left
        root.right = rotate_right(root.right)
        return rotate_left(root)
    return root

def preorder(root):
    if root:
        print(root.key, end=" ")
        preorder(root.left)
        preorder(root.right)

def build(keys):
    root = None
    for k in keys:
        root = insert(root, k)
    return root

for label, keys in (("LL", (20, 15, 5)), ("RR", (100, 200, 300)), ("LR", (30, 10, 20)), ("RL", (10, 30, 20))):
    root = build(keys)
    print(label, " ".join(map(str, keys)) + ": root", str(root.key) + ", preorder", end=" ")
    preorder(root); print()
root = build((20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7))
print("sample keys: preorder", end=" "); preorder(root); print()
print("height:", root.height)
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key, height = 1;                 // a new node is a leaf (node-counting convention)
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

int height(Node* n) { return n ? n->height : 0; }
int balance(Node* n) { return height(n->left) - height(n->right); }
void update(Node* n) { n->height = 1 + max(height(n->left), height(n->right)); }

Node* rotateRight(Node* x) {             // x's left child y becomes the subtree root
    Node* y = x->left;
    x->left = y->right;                  // T2 moves across
    y->right = x;
    update(x); update(y);                // x first: it is now below y
    return y;
}

Node* rotateLeft(Node* x) {              // mirror image
    Node* y = x->right;
    x->right = y->left;
    y->left = x;
    update(x); update(y);
    return y;
}

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    else return root;                                   // duplicate
    update(root);                                       // on the way back up
    int bf = balance(root);
    if (bf > 1 && key < root->left->key) return rotateRight(root);       // Left-Left
    if (bf < -1 && key > root->right->key) return rotateLeft(root);      // Right-Right
    if (bf > 1 && key > root->left->key) {                               // Left-Right
        root->left = rotateLeft(root->left);
        return rotateRight(root);
    }
    if (bf < -1 && key < root->right->key) {                             // Right-Left
        root->right = rotateRight(root->right);
        return rotateLeft(root);
    }
    return root;
}

void preorder(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    cout << root->key << " ";
    preorder(root->left);
    preorder(root->right);
}

Node* build(const vector<int>& keys) {
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int k : keys) root = insert(root, k);
    return root;
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<string, vector<int>>> cases = {
        {"LL", {20, 15, 5}}, {"RR", {100, 200, 300}}, {"LR", {30, 10, 20}}, {"RL", {10, 30, 20}}};
    for (auto& [label, keys] : cases) {
        Node* root = build(keys);
        cout << label;
        for (int k : keys) cout << " " << k;
        cout << ": root " << root->key << ", preorder ";
        preorder(root); cout << "\n";
    }
    Node* root = build({20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7});
    cout << "sample keys: preorder "; preorder(root); cout << "\n";
    cout << "height: " << root->height << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key, height = 1;             // a new node is a leaf (node-counting convention)
        Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static int height(Node n) { return n == null ? 0 : n.height; }
    static int balance(Node n) { return height(n.left) - height(n.right); }
    static void update(Node n) { n.height = 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right)); }

    static Node rotateRight(Node x) {    // x's left child y becomes the subtree root
        Node y = x.left;
        x.left = y.right;                // T2 moves across
        y.right = x;
        update(x); update(y);            // x first: it is now below y
        return y;
    }

    static Node rotateLeft(Node x) {     // mirror image
        Node y = x.right;
        x.right = y.left;
        y.left = x;
        update(x); update(y);
        return y;
    }

    static Node insert(Node root, int key) {
        if (root == null) return new Node(key);
        if (key < root.key) root.left = insert(root.left, key);
        else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);
        else return root;                                   // duplicate
        update(root);                                       // on the way back up
        int bf = balance(root);
        if (bf > 1 && key < root.left.key) return rotateRight(root);       // Left-Left
        if (bf < -1 && key > root.right.key) return rotateLeft(root);      // Right-Right
        if (bf > 1 && key > root.left.key) {                               // Left-Right
            root.left = rotateLeft(root.left);
            return rotateRight(root);
        }
        if (bf < -1 && key < root.right.key) {                             // Right-Left
            root.right = rotateRight(root.right);
            return rotateLeft(root);
        }
        return root;
    }

    static void preorder(Node root) {
        if (root == null) return;
        System.out.print(root.key + " ");
        preorder(root.left);
        preorder(root.right);
    }

    static Node build(int[] keys) {
        Node root = null;
        for (int k : keys) root = insert(root, k);
        return root;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] labels = {"LL", "RR", "LR", "RL"};
        int[][] cases = {{20, 15, 5}, {100, 200, 300}, {30, 10, 20}, {10, 30, 20}};
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
            Node root = build(cases[i]);
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(labels[i]);
            for (int k : cases[i]) sb.append(" ").append(k);
            System.out.print(sb + ": root " + root.key + ", preorder ");
            preorder(root); System.out.println();
        }
        Node root = build(new int[]{20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7});
        System.out.print("sample keys: preorder "); preorder(root); System.out.println();
        System.out.println("height: " + root.height);
    }
}

class Node {
    constructor(key) { this.key = key; this.left = null; this.right = null; this.height = 1; }
}                                        // a new node is a leaf (node-counting convention)

const height = (n) => n === null ? 0 : n.height;
const balance = (n) => height(n.left) - height(n.right);
const update = (n) => { n.height = 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right)); };

function rotateRight(x) {                // x's left child y becomes the subtree root
    const y = x.left;
    x.left = y.right;                    // T2 moves across
    y.right = x;
    update(x); update(y);                // x first: it is now below y
    return y;
}

function rotateLeft(x) {                 // mirror image
    const y = x.right;
    x.right = y.left;
    y.left = x;
    update(x); update(y);
    return y;
}

function insert(root, key) {
    if (root === null) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root.key) root.left = insert(root.left, key);
    else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);
    else return root;                                   // duplicate
    update(root);                                       // on the way back up
    const bf = balance(root);
    if (bf > 1 && key < root.left.key) return rotateRight(root);       // Left-Left
    if (bf < -1 && key > root.right.key) return rotateLeft(root);      // Right-Right
    if (bf > 1 && key > root.left.key) {                               // Left-Right
        root.left = rotateLeft(root.left);
        return rotateRight(root);
    }
    if (bf < -1 && key < root.right.key) {                             // Right-Left
        root.right = rotateRight(root.right);
        return rotateLeft(root);
    }
    return root;
}

function preorder(root) {
    if (root === null) return;
    process.stdout.write(root.key + " ");
    preorder(root.left);
    preorder(root.right);
}

const build = (keys) => keys.reduce((root, k) => insert(root, k), null);

for (const [label, keys] of [["LL", [20, 15, 5]], ["RR", [100, 200, 300]], ["LR", [30, 10, 20]], ["RL", [10, 30, 20]]]) {
    const root = build(keys);
    process.stdout.write(`${label} ${keys.join(" ")}: root ${root.key}, preorder `);
    preorder(root); console.log();
}
const root = build([20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7]);
process.stdout.write("sample keys: preorder "); preorder(root); console.log();
console.log("height:", root.height);
Output
LL 20 15 5: root 15, preorder 15 5 20
RR 100 200 300: root 200, preorder 200 100 300
LR 30 10 20: root 20, preorder 20 10 30
RL 10 30 20: root 20, preorder 20 10 30
sample keys: preorder 20 15 12 7 18 40 30 35 50 80
height: 4
Time O(log n) per insert — one path down plus at most two rotationsSpace O(log n) recursion stack
Key point

Why at most two rotations: after an insert, fixing the lowest unbalanced node restores that subtree to its original height, so no ancestor can still be unbalanced. Deletion is different — a rotation may shorten the subtree, so the fix can cascade up the whole path, O(log n) rotations.

Pitfall

The notes wrote the AVL condition as |lh − rh| < 1; it is |lh − rh| ≤ 1. With < 1 only perfect trees would qualify and no tree with n = 2 nodes could exist.

Red-black tree

Red-black tree — a BST in which every node carries one extra bit — a colour, red or black — and four rules on the colours keep the longest root-to-leaf path at most twice as long as the shortest. This guarantees h ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1), so all operations are O(log n).

  1. Every node is either red or black.
  2. The root is always black.
  3. No two consecutive reds: a red node has only black children (a red node's parent is black).
  4. Every path from a node down to its descendant null leaves has the same number of black nodes (the black height).
A valid red-black tree holding the sample keys — the colouring the notes drew violated rule 4, so it is redrawn here
                 20 (B)
              /         \
         15 (B)           40 (B)
        /     \          /      \
   12 (B)    18 (B)   30 (B)    50 (B)
   /                      \         \
7 (R)                    35 (R)    80 (R)

black nodes on every root → null path: 3   (20-15-12, 20-15-18, 20-40-30, 20-40-50, …)
longest path: 20-15-12-7-null (4 nodes)   shortest: 20-15-18-null (3 nodes)  → ≤ 2×

Why the rules bound the height. Rule 4 says every path has the same number b of black nodes; rule 3 says reds cannot be adjacent, so a path has at most b reds squeezed between its blacks. The shortest possible path is all black (b nodes); the longest alternates (2b nodes). Hence no path is more than twice as long as any other — the statement at the end of the notes — and since a tree with b blacks on every path has at least 2^b − 1 nodes, b ≤ log₂(n + 1) and h ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1).

Insertion colours the new node red (that never breaks rule 4), then fixes any red-red violation by recolouring and at most two rotations. Deletion is more involved but also needs at most three rotations. The code is long and rarely asked in interviews; the properties and the comparison below are.

AVL treeRed-black tree
Balance rule|hL − hR| ≤ 1 at every node (strict)Colour rules; longest path ≤ 2 × shortest (loose)
Height bound≤ 1.44 log₂ n — shorter≤ 2 log₂ n — a bit taller
SearchFaster (shorter tree)Slightly slower
Insert≤ 2 rotations, but more frequent rebalancing≤ 2 rotations, mostly just recolouring
DeleteUp to O(log n) rotations≤ 3 rotations
Extra data per nodeHeight (an int) or balance factor1 bit (the colour)
Best forLookup-heavy data that changes rarely (databases, dictionaries)Frequent inserts/deletes
Used inSome database indexes, Windows kernelstd::map/set, Java TreeMap/TreeSet, Linux scheduler (CFS) and memory manager
Applications of a BST

Sorted dynamic data

Keep a stream of keys sorted while they keep arriving: inorder is always sorted, insert/delete stay O(log n) — std::set, TreeMap.

Double-ended priority queue

A heap gives only the min or the max; a BST gives both (leftmost and rightmost) plus delete-any in O(log n).

Floor, ceiling, nearest in a stream

What is the largest value ≤ x among the values seen so far? — floor/ceiling on a self-balancing BST.

Count smaller / greater in a stream

Augment each node with the size of its subtree; rank queries then take one walk down, O(log n).

Range queries

All keys in [lo, hi]: go down to lo, then inorder until hi — O(h + k) for k results.

Language libraries

C++ map/set/multimap/multiset, Java TreeMap/TreeSet are red-black trees; database B-trees are the same idea with many keys per node.

Interview Q&A
How do you check whether a binary tree is a BST?

Not by comparing each node with its two children — that misses a grandchild on the wrong side. Either do an inorder traversal and check that the sequence is strictly increasing, or pass a valid range (lo, hi) down the recursion: the left child must be in (lo, node.key), the right in (node.key, hi). Both are O(n).

What is the worst-case complexity of search in a BST, and how do you avoid it?

O(n), when the tree is skewed (keys inserted in sorted order make a linked list). Avoid it with a self-balancing tree — AVL or red-black — which guarantees h = O(log n) by rotating after inserts and deletes.

How do you delete a node that has two children?

Replace its key with the inorder successor (the minimum of the right subtree) or the inorder predecessor (maximum of the left), then delete that successor from the subtree it came from. The successor has at most one child, so the second deletion is the easy case. Total O(h).

How do you find the kth smallest element in a BST?

An inorder traversal visits keys in ascending order, so stop at the kth visited node — O(h + k). If the query is frequent, store the subtree size in each node: at a node with s keys in its left subtree, go left if k ≤ s, return the node if k = s + 1, else go right with k − s − 1. That is O(h).

AVL or red-black — which would you choose?

AVL for lookup-heavy workloads: its stricter balance keeps the tree shorter. Red-black for insert/delete-heavy workloads: fewer rotations per update and only one bit of extra storage. Most standard libraries (std::map, TreeMap) chose red-black.

How do a BST and a hash table compare?

A hash table gives O(1) average search/insert/delete but has no notion of order: no min/max, floor/ceiling, sorted traversal or range queries. A balanced BST gives all of those in O(log n) and has no worst-case collisions. Use a hash table for pure key lookups, a BST when order matters.

Trees & Heaps

Binary Heap

A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in a plain array in which every parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children. It gives the minimum in O(1) and insert / extract-min in O(log n) with no pointers at all — it is the structure behind every priority queue and heap sort.

Binary heap — an array a viewed as a complete binary tree — a[0] is the root, the children of a[i] are a[2i + 1] and a[2i + 2] — that satisfies the heap property: in a min-heap every node is ≤ its children (so the minimum is at the root); in a max-heap every node is ≥ its children (the maximum is at the root).

A min-heap: the array is the tree, read level by level, left to right
index:   0     1     2     3     4     5
       ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
       │  2  │  3  │ 15  │  5  │  4  │ 45  │        parent(i) = (i − 1) / 2
       └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘        left(i)   = 2i + 1
                                                    right(i)  = 2i + 2
                     2 [0]
                   /      \
               3 [1]       15 [2]         e.g. 15 at index 2: parent (2−1)/2 = 0 → 2
              /    \       /                               left 2·2+1 = 5 → 45
          5 [3]   4 [4]  45 [5]                           right 2·2+2 = 6 → none

Used in heap sort and to implement a priority queue — the data structure of always give me the most urgent item: Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms, Huffman coding, event schedulers, the k largest and running median problems.

A complete binary tree stored as an array

The array trick only works because a heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, and that one is filled strictly from left to right. Reading such a tree level by level leaves no gaps, so position in the array ↔ position in the tree, and the parent/child relations become arithmetic.

Every level must be filled from left to right with no gap
    COMPLETE                          NOT COMPLETE
       ●                                  ●
     /   \                              /   \
    ●     ●                            ●     ●
   / \                                  \
  ●   ●                                  ●      ← the last level has a gap on its left:
                                                  index 3 would be empty while index 4 is used
array: ● ● ● ● ●  (indices 0–4)        the array would need a hole → not a heap shape
Relation0-based array (used here)1-based array (the notes' first version)
Roota[0]a[1]
Parent of i(i − 1) / 2 (integer division)i / 2
Left child of i2i + 12i
Right child of i2i + 22i + 1
Leavesindices n/2 … n − 1indices n/2 + 1 … n
Last internal noden/2 − 1n/2

Because a complete tree of n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋, every root-to-leaf walk — which is what insert and extract do — takes O(log n) steps. And because there are no pointers, a heap of n ints is exactly n ints of memory, laid out contiguously and cache-friendly.

Key point

A heap is not a search structure. The heap property says nothing about the relation between the two subtrees of a node — 15 is left of 5 in the example above — so finding an arbitrary value is O(n). If you need search and min/max, use a balanced BST.

Min-heap and max-heap
Min-heapMax-heap
Heap propertyevery node ≤ its children (and so ≤ all its descendants)every node ≥ its children
Root holdsthe minimumthe maximum
Priority queuethe item with the lowest value has the highest prioritythe item with the highest value has the highest priority
Default inPython heapq, Java PriorityQueueC++ std::priority_queue

Everything below is written for a min-heap; a max-heap is the same code with every comparison flipped — or, cheaper, a min-heap of the negated values.

Which of these are min-heaps? (from the notes)

Both conditions are needed: the shape (complete) and the order (heap property)
(a)       10                        (b)        10
        /    \                               /    \
      20      30                           40      50
              /                           /  \
            40                          44    100

(a) NOT a heap — 40 hangs under 30 while 20 has no child, so the last level is not
    filled left to right: the tree is not complete (array would be 10 20 30 _ _ 40).
(b) a min-heap — complete, and 10 ≤ 40, 50;  40 ≤ 44, 100.
Operations and their cost
OperationHowTimeWhy
getMin() / peek()Return a[0]O(1)The root is always the minimum
insert(x)Append at the end, then sift up while smaller than the parentO(log n)Climbs at most the height of the tree
extractMin()Move the last element to the root, then sift down (heapify)O(log n)Descends at most the height

delete(i)decreaseKey(i, −∞) then extractMin()O(log n)Two logarithmic steps
buildHeap(arr)Heapify every internal node from the last one up to the rootO(n)Most nodes are near the bottom and move only a few levels
search for a valueScan the arrayO(n)No ordering between siblings
Insert (sift up)
Example

Input: insert 3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45 into an empty min-heap
Output: array 2 3 15 5 4 45 — min 2

Idea

Put the new element in the first free slot (a[n]) — that keeps the tree complete. The only thing that can now be wrong is that the new element is smaller than its parent, so swap it upward until its parent is smaller or it reaches the root. Each swap fixes the pair without disturbing anything else, and the walk is at most h = ⌊log₂ n⌋ steps.

Sift up: compare with the parent, swap while smaller
insert 2 into [3]:          append at the end        2 < parent 3: swap

      3          ──────▶         3          ──────▶         2
                                /                          /
                               2                          3

insert 4 into [2, 3, 15, 5]:  append at index 4; parent is index 1 (3) ≤ 4 → stop

      2                       2
    /   \       ──────▶     /   \
   3     15                3     15        array: 2 3 15 5 4
  /                       / \
 5                       5   4
Python
class MinHeap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = []

    def parent(self, i):
        return (i - 1) // 2

    def insert(self, x):
        a = self.a
        a.append(x)                              # 1. first free slot: tree stays complete
        i = len(a) - 1
        while i > 0 and a[self.parent(i)] > a[i]:   # 2. sift up while the parent is larger
            p = self.parent(i)
            a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]
            i = p

    def get_min(self):
        return self.a[0]

h = MinHeap()
for x in (3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45):
    h.insert(x)
    print(f"insert {x}:", *h.a)
print("min:", h.get_min())

#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class MinHeap {
    vector<int> a;
public:
    int parent(int i) { return (i - 1) / 2; }

    void insert(int x) {
        a.push_back(x);                              // 1. first free slot: tree stays complete
        int i = (int)a.size() - 1;
        while (i > 0 && a[parent(i)] > a[i]) {       // 2. sift up while the parent is larger
            swap(a[i], a[parent(i)]);
            i = parent(i);
        }
    }

    int getMin() { return a[0]; }
    void print() { for (int x : a) cout << x << " "; cout << "\n"; }
};

int main() {
    MinHeap h;
    for (int x : {3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45}) {
        h.insert(x);
        cout << "insert " << x << ": "; h.print();
    }
    cout << "min: " << h.getMin() << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class MinHeap {
        ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();

        int parent(int i) { return (i - 1) / 2; }

        void swap(int i, int j) { int t = a.get(i); a.set(i, a.get(j)); a.set(j, t); }

        void insert(int x) {
            a.add(x);                                    // 1. first free slot: tree stays complete
            int i = a.size() - 1;
            while (i > 0 && a.get(parent(i)) > a.get(i)) {   // 2. sift up while the parent is larger
                swap(i, parent(i));
                i = parent(i);
            }
        }

        int getMin() { return a.get(0); }
        void print() { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int x : a) sb.append(x).append(' '); System.out.println(sb.toString().trim()); }
    }

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

In JavaScript (i - 1) / 2 is a float — Math.floor is required. In Python use //. Forgetting this gives fractional indices and a heap that silently never sifts.

Extract min (sift down / heapify)
Example

Input: the heap 2 3 15 5 4 45
Output: returns 2; heap becomes 3 4 15 5 45
Input: extract again
Output: returns 3; heap becomes 4 5 15 45

Idea

The minimum is the root, but removing the root leaves a hole at the top and a complete tree can only lose its last slot. So: save a[0], move the last element into the root, shrink the array by one. The only violation now is at the root, which may be larger than a child — sift it down: swap it with the smaller of its two children (so the new parent is ≤ both) and repeat from there until it is ≤ both children or becomes a leaf. This repair step is minHeapify(i) — it assumes both subtrees of i are valid heaps and fixes node i.

Extract-min moves the last element to the root and sifts it down along one path
heap 2 3 15 5 4 45        take out 2,        heapify(0): smaller child of 45    heapify(1): smaller child
                          move 45 to root     is 3 → swap                        of 45 is 4 → swap
       2                       45                      3                              3
     /   \                   /    \                  /   \                          /   \
    3     15                3      15              45     15                       4     15
   / \   /                 / \                    / \                            / \
  5   4 45                5   4                   5   4                          5   45

returned 2;  heap is now 3 4 15 5 45
Python
class MinHeap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = []

    def parent(self, i): return (i - 1) // 2
    def left(self, i): return 2 * i + 1
    def right(self, i): return 2 * i + 2

    def insert(self, x):
        a = self.a
        a.append(x)
        i = len(a) - 1
        while i > 0 and a[self.parent(i)] > a[i]:
            p = self.parent(i)
            a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]
            i = p

    def min_heapify(self, i):            # subtrees of i are heaps; fix node i
        a, n = self.a, len(self.a)
        l, r, smallest = self.left(i), self.right(i), i
        if l < n and a[l] < a[smallest]:
            smallest = l
        if r < n and a[r] < a[smallest]:
            smallest = r
        if smallest != i:                # a child is smaller: swap and continue below
            a[i], a[smallest] = a[smallest], a[i]
            self.min_heapify(smallest)

    def extract_min(self):
        a = self.a
        if not a:
            return None
        res = a[0]                       # 1. the answer is the root
        a[0] = a[-1]                     # 2. last element moves to the root
        a.pop()
        if a:
            self.min_heapify(0)          # 3. sift it down
        return res

h = MinHeap()
for x in (3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45):
    h.insert(x)
print("heap:", *h.a)
print("extract min:", h.extract_min())
print("heap:", *h.a)
print("extract min:", h.extract_min())
print("heap:", *h.a)

#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class MinHeap {
    vector<int> a;
    int parent(int i) { return (i - 1) / 2; }
    int left(int i) { return 2 * i + 1; }
    int right(int i) { return 2 * i + 2; }
public:
    void insert(int x) {
        a.push_back(x);
        int i = (int)a.size() - 1;
        while (i > 0 && a[parent(i)] > a[i]) { swap(a[i], a[parent(i)]); i = parent(i); }
    }

    void minHeapify(int i) {                     // subtrees of i are heaps; fix node i
        int n = (int)a.size();
        int l = left(i), r = right(i), smallest = i;
        if (l < n && a[l] < a[smallest]) smallest = l;
        if (r < n && a[r] < a[smallest]) smallest = r;
        if (smallest != i) {                     // a child is smaller: swap and continue below
            swap(a[i], a[smallest]);
            minHeapify(smallest);
        }
    }

    int extractMin() {
        int res = a[0];                          // 1. the answer is the root
        a[0] = a.back();                         // 2. last element moves to the root
        a.pop_back();
        if (!a.empty()) minHeapify(0);           // 3. sift it down
        return res;
    }

    void print() { cout << "heap: "; for (int x : a) cout << x << " "; cout << "\n"; }
};

int main() {
    MinHeap h;
    for (int x : {3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45}) h.insert(x);
    h.print();
    cout << "extract min: " << h.extractMin() << "\n";
    h.print();
    cout << "extract min: " << h.extractMin() << "\n";
    h.print();
}

import java.util.ArrayList;

public class Main {
    static class MinHeap {
        ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();
        int parent(int i) { return (i - 1) / 2; }
        int left(int i) { return 2 * i + 1; }
        int right(int i) { return 2 * i + 2; }
        void swap(int i, int j) { int t = a.get(i); a.set(i, a.get(j)); a.set(j, t); }

        void insert(int x) {
            a.add(x);
            int i = a.size() - 1;
            while (i > 0 && a.get(parent(i)) > a.get(i)) { swap(i, parent(i)); i = parent(i); }
        }

        void minHeapify(int i) {                     // subtrees of i are heaps; fix node i
            int n = a.size();
            int l = left(i), r = right(i), smallest = i;
            if (l < n && a.get(l) < a.get(smallest)) smallest = l;
            if (r < n && a.get(r) < a.get(smallest)) smallest = r;
            if (smallest != i) {                     // a child is smaller: swap and continue below
                swap(i, smallest);
                minHeapify(smallest);
            }
        }

        int extractMin() {
            int res = a.get(0);                      // 1. the answer is the root
            a.set(0, a.get(a.size() - 1));           // 2. last element moves to the root
            a.remove(a.size() - 1);
            if (!a.isEmpty()) minHeapify(0);         // 3. sift it down
            return res;
        }

        void print() { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("heap:"); for (int x : a) sb.append(' ').append(x); System.out.println(sb); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MinHeap h = new MinHeap();
        for (int x : new int[]{3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45}) h.insert(x);
        h.print();
        System.out.println("extract min: " + h.extractMin());
        h.print();
        System.out.println("extract min: " + h.extractMin());
        h.print();
    }
}

class MinHeap {
    constructor() { this.a = []; }
    parent(i) { return Math.floor((i - 1) / 2); }
    left(i) { return 2 * i + 1; }
    right(i) { return 2 * i + 2; }

    insert(x) {
        const a = this.a;
        a.push(x);
        let i = a.length - 1;
        while (i > 0 && a[this.parent(i)] > a[i]) {
            const p = this.parent(i);
            [a[i], a[p]] = [a[p], a[i]];
            i = p;
        }
    }

    minHeapify(i) {                              // subtrees of i are heaps; fix node i
        const a = this.a, n = a.length;
        const l = this.left(i), r = this.right(i);
        let smallest = i;
        if (l < n && a[l] < a[smallest]) smallest = l;
        if (r < n && a[r] < a[smallest]) smallest = r;
        if (smallest !== i) {                    // a child is smaller: swap and continue below
            [a[i], a[smallest]] = [a[smallest], a[i]];
            this.minHeapify(smallest);
        }
    }

    extractMin() {
        const a = this.a;
        if (a.length === 0) return null;
        const res = a[0];                        // 1. the answer is the root
        a[0] = a[a.length - 1];                  // 2. last element moves to the root
        a.pop();
        if (a.length) this.minHeapify(0);        // 3. sift it down
        return res;
    }
}

extract min: 3
heap: 4 5 15 45
Time O(log n)Space O(log n) for the recursive heapify — O(1) if written as a loop
Pitfall

minHeapify must swap with the smaller child, not just any smaller child. Swapping with the larger one puts it above its sibling and breaks the heap property. Also check l < n / r < n before reading — the notes' first version read a[rightChild] past the end when a node had only a left child.

Decrease key and delete
Example

Input: the heap 2 3 15 5 4 45; decreaseKey(index 2, 1)
Output: 15 becomes 1 and rises to the root: 1 3 2 5 4 45
Input: then delete(index 1)
Output: the value 3 is removed: 1 4 2 5 45

Idea

Decrease key lowers one value. A smaller value can only violate the heap property with its parent, so the fix is the same sift-up as insert. Delete at index i needs no new mechanism: decrease the key to −∞ so it rises to the root, then extractMin() throws it away. Both are O(log n). (Increase key would be the mirror: set the value, then minHeapify(i).)

Python
import math

class MinHeap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = []

    def parent(self, i): return (i - 1) // 2

    def sift_up(self, i):                    # shared by insert and decrease_key
        a = self.a
        while i > 0 and a[self.parent(i)] > a[i]:
            p = self.parent(i)
            a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]
            i = p

    def insert(self, x):
        self.a.append(x)
        self.sift_up(len(self.a) - 1)

    def min_heapify(self, i):
        a, n = self.a, len(self.a)
        l, r, smallest = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2, i
        if l < n and a[l] < a[smallest]: smallest = l
        if r < n and a[r] < a[smallest]: smallest = r
        if smallest != i:
            a[i], a[smallest] = a[smallest], a[i]
            self.min_heapify(smallest)

    def extract_min(self):
        a = self.a
        res = a[0]
        a[0] = a[-1]
        a.pop()
        if a:
            self.min_heapify(0)
        return res

    def decrease_key(self, i, x):            # x must be <= a[i]
        self.a[i] = x
        self.sift_up(i)                      # only the path to the root can be wrong

    def delete(self, i):
        self.decrease_key(i, -math.inf)      # 1. send it to the root ...
        self.extract_min()                   # 2. ... and remove the root

h = MinHeap()
for x in (3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45):
    h.insert(x)
print("heap:", *h.a)
h.decrease_key(2, 1)
print("decrease key at index 2 (15 -> 1):", *h.a)
h.delete(1)
print("delete index 1 (value 3):", *h.a)
print("min:", h.a[0])

#include <climits>

using namespace std;

class MinHeap {
    vector<int> a;
    int parent(int i) { return (i - 1) / 2; }

    void siftUp(int i) {                         // shared by insert and decreaseKey
        while (i > 0 && a[parent(i)] > a[i]) { swap(a[i], a[parent(i)]); i = parent(i); }
    }

    void minHeapify(int i) {
        int n = (int)a.size();
        int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, smallest = i;
        if (l < n && a[l] < a[smallest]) smallest = l;
        if (r < n && a[r] < a[smallest]) smallest = r;
        if (smallest != i) { swap(a[i], a[smallest]); minHeapify(smallest); }
    }
public:
    void insert(int x) { a.push_back(x); siftUp((int)a.size() - 1); }

    int extractMin() {
        int res = a[0];
        a[0] = a.back();
        a.pop_back();
        if (!a.empty()) minHeapify(0);
        return res;
    }

    void decreaseKey(int i, int x) {             // x must be <= a[i]
        a[i] = x;
        siftUp(i);                               // only the path to the root can be wrong
    }

    void erase(int i) {                          // "delete" is a keyword in C++
        decreaseKey(i, INT_MIN);                 // 1. send it to the root ...
        extractMin();                            // 2. ... and remove the root
    }

    int getMin() { return a[0]; }
    void print() { for (int x : a) cout << x << " "; cout << "\n"; }
};

int main() {
    MinHeap h;
    for (int x : {3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45}) h.insert(x);
    cout << "heap: "; h.print();
    h.decreaseKey(2, 1);
    cout << "decrease key at index 2 (15 -> 1): "; h.print();
    h.erase(1);
    cout << "delete index 1 (value 3): "; h.print();
    cout << "min: " << h.getMin() << "\n";
}

import java.util.ArrayList;

public class Main {
    static class MinHeap {
        ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();
        int parent(int i) { return (i - 1) / 2; }
        void swap(int i, int j) { int t = a.get(i); a.set(i, a.get(j)); a.set(j, t); }

        void siftUp(int i) {                         // shared by insert and decreaseKey
            while (i > 0 && a.get(parent(i)) > a.get(i)) { swap(i, parent(i)); i = parent(i); }
        }

        void minHeapify(int i) {
            int n = a.size();
            int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, smallest = i;
            if (l < n && a.get(l) < a.get(smallest)) smallest = l;
            if (r < n && a.get(r) < a.get(smallest)) smallest = r;
            if (smallest != i) { swap(i, smallest); minHeapify(smallest); }
        }

        void insert(int x) { a.add(x); siftUp(a.size() - 1); }

        int extractMin() {
            int res = a.get(0);
            a.set(0, a.get(a.size() - 1));
            a.remove(a.size() - 1);
            if (!a.isEmpty()) minHeapify(0);
            return res;
        }

        void decreaseKey(int i, int x) {             // x must be <= a[i]
            a.set(i, x);
            siftUp(i);                               // only the path to the root can be wrong
        }

        void delete(int i) {
            decreaseKey(i, Integer.MIN_VALUE);       // 1. send it to the root ...
            extractMin();                            // 2. ... and remove the root
        }

        String show() { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int x : a) sb.append(x).append(' '); return sb.toString().trim(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MinHeap h = new MinHeap();
        for (int x : new int[]{3, 2, 15, 5, 4, 45}) h.insert(x);
        System.out.println("heap: " + h.show());
        h.decreaseKey(2, 1);
        System.out.println("decrease key at index 2 (15 -> 1): " + h.show());
        h.delete(1);
        System.out.println("delete index 1 (value 3): " + h.show());
        System.out.println("min: " + h.a.get(0));
    }
}

class MinHeap {
    constructor() { this.a = []; }
    parent(i) { return Math.floor((i - 1) / 2); }

    siftUp(i) {                                  // shared by insert and decreaseKey
        const a = this.a;
        while (i > 0 && a[this.parent(i)] > a[i]) {
            const p = this.parent(i);
            [a[i], a[p]] = [a[p], a[i]];
            i = p;
        }
    }

    insert(x) { this.a.push(x); this.siftUp(this.a.length - 1); }

    minHeapify(i) {
        const a = this.a, n = a.length;
        const l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2;
        let smallest = i;
        if (l < n && a[l] < a[smallest]) smallest = l;
        if (r < n && a[r] < a[smallest]) smallest = r;
        if (smallest !== i) { [a[i], a[smallest]] = [a[smallest], a[i]]; this.minHeapify(smallest); }
    }

    extractMin() {
        const a = this.a;
        const res = a[0];
        a[0] = a[a.length - 1];
        a.pop();
        if (a.length) this.minHeapify(0);
        return res;
    }

    decreaseKey(i, x) {                          // x must be <= a[i]
        this.a[i] = x;
        this.siftUp(i);                          // only the path to the root can be wrong
    }

    delete(i) {
        this.decreaseKey(i, -Infinity);          // 1. send it to the root ...
        this.extractMin();                       // 2. ... and remove the root
    }
}

Time O(log n) eachSpace O(1)
Key point

decreaseKey is what Dijkstra's algorithm needs when a shorter path to a vertex is found. It requires knowing the index of the element, which the array can only provide with an extra value → index map; the library priority queues below do not offer it, so Dijkstra implementations usually push a fresh entry instead (lazy deletion).

Pitfall

The notes' second implementation had two typos that make it silently wrong: lchild returned 2 * 1 + 1 (always 3) instead of 2 * i + 1, and decreasekey compared arr[self.parent(i) > arr[i]] — indexing with a boolean — instead of arr[self.parent(i)] > arr[i]. Running the code with a known heap and checking the array after every operation, as above, catches both.

Build heap in O(n)
Example

Input: arr = 40 10 30 50 20 15
Output: min-heap 10 20 15 50 40 30

Idea

Inserting n elements one by one costs O(n log n). Building bottom-up is faster: the leaves (indices n/2 … n − 1) are already one-node heaps, so call minHeapify(i) for i = n/2 − 1 down to 0. Each call assumes both subtrees are heaps — true, because every index below i was fixed first — and repairs node i by sifting it down.

Build-heap fixes the internal nodes from the bottom up; each sift-down only goes as far as it must
arr = 40 10 30 50 20 15        n = 6, last internal node = 6/2 − 1 = 2

          40 [0]            heapify(2): 30 vs child 15 → swap        40
        /       \                                                  /    \
    10 [1]      30 [2]      heapify(1): 10 ≤ 50, 20 → nothing      10     15
    /   \       /                                                 / \    /
50 [3] 20 [4] 15 [5]        heapify(0): 40 vs 10, 15 → swap 10   50  20  30
                                then 40 vs 50, 20 → swap 20
result: 10 20 15 50 40 30

Why O(n) and not O(n log n). A node at height h (leaves at height 0) sifts down at most h steps, and there are at most n / 2^(h+1) nodes at that height. Total work is Σ h · n / 2^(h+1) = n · Σ h / 2^(h+1) ≤ n · 1 = O(n) — half the nodes are leaves and cost nothing, a quarter move at most one level, and so on. The O(n log n) bound counts log n for every node, which is far too pessimistic.

Python
def min_heapify(a, n, i):                # fix node i, given that its subtrees are heaps
    l, r, smallest = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2, i
    if l < n and a[l] < a[smallest]: smallest = l
    if r < n and a[r] < a[smallest]: smallest = r
    if smallest != i:
        a[i], a[smallest] = a[smallest], a[i]
        min_heapify(a, n, smallest)

def build_heap(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):  # last internal node down to the root
        min_heapify(a, n, i)

def extract_min(a):
    res = a[0]
    a[0] = a[-1]
    a.pop()
    if a:
        min_heapify(a, len(a), 0)
    return res

a = [40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 15]
build_heap(a)
print("build heap from 40 10 30 50 20 15:", *a)
out = []
while a:
    out.append(extract_min(a))
print("extract all:", *out)

#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void minHeapify(vector<int>& a, int n, int i) {   // fix node i, given that its subtrees are heaps
    int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, smallest = i;
    if (l < n && a[l] < a[smallest]) smallest = l;
    if (r < n && a[r] < a[smallest]) smallest = r;
    if (smallest != i) {
        swap(a[i], a[smallest]);
        minHeapify(a, n, smallest);
    }
}

void buildHeap(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    for (int i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--)          // last internal node down to the root
        minHeapify(a, n, i);
}

int extractMin(vector<int>& a) {
    int res = a[0];
    a[0] = a.back();
    a.pop_back();
    if (!a.empty()) minHeapify(a, (int)a.size(), 0);
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a = {40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 15};
    buildHeap(a);
    cout << "build heap from 40 10 30 50 20 15:";
    for (int x : a) cout << " " << x;
    cout << "\nextract all:";
    while (!a.empty()) cout << " " << extractMin(a);
    cout << "\n";
}

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static void minHeapify(ArrayList<Integer> a, int n, int i) {   // fix node i, given that its subtrees are heaps
        int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, smallest = i;
        if (l < n && a.get(l) < a.get(smallest)) smallest = l;
        if (r < n && a.get(r) < a.get(smallest)) smallest = r;
        if (smallest != i) {
            int t = a.get(i); a.set(i, a.get(smallest)); a.set(smallest, t);
            minHeapify(a, n, smallest);
        }
    }

    static void buildHeap(ArrayList<Integer> a) {
        int n = a.size();
        for (int i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--)          // last internal node down to the root
            minHeapify(a, n, i);
    }

    static int extractMin(ArrayList<Integer> a) {
        int res = a.get(0);
        a.set(0, a.get(a.size() - 1));
        a.remove(a.size() - 1);
        if (!a.isEmpty()) minHeapify(a, a.size(), 0);
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 15));
        buildHeap(a);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("build heap from 40 10 30 50 20 15:");
        for (int x : a) sb.append(' ').append(x);
        System.out.println(sb);
        sb = new StringBuilder("extract all:");
        while (!a.isEmpty()) sb.append(' ').append(extractMin(a));
        System.out.println(sb);
    }
}

Time O(n) to build; O(n log n) to extract everythingSpace O(1) extra (in place)
Key point

Build heap, then extract everything is already a sorting algorithm — the extraction order is ascending. Heap sort below does the same thing in place, without a second array, by using a max-heap.

Heap sort
Example

Input: arr = 40 10 30 50 20 15
Output: 10 15 20 30 40 50

Idea

Build a max-heap in place (O(n)). The maximum is now at a[0]; swap it with the last element so it sits in its final sorted position, shrink the heap by one and maxHeapify(0) to restore the heap on the remaining prefix. Repeat n − 1 times: each round places one more element at the end, so the sorted suffix grows while the heap prefix shrinks — all inside the same array.

1
Build max-heap
for i = n/2 − 1 … 0: maxHeapify(a, n, i) — the largest element is at a[0].
2
Repeat for end = n − 1 … 1
Swap a[0] and a[end] (the max is now in place), then maxHeapify(a, end, 0) on the prefix of length end.
3
Done
The prefix shrinks to one element; the array is sorted ascending.
Each round moves the current maximum to the front of the sorted suffix
max-heap:  50 40 30 10 20 15   | sorted suffix
swap 50 ↔ 15, heapify prefix:  40 20 30 10 15 | 50
swap 40 ↔ 15, heapify prefix:  30 20 15 10 | 40 50
swap 30 ↔ 10, heapify prefix:  20 10 15 | 30 40 50
swap 20 ↔ 15, heapify prefix:  15 10 | 20 30 40 50
swap 15 ↔ 10:                  10 | 15 20 30 40 50
Python
def max_heapify(a, n, i):
    l, r, largest = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2, i
    if l < n and a[l] > a[largest]: largest = l
    if r < n and a[r] > a[largest]: largest = r
    if largest != i:
        a[i], a[largest] = a[largest], a[i]
        max_heapify(a, n, largest)

def heap_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):          # 1. build max-heap: O(n)
        max_heapify(a, n, i)
    print("max-heap:", *a)
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):              # 2. n − 1 rounds
        a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]              #    max goes to its final place
        max_heapify(a, end, 0)                   #    restore the heap on a[0..end)

a = [40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 15]
heap_sort(a)
print("sorted:", *a)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void maxHeapify(vector<int>& a, int n, int i) {
    int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, largest = i;
    if (l < n && a[l] > a[largest]) largest = l;
    if (r < n && a[r] > a[largest]) largest = r;
    if (largest != i) { swap(a[i], a[largest]); maxHeapify(a, n, largest); }
}

void print(const char* label, const vector<int>& a) {
    cout << label; for (int x : a) cout << " " << x; cout << "\n";
}

void heapSort(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    for (int i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--) maxHeapify(a, n, i);   // 1. build max-heap: O(n)
    print("max-heap:", a);
    for (int end = n - 1; end > 0; end--) {                    // 2. n − 1 rounds
        swap(a[0], a[end]);                                    //    max goes to its final place
        maxHeapify(a, end, 0);                                 //    restore the heap on a[0..end)
    }
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a = {40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 15};
    heapSort(a);
    print("sorted:", a);
}

        if (r < n && a[r] > a[largest]) largest = r;
        if (largest != i) {
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[largest]; a[largest] = t;

Built-in priority queues

You will rarely write a heap by hand outside an interview. Every language but JavaScript ships one; the API is always push, pop the best, peek.

LanguagePriority queueDefault orderpush / pop / peekMax-heap instead
Pythonheapq — functions on a plain listmin-heapheappush(h, x) / heappop(h) / h[0]push -x, or (−priority, item) tuples
C++std::priority_queue<T>max-heappush(x) / pop() (returns nothing) / top()it is max by default; min: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>
Javajava.util.PriorityQueue<T>min-heapoffer(x) / poll() / peek()new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder())
JavaScript— none built inwrite a MinHeap class (below) or use a library
Example

Input: start from 5 20 1 30 4; push 3; pop everything
Output: min 1; popped order 1 3 4 5 20 30

Python
import heapq

h = [5, 20, 1, 30, 4]
heapq.heapify(h)                     # O(n) build, in place
print("min:", h[0])
heapq.heappush(h, 3)                 # O(log n)
print("after push 3, min:", h[0])
out = []
while h:
    out.append(heapq.heappop(h))     # O(log n) each
print("popped in order:", *out)

#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    vector<int> v = {5, 20, 1, 30, 4};
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq(v.begin(), v.end());   // min-heap; O(n) build
    cout << "min: " << pq.top() << "\n";
    pq.push(3);                                                             // O(log n)
    cout << "after push 3, min: " << pq.top() << "\n";
    cout << "popped in order:";
    while (!pq.empty()) { cout << " " << pq.top(); pq.pop(); }              // O(log n) each
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Arrays.asList(5, 20, 1, 30, 4));   // min-heap
        System.out.println("min: " + pq.peek());
        pq.offer(3);                                                         // O(log n)
        System.out.println("after push 3, min: " + pq.peek());
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("popped in order:");
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) sb.append(' ').append(pq.poll());              // O(log n) each
        System.out.println(sb);
    }
}
JavaScript
class MinHeap {                          // JavaScript has no built-in priority queue
    constructor(items = []) { this.a = [...items]; for (let i = (this.a.length >> 1) - 1; i >= 0; i--) this.down(i); }
    size() { return this.a.length; }
    peek() { return this.a[0]; }
    push(x) { this.a.push(x); this.up(this.a.length - 1); }
    pop() {
        const a = this.a, res = a[0], last = a.pop();
        if (a.length) { a[0] = last; this.down(0); }
        return res;
    }
    up(i) {
        const a = this.a;
        while (i > 0) {
            const p = (i - 1) >> 1;
            if (a[p] <= a[i]) break;
            [a[p], a[i]] = [a[i], a[p]]; i = p;
        }
    }
    down(i) {
        const a = this.a, n = a.length;
        for (;;) {
            const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
            let s = i;
            if (l < n && a[l] < a[s]) s = l;
            if (r < n && a[r] < a[s]) s = r;
            if (s === i) break;
            [a[s], a[i]] = [a[i], a[s]]; i = s;
        }
    }
}

const pq = new MinHeap([5, 20, 1, 30, 4]);   // O(n) build
console.log("min:", pq.peek());
pq.push(3);                                  // O(log n)
console.log("after push 3, min:", pq.peek());
const out = [];
while (pq.size()) out.push(pq.pop());        // O(log n) each
console.log("popped in order:", out.join(" "));
Output
min: 1
after push 3, min: 1
popped in order: 1 3 4 5 20 30
Time O(log n) push / pop, O(1) peekSpace O(n)

heapq also has a few conveniences worth knowing — nlargest, nsmallest and heapreplace (pop then push in a single sift, faster than the two calls). The list is the heap, so you can print it and see the array layout from the diagrams:

Python
import heapq

p = [5, 20, 1, 30, 4]
heapq.heapify(p)
print(p)                          # [1, 4, 5, 30, 20]   ← a valid min-heap, not a sorted list
heapq.heappush(p, 3)
print(p)                          # [1, 4, 3, 30, 20, 5]
print(heapq.heappop(p))           # 1
print(p)                          # [3, 4, 5, 30, 20]
print(heapq.nlargest(2, p))       # [30, 20]
print(heapq.nsmallest(2, p))      # [3, 4]
print(heapq.heapreplace(p, -1))   # 3   ← pops the min, then pushes -1 (one sift instead of two)
print(p)                          # [-1, 4, 5, 30, 20]
Pitfall

A heap is not sorted — only h[0] is guaranteed to be the minimum. Iterating over heapq's list, PriorityQueue's iterator or printing the array gives level order, not ascending order. To get sorted output, pop repeatedly.

Key point

For a max-heap in Python push the negated values (heappush(h, -x), read -h[0]); for tuples (priority, item) the heap orders by priority first — make sure items are comparable or add a tie-breaking counter. In Java pass Collections.reverseOrder() or a Comparator; in C++ the default priority_queue<int> already is a max-heap.

Where heaps are used

Priority queue

Task scheduling, event simulation, bandwidth management — serve the most urgent item first, O(log n) per operation.

Heap sort

O(n log n) worst case with O(1) extra space; the fallback inside introsort.

Graph algorithms

Dijkstra's shortest paths and Prim's minimum spanning tree pop the closest vertex from a min-heap.

k largest / smallest

Keep a min-heap of size k; push each element and pop when the size exceeds k — O(n log k) instead of sorting everything.

Median of a stream

A max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half; the median is at the roots.

Merge k sorted lists

Push the head of each list; pop the smallest and push its successor — O(N log k). Huffman coding uses the same pattern.

Interview Q&A
Why can a heap be stored in an array but a BST cannot?

A heap is a complete binary tree, so reading it level by level leaves no gaps and parent/child positions are pure arithmetic ((i−1)/2, 2i+1, 2i+2). A BST can have any shape; storing it the same way would need an array of size 2^h with mostly empty slots.

Why is building a heap O(n) when a single insert is O(log n)?

Bottom-up build calls heapify on the internal nodes from the bottom, and a node at height h sifts down at most h levels. Half of the nodes are leaves (cost 0), a quarter are at height 1, an eighth at height 2 … so the total is n · Σ h / 2^(h+1), a series that converges to n. Inserting one by one instead sifts up, and most elements are deep, so that is Θ(n log n).

Heap or balanced BST for a priority queue?

A heap: O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop, O(n) build, no pointers and great cache behaviour. A BST gives the same O(log n) bounds plus search, predecessor/successor and delete-by-value, at the cost of pointers and constants — use it only when you need those extras (e.g. a double-ended priority queue).

How do you find the k largest elements of a stream, and why a min-heap?

Keep a min-heap of size k. For each element, push it; if the size exceeds k, pop the minimum — the smallest of the current candidates leaves. The root is always the kth largest so far. O(n log k) time and O(k) space, versus O(n log n) for sorting. A max-heap would make the largest easy to find but the one to evict hard.

Is heap sort stable? Is it used in practice?

Not stable — the long-range swaps reorder equal keys. In practice it loses to quick sort on arrays because of cache misses, but its guaranteed O(n log n) and O(1) space make it the fallback in introsort (C++ std::sort), which switches to heap sort when quick sort's recursion gets too deep.

What does decreaseKey need that a library priority queue does not provide?

The index of the element inside the heap. Library queues hide the array, so you cannot address an element. Dijkstra implementations therefore push a new (distance, vertex) pair whenever a shorter path is found and skip stale pairs when they are popped — lazy deletion — which keeps the same O(E log V) bound.
